nodes.label: Net Income
nodes.formula_human: Pre-Tax Income − Income Tax Expense
nodes.definition: The final, bottom-line profit or loss after all revenues, costs, expenses, non-operating items, and taxes.
nodes.example: Apple FY2024 reported net income of $93.7B, reflecting all costs deducted from $391B in revenue.

playbook.if_increased: (1) revenue growth exceeding cost growth, (2) margin expansion from operating leverage, (3) lower effective tax rate, (4) one-time gains in non-operating items
playbook.if_decreased: (1) revenue decline or deceleration, (2) cost increases outpacing revenue (margin compression), (3) higher effective tax rate, (4) impairment or restructuring charges

comparability.variations: All companies report Net Income. Some report 'Net Income attributable to common shareholders' after deducting minority interest. Non-GAAP measures (Adjusted Net Income) exclude SBC and restructuring.

examples.treatment: Net Income
Net Income
Net earnings attributable to Berkshire Hathaway shareholders

nodes.label: Pre-Tax Income (EBT)
nodes.formula_human: Operating Income + Non-Operating Income − Non-Operating Expenses
nodes.definition: Operating Income adjusted for non-operating income and expenses. The basis for calculating income tax expense.
nodes.example: A manufacturer with $10M operating income and $1M interest expense has $9M EBT.
nodes.classification_notes: EBT is the figure to which the effective tax rate is applied. The difference between statutory and effective tax rates is a key analytical metric.

playbook.if_increased: (1) operating income growth, (2) non-operating income gains (investment gains, FX), (3) reduced interest expense from debt paydown, (4) one-time non-operating gains
playbook.if_decreased: (1) operating income decline, (2) increased interest expense from higher debt or rates, (3) impairment or restructuring charges, (4) FX losses

comparability.variations: All companies report pre-tax income. Terminology varies: 'Income before income taxes', 'Earnings before income taxes', 'Income before provision for income taxes'.

examples.treatment: Income before provision for income taxes
Income before income tax expense
Income before income taxes

nodes.label: Operating Income (EBIT)
nodes.formula_human: Gross Profit − Operating Expenses (Selling + G&A + R&D + D&A)
nodes.definition: Gross Profit minus all operating expenses. Measures profitability from core operations before capital structure and tax effects. The primary measure of operational efficiency.
nodes.example: A SaaS company with 80% gross margins but heavy R&D investment may have slim EBIT.
nodes.classification_notes: Some companies present Operating Income explicitly; others require calculation from disclosed items. Tech companies often show 'Income from Operations'. Manufacturing companies may include or exclude certain restructuring charges depending on materiality.

playbook.if_increased: (1) revenue growth outpacing OpEx growth (operating leverage), (2) gross margin expansion from pricing or COGS efficiency, (3) OpEx reductions from restructuring or efficiency, (4) favorable product mix shift
playbook.if_decreased: (1) revenue decline reducing contribution margin, (2) gross margin compression from input cost increases, (3) OpEx increases from hiring or marketing spend, (4) one-time charges classified as operating

comparability.variations: Most companies report Operating Income or Income from Operations. Some combine it with non-operating items. SaaS companies often highlight non-GAAP operating income excluding SBC.

examples.treatment: Operating income
Operating income
Operating income

nodes.label: Gross Profit
nodes.formula_human: Net Revenue − Cost of Goods Sold
nodes.definition: The residual profit after deducting direct costs (COGS) from Net Revenue. Represents the margin available to cover operating expenses, interest, taxes, and generate net income.
nodes.example: A retail company with $500M net revenue and $350M COGS reports $150M gross profit (30% gross margin).
nodes.classification_notes: Gross Profit is not always explicitly reported as a line item. Some companies go directly from Revenue to Operating Income. Financial services companies typically do not report Gross Profit — their equivalent is Net Interest Income or Net Revenue after provisions.

playbook.if_increased: (1) revenue growth outpacing COGS growth, (2) pricing power — price increases not offset by cost increases, (3) favorable product/service mix shift toward higher-margin offerings, (4) cost reduction initiatives in direct costs, (5) operating leverage in cost of revenue
playbook.if_decreased: (1) input cost inflation eroding margins, (2) competitive pricing pressure forcing price reductions, (3) unfavorable mix shift toward lower-margin products, (4) supply chain disruptions, (5) revenue decline without proportional cost reduction

comparability.variations: Most companies report Gross Profit. SaaS companies typically show 70-85% gross margins; manufacturing 25-45%; retail 20-40%. Financial services companies generally do not present Gross Profit.

examples.treatment: Gross margin (products + services combined)
Gross profit (subscription + professional services)
Net sales minus merchandise costs
Not reported — uses Net Interest Income

nodes.label: Net Revenue
nodes.formula_human: Gross Revenue − Revenue Deductions
nodes.definition: Gross Revenue minus all revenue deductions (returns, discounts, allowances). The top line of the income statement as reported under ASC 606.
nodes.example: A SaaS company with $100M gross revenue and $5M in volume discounts shows $95M net revenue.

playbook.if_increased: (1) customer/unit volume growth, (2) price increases, (3) new product/service launches, (4) expansion into new markets, (5) favorable product mix shift
playbook.if_decreased: (1) customer churn, (2) competitive pricing pressure, (3) market contraction, (4) unfavorable FX impact, (5) loss of key customer

comparability.variations: Some companies report Gross Revenue; most report Net Revenue as the top line per ASC 606. Financial services companies use Net Interest Income instead.

examples.treatment: Revenue (net)
Net sales
Net sales

nodes.label: Gross Revenue
nodes.formula_human: Product Revenue + Service Revenue + Other Revenue
nodes.definition: Total revenue recognized before any deductions. Consists of all revenue streams from the company's primary business activities.
nodes.example: A diversified tech company recognizing $80M product revenue + $50M service revenue + $5M other = $135M gross revenue.

playbook.if_increased: (1) growth in product or service revenue streams, (2) new revenue stream added, (3) price increases
playbook.if_decreased: (1) decline in core revenue stream, (2) product discontinuation, (3) competitive losses

comparability.variations: Most companies report Net Revenue, not Gross. Gross Revenue is typically only visible in the revenue footnote or for companies with material deductions.

examples.treatment: Shows gross billings separately
Reports gross vs. net revenue for agency vs. merchant

nodes.label: OTHER REVENUE
nodes.formula_human: Franchise Revenue + Royalty Revenue + Other Operating Revenue
nodes.definition: Revenue from secondary or ancillary business activities not classified as product or service revenue.
nodes.example: A manufacturer earning $2M in franchise fees and $500K in patent royalties alongside its $80M in product sales.
nodes.classification_notes: Other revenue captures ancillary operating income streams that are not core product or service revenue. Companies may reclassify items between other revenue and non-operating income depending on materiality and whether the activity is part of ordinary operations.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new franchise agreements signed, (2) increased royalty income from IP licensing deals, (3) one-time licensing or settlement payments, (4) monetization of previously idle assets
playbook.if_decreased: (1) franchise closures or non-renewals, (2) expiration of key IP licenses or patents, (3) reclassification of revenue streams to product or service revenue, (4) regulatory changes limiting licensing arrangements

comparability.variations: Franchise-heavy companies (QSR, hotels) report franchise revenue as a primary line item. IP-intensive companies report royalty revenue separately. Many companies bundle small ancillary items into a single 'Other Revenue' line.

examples.treatment: Franchised restaurants revenue (franchise fees + royalties)
QTL (licensing) segment revenue
Franchise fees reported as a separate revenue line

nodes.label: Franchise Revenue
nodes.definition: Fees paid by franchisees for the right to operate under the company's brand.
nodes.example: McDonald's recognizing ~$15.4B (FY2023) in franchised restaurant revenues from royalties (% of sales) and initial franchise fees from 40,000+ franchisees.
nodes.classification_notes: Franchise revenue includes both initial franchise fees (recognized over time as the franchisor satisfies performance obligations) and ongoing royalties (typically a percentage of franchisee sales, recognized as earned). Under ASC 606, initial franchise fees are often recognized over the franchise term rather than upfront. Note: the original XBRL tag us-gaap:FranchiseRevenue was deprecated in 2018; filers now use us-gaap:RevenueFromContractWithCustomerExcludingAssessedTax.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new franchise unit openings, (2) higher franchisee same-store sales driving royalty growth, (3) franchise fee rate increases in new agreements, (4) conversion of company-operated locations to franchise model, (5) international market expansion
playbook.if_decreased: (1) franchisee closures or non-renewals, (2) declining franchisee same-store sales, (3) refranchising moratoriums or regulatory restrictions, (4) franchisee financial distress leading to fee concessions, (5) conversion of franchised units to company-operated

comparability.variations: QSR and hotel companies report franchise revenue as a major line item. Some companies combine franchise fees with royalty revenue. Others separate initial fees from ongoing royalties in footnotes.

examples.treatment: Franchised restaurants revenue (royalties + rent from franchisees)
Franchise and property revenues
Franchise and licensing fees

nodes.label: Other Operating Revenue
nodes.definition: Catch-all for revenue from incidental operating activities not otherwise classified.
nodes.example: A software company recognizing $800K in other operating revenue from subleasing excess office space and $200K from selling scrap hardware equipment.
nodes.classification_notes: Other operating revenue is a catch-all for operating income streams not material enough to warrant their own line item. Items here should be from recurring or semi-recurring operating activities. One-time gains (asset sales, insurance recoveries) are typically classified as other income/expense below operating income, not as other operating revenue. If an item becomes material, it should be reclassified to its own line.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new incidental revenue streams (subleasing, scrap sales), (2) one-time settlements or insurance recoveries classified as operating, (3) government grants or subsidies, (4) reclassification of items from non-operating to operating
playbook.if_decreased: (1) discontinuation of ancillary activities, (2) reclassification of material items to specific revenue lines, (3) expiration of government grants, (4) cessation of sublease arrangements

comparability.variations: This line varies widely across companies and industries. Manufacturing companies may include scrap sales. Real estate companies may include ancillary service revenue. The lack of standardization makes cross-company comparison difficult.

examples.treatment: Other income/expense (includes miscellaneous operating items)
Other revenue within automotive segment
Other revenues (non-advertising revenue within Google Services)

nodes.label: Royalty Revenue
nodes.definition: Revenue from licensing intellectual property (patents, trademarks, content) to third parties.
nodes.example: Qualcomm earning $6.4B in QTL (licensing) revenue from royalties on 3G/4G/5G patents, calculated as a percentage of handset selling prices.
nodes.classification_notes: Under ASC 606, sales-based or usage-based royalties for IP licenses are recognized when the subsequent sale or usage occurs (the royalty constraint exception). Fixed or minimum guarantee royalties follow standard ASC 606 recognition. Royalty revenue is distinct from franchise revenue though both involve licensing rights.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new licensing agreements signed, (2) higher licensee sales driving usage-based royalties, (3) patent portfolio expansion, (4) favorable litigation outcomes enforcing IP rights, (5) new geographic markets for licensed IP
playbook.if_decreased: (1) patent expirations reducing licensable IP, (2) licensee sales declines, (3) contract non-renewals or renegotiations at lower rates, (4) adverse court rulings invalidating patents, (5) open-source alternatives eroding licensing demand

comparability.variations: Pharma companies report royalties on out-licensed drugs. Tech companies report licensing/IP revenue. Media companies report content royalties. Some companies combine royalty and franchise revenue.

examples.treatment: QTL segment (technology licensing revenue)
Alliance and royalty revenues
Licensing and merchandise royalties within Consumer Products segment

nodes.label: Product Revenue
nodes.formula_human: Finished Goods Sales + Component/Parts Sales + Licensing of Physical Products
nodes.definition: Revenue from the sale of physical goods, recognized at point of transfer of control.
nodes.example: A manufacturer recognizes product revenue when goods ship to customers.
nodes.classification_notes: Product revenue is typically recognized at a point in time when control transfers to the customer (usually upon shipment or delivery, depending on shipping terms). FOB shipping point vs. FOB destination affects the timing of recognition.

playbook.if_increased: (1) unit volume growth from market expansion, (2) price increases on products, (3) new product launches, (4) favorable product mix shift to higher-ASP items, (5) seasonal demand peaks
playbook.if_decreased: (1) competitive market share loss, (2) product obsolescence or lifecycle decline, (3) pricing pressure from competitors, (4) supply chain constraints limiting shipments, (5) channel destocking

comparability.variations: Manufacturing and retail companies report product revenue prominently. Some companies combine product and service revenue into a single 'Net Sales' line. Tech companies may report 'Products' and 'Services' separately.

examples.treatment: Products (iPhone, Mac, iPad, Wearables)
Net Sales by segment
Automotive revenues

nodes.label: Component / Parts Sales
nodes.definition: Revenue from selling individual components or spare parts.
nodes.example: An electronics company selling replacement components to repair shops.
nodes.classification_notes: Distinguish from finished goods revenue. Parts sold as part of a bundled service contract may require allocation under ASC 606 (multiple performance obligations). Warranty replacement parts are not revenue but a warranty expense. Aftermarket parts often carry higher margins than OEM sales.

playbook.if_increased:
1. Growing installed base of equipment driving aftermarket demand
2. Expansion of parts catalog or new product lines
3. Price increases on replacement components
4. Equipment aging cycles driving higher replacement rates
playbook.if_decreased:
1. Decline in installed base from customer attrition
2. Competitive third-party parts suppliers capturing market share
3. Improved product reliability reducing replacement frequency
4. Customer shift to full-unit replacement over component repair

comparability.variations: Some manufacturers report component/parts sales within a single product revenue line; others separate aftermarket parts from OEM product sales. Automotive companies often have a dedicated "Parts & Accessories" segment.

examples.treatment: Reports parts revenue within its product segment, with aftermarket parts disclosed as a key growth driver
Includes parts sales in Equipment Operations revenue, separately discusses parts and service trends
Reports aftermarket parts and components within each operating segment

nodes.label: Finished Goods Sales
nodes.definition: Revenue from selling completed manufactured products.
nodes.example: An auto manufacturer recognizing revenue from vehicle sales to dealerships.
nodes.classification_notes: Revenue recognized at the point in time when control transfers to the customer (ASC 606). Shipping terms (FOB shipping point vs. destination) affect timing. Variable consideration (volume rebates, returns) must be estimated and constrained. Distinguish from service revenue, licensing revenue, and component/parts sales.

playbook.if_increased:
1. Higher unit volumes from market share gains or new customers
2. Price increases passed through to customers
3. New product launches expanding the finished goods portfolio
4. Favorable foreign exchange on international sales
5. Channel expansion (new distributors, geographies, e-commerce)
playbook.if_decreased:
1. Market demand softening or economic downturn
2. Loss of key customer accounts or distributor relationships
3. Product recalls or quality issues reducing shipments
4. Competitive pressure forcing price reductions
5. Supply chain disruptions limiting production output

comparability.variations: Some manufacturers report all product sales in one line; others disaggregate by product type, geography, or channel as required by ASC 606. Companies selling through distributors may face timing differences based on sell-in vs. sell-through recognition. Consignment arrangements delay recognition.

examples.treatment: Reports vehicle sales revenue by geographic segment with detailed unit volume and average selling price disclosures
Disaggregates product revenue into iPhone, Mac, iPad, Wearables, and Accessories
Reports net sales by product segment (Beauty, Grooming, Health Care, Fabric & Home Care, Baby/Feminine/Family)

nodes.label: Licensing of Physical Products
nodes.definition: Revenue from licensing rights to use a physical product design (distinct from software licensing).
nodes.example: A consumer electronics company earns $8M/year licensing its patented hardware design to a third-party manufacturer in Asia.
nodes.classification_notes: Distinct from software licensing revenue. Applies when the company grants rights to manufacture or sell a physical product design. If the company manufactures and sells the product directly, classify under product sales revenue instead.

playbook.if_increased:
1. Signed new licensing agreements with additional manufacturers
2. Existing licensees increased production volumes driving royalty growth
3. Launched new product designs attracting licensing interest
4. Expanded into new geographic markets through licensing partners
playbook.if_decreased:
1. Key licensing agreements expired or were not renewed
2. Licensees reduced production volumes due to market softness
3. Competitive designs reduced demand for licensed products
4. Transitioned from licensing model to direct manufacturing

comparability.variations: Some companies report licensing revenue within product revenue; others break it out as a separate revenue stream. Royalty-based licensing may be recognized over time vs. upfront depending on contract structure under ASC 606.

examples.treatment: Reports technology licensing fees as a separate QTL segment, distinct from chip sales revenue
Reports licensing revenue separately from products and services revenue in its segment reporting
Separates license revenue (upfront design fees) from royalty revenue (per-unit shipments)

nodes.label: RECURRING VS. NON-RECURRING REVENUE
nodes.definition: Analytical classification overlay that segments revenue into recurring (subscription, maintenance, usage-based) vs. non-recurring (one-time sales, implementation fees, license fees) components for quality-of-earnings analysis.
nodes.example: A SaaS company reporting 85% recurring revenue ($170M subscriptions + $15M maintenance) vs. 15% non-recurring ($25M implementation + $10M one-time licenses) to highlight revenue predictability.
nodes.classification_notes: Not a separate GL account — a classification overlay for analytical purposes.

playbook.if_increased: (1) shift from perpetual licenses to subscription model increasing recurring share, (2) higher renewal rates improving recurring base, (3) growth in maintenance attach rates, (4) expansion revenue from existing customers
playbook.if_decreased: (1) large one-time deals increasing non-recurring share, (2) declining renewal rates, (3) customer downgrades from annual to month-to-month, (4) revenue mix shifting toward professional services

comparability.variations: SaaS companies emphasize ARR/MRR metrics. Some companies disclose recurring vs. non-recurring breakdown in earnings supplements. The definition of 'recurring' varies — some include usage-based, others exclude it.

examples.treatment: Reports subscription revenue as % of total to highlight recurring mix
Tracks recurring revenue % as key metric during license-to-subscription transition
Reports 'more predictable revenue' (cloud + software support) vs. less predictable

coa_mapping.quickbooks: N/A - analytical overlay, not a GL account
coa_mapping.netsuite: N/A - analytical overlay, not a GL account
coa_mapping.sap: N/A - analytical overlay, not a GL account

nodes.label: Service Revenue
nodes.formula_human: Professional Services Revenue + Subscription Revenue + Maintenance & Support Revenue + Usage-Based Revenue
nodes.definition: Revenue recognized over time or at completion of a performance obligation for services rendered.
nodes.example: A consulting firm recognizing revenue as hours are worked under a time-and-materials contract.
nodes.classification_notes: Service revenue is recognized over time when the customer simultaneously receives and consumes the benefits (ASC 606-10-25-27). For SaaS, subscription revenue is the dominant sub-component. Professional services may be recognized over time or at a point in time depending on contract terms.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new customer acquisition, (2) price increases on renewals, (3) upsell/cross-sell expanding customer spend, (4) improved retention reducing churn, (5) new service line launch
playbook.if_decreased: (1) customer churn or downgrades, (2) competitive pricing pressure, (3) delayed project starts (professional services), (4) consumption decline (usage-based), (5) contract non-renewals

comparability.variations: SaaS companies report subscription revenue as the primary component. Professional services firms may report consulting revenue separately. Some companies disaggregate by geography rather than service type.

examples.treatment: Subscription and support revenue
Revenue from services
Net sales (usage-based)

nodes.label: Maintenance & Support Revenue
nodes.definition: Revenue from post-sale technical support or maintenance agreements.
nodes.example: Oracle recognizing annual support fees on database licenses.
nodes.classification_notes: Maintenance and support revenue is a stand-ready obligation recognized ratably over the contract period (typically 12 months). When bundled with software licenses, it must be separated as a distinct performance obligation under ASC 606. Renewal rates are a key KPI as this is highly recurring revenue.

playbook.if_increased: (1) higher renewal rates on existing contracts, (2) price increases on annual support contracts, (3) growth in installed base driving new support agreements, (4) expansion of support coverage tiers (basic to premium), (5) multi-year contract signings
playbook.if_decreased: (1) customer churn or non-renewal of support contracts, (2) migration from on-premise (with support) to cloud/SaaS, (3) competitive support alternatives or self-service adoption, (4) discount pressure from large enterprise renewals, (5) product end-of-life reducing supportable installed base

comparability.variations: Enterprise software companies report maintenance and support as a separate revenue line. Some companies bundle support with subscription revenue. Hardware companies may include warranty support separately.

examples.treatment: Cloud services and license support (includes maintenance)
Software support revenue
Included in Software segment recurring revenue

nodes.label: Professional Services Revenue
nodes.definition: Revenue from consulting, advisory, implementation, or other project-based services.
nodes.example: Deloitte recognizing revenue as consulting hours are delivered.
nodes.classification_notes: Professional services revenue is recognized based on the pattern of transfer: time-and-materials contracts use an input method (hours incurred), while fixed-price contracts typically use an output method or percentage-of-completion. In SaaS companies, professional services are often sold below cost as an enabler for subscription revenue.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new implementation projects from product launches, (2) higher billing rates, (3) increased headcount enabling more delivery capacity, (4) large digital transformation engagements, (5) higher utilization rates
playbook.if_decreased: (1) project delays or cancellations, (2) lower utilization rates (bench time), (3) pricing pressure from offshore competitors, (4) customer shift to self-implementation or partner-led delivery, (5) seasonal slowdowns in Q1 or summer months

comparability.variations: Pure-play consulting firms report this as their primary revenue. SaaS companies typically report professional services as a separate, lower-margin revenue line. Some companies combine implementation and training revenue.

examples.treatment: Consulting revenue and Managed Services revenue
Professional services revenue (separate from subscription)
Consulting and Advisory revenue

nodes.label: Subscription Revenue
nodes.formula_human: Revenue recognized ratably over subscription periods
nodes.definition: Revenue recognized ratably over a subscription period (monthly/annually). Most common in SaaS.
nodes.example: Salesforce recognizing $10K/month from a $120K annual CRM contract.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new customer acquisition, (2) expansion revenue (upsells/cross-sells), (3) price increases on renewals, (4) lower churn rate
playbook.if_decreased: (1) increased churn/downgrades, (2) slower new logo acquisition, (3) competitive pricing pressure, (4) contract term changes (annual→monthly)

comparability.variations: Some companies split subscription vs. consumption revenue. Others bundle subscription with maintenance/support.

examples.treatment: Subscription and Support Revenue
Included in Intelligent Cloud and Productivity segments
Subscription revenue (Digital Media + Digital Experience)

nodes.label: Usage-Based Revenue
nodes.definition: Revenue recognized based on actual consumption or usage (per-API-call, per-GB, per-transaction).
nodes.example: AWS recognizing revenue based on EC2 compute hours consumed each month.
nodes.classification_notes: Usage-based revenue is recognized as the customer consumes the service (right-to-access model). Under ASC 606, usage-based royalties for IP licenses follow the royalty constraint exception. For non-IP usage fees, revenue is recognized as the usage occurs. Companies may offer committed-use contracts with minimum consumption floors, creating hybrid recognition patterns.

playbook.if_increased: (1) customer workload growth driving higher consumption, (2) new customer onboarding with high usage patterns, (3) price-per-unit increases, (4) expansion into new use cases (AI/ML workloads), (5) seasonal traffic peaks (e.g., holiday e-commerce)
playbook.if_decreased: (1) customer workload optimization reducing consumption, (2) customer churn or migration to competitors, (3) pricing pressure from competitive cloud providers, (4) macroeconomic slowdowns reducing customer activity, (5) customers shifting from pay-as-you-go to reserved/committed plans

comparability.variations: Cloud infrastructure companies report usage-based revenue as their primary model. Some companies blend subscription and usage in a single line. Payment processors report per-transaction revenue similarly.

examples.treatment: Net sales recognized based on compute/storage/data transfer consumption
Product revenue (consumption-based credits)
Usage-based revenue from API calls (messaging, voice)

nodes.label: Revenue Deductions
nodes.formula_human: Sales Returns & Allowances + Sales Discounts + Rebates & Credits
nodes.definition: Reductions to Gross Revenue required under ASC 606 to arrive at Net Revenue. These are contra-revenue items (credit-balance offsets to revenue) — they reduce the top line but are not expenses.
nodes.example: A software company reporting $100M gross revenue with $5M in volume discounts shows $95M net revenue.
nodes.classification_notes: Revenue deductions are contra-revenue items with a normal DEBIT balance that offset CREDIT revenue. Under ASC 606, variable consideration (discounts, rebates, returns) must be estimated and deducted from revenue at the time of recognition. Most companies report only Net Revenue, making these deductions visible only in footnotes.

playbook.if_increased: (1) higher return rates from quality issues or seasonal patterns, (2) increased promotional discounting, (3) new volume discount tiers triggered by customer growth, (4) channel partner rebate accrual increases
playbook.if_decreased: (1) improved product quality reducing returns, (2) reduced promotional activity, (3) tighter discount policies, (4) shift to less discount-sensitive channels

comparability.variations: Most companies report Net Revenue only; gross-to-net bridge is rarely visible on the face of the P&L. E-commerce and retail companies tend to have higher return rates. SaaS companies typically have minimal deductions.

examples.treatment: Returns netted against revenue; not separately disclosed
Net sales (after returns and allowances)
Revenue deductions for Medicaid/Medicare rebates disclosed in notes

nodes.label: REBATES & CREDITS
nodes.definition: Post-sale cash payments or credits back to customers tied to cumulative purchase milestones.
nodes.example: A pharmaceutical company pays $14M in annual volume rebates to pharmacy benefit managers when cumulative purchases exceed tiered thresholds.
nodes.classification_notes: Under ASC 606, rebates are variable consideration estimated at contract inception and recorded as a reduction of revenue. Distinguish from sales returns (physical goods sent back) and promotional discounts (point-of-sale reductions). Rebates often require estimation of breakage (customers who qualify but do not claim).

playbook.if_increased:
1. More customers reaching volume rebate thresholds due to strong sales
2. Introduced more aggressive rebate programs to drive customer retention
3. Updated rebate accrual estimates upward based on actual redemption rates
4. Expanded channel partner programs with higher rebate tiers
5. Competitive pressure forcing richer incentive structures
playbook.if_decreased:
1. Restructured rebate programs with higher qualification thresholds
2. Fewer customers reaching volume milestones due to market softness
3. Reduced rebate accruals based on lower-than-expected redemption
4. Eliminated underperforming rebate programs
5. Shifted from rebates to upfront discounting

comparability.variations: Some companies report rebates as a contra-revenue deduction before net revenue; others disclose them separately. Pharma and consumer goods industries have complex rebate structures that require significant estimation. SaaS companies may use credits rather than cash rebates.

examples.treatment: Reports trade promotions and rebates as a reduction of net sales, disclosed in significant accounting policies
Records rebates as variable consideration reducing net revenue, with material estimates for Medicaid and managed care rebates
Reports volume incentive rebates and credits as a reduction of revenue, estimating based on historical patterns

nodes.label: Channel / Distributor Rebates
nodes.definition: Rebates paid to distributors or channel partners for hitting sales volume targets.
nodes.example: A semiconductor company paying $15M in quarterly rebates to its top 5 distributors who exceeded $300M in combined purchase targets, recorded as a reduction of revenue.
nodes.classification_notes: Channel rebates are classified as a reduction of revenue (not an expense) under ASC 606 when the payment to the customer (distributor) does not provide a distinct good or service. If the distributor provides identifiable marketing services, the rebate may be partially classified as a marketing expense. Estimation of rebate accruals requires judgment on whether volume targets will be met.

playbook.if_increased: (1) distributors exceeding volume targets triggering higher rebate tiers, (2) new channel partner agreements with rebate incentives, (3) increased reliance on indirect channel vs. direct sales, (4) competitive pressure requiring richer channel incentives, (5) channel expansion into new geographies
playbook.if_decreased: (1) shift to direct sales model bypassing distributors, (2) renegotiated partner agreements with lower rebate rates, (3) distributors falling short of volume targets, (4) channel partner consolidation reducing number of rebate agreements, (5) tighter rebate program qualification criteria

comparability.variations: Technology, pharma, and CPG companies commonly use channel rebate programs. Indirect-channel-heavy companies (Cisco, HP) have significant rebate accruals. Some companies disclose rebate liabilities on the balance sheet.

examples.treatment: Channel partner rebates accrued as reduction of revenue; rebate liability on balance sheet
Partner rebates and incentives netted against net revenue
Wholesaler chargebacks and distribution fees recorded as gross-to-net adjustments

nodes.label: Customer Loyalty Credits
nodes.definition: Credits issued to customers under loyalty programs redeemable against future purchases.
nodes.example: Starbucks deferring $1.6B in revenue from its Rewards program loyalty points, recognizing revenue only when stars are redeemed or expire (breakage).
nodes.classification_notes: Under ASC 606, loyalty points are a material right (separate performance obligation). A portion of the transaction price is allocated to the loyalty points based on their standalone selling price and deferred until redemption. Breakage (unredeemed points) is recognized proportionally as points are redeemed. This creates a contract liability on the balance sheet that can be substantial for large loyalty programs.

playbook.if_increased: (1) loyalty program expansion increasing points issuance, (2) higher sales volume generating more loyalty credits, (3) reduced breakage estimates requiring more deferred revenue, (4) richer reward tiers increasing per-transaction credit allocation, (5) new partnership earning opportunities
playbook.if_decreased: (1) higher point redemption rates releasing deferred revenue, (2) increased breakage estimates, (3) program restructuring reducing earn rates, (4) loyalty program wind-down or elimination, (5) expiration policy changes accelerating breakage recognition

comparability.variations: Airlines, hotels, and retailers have the largest loyalty programs. The accounting treatment creates significant deferred revenue (contract liability) on the balance sheet. Some companies operate third-party loyalty programs (credit card co-brands) adding complexity.

examples.treatment: Stored value card and loyalty deferred revenue ($1.6B+ contract liability)
SkyMiles loyalty program deferred revenue; breakage recognized over time
Prime rewards and loyalty credits allocated as material rights

nodes.label: Contract Rebates & True-ups
nodes.definition: Adjustments to rebate accruals at contract anniversary dates when actual volumes differ from estimates.
nodes.example: A pharma distributor accruing $8M in rebates during the year based on estimated purchase volumes, then recording a $1.5M true-up (reduction of rebate liability) when actual volumes came in 10% below estimates at year-end.
nodes.classification_notes: True-ups occur when actual volumes or sales data become available and differ from estimates used to accrue rebates. Under ASC 606, the constraint on variable consideration requires that revenue recognized is not subject to significant reversal. True-up adjustments can increase or decrease revenue depending on whether actuals exceeded or fell short of estimates. These adjustments often create quarter-to-quarter volatility.

playbook.if_increased: (1) actual volumes exceeding estimates requiring higher rebate payments, (2) new multi-year contracts with escalating rebate tiers, (3) contract anniversary dates triggering retroactive rebate calculations, (4) change in estimation methodology increasing accruals
playbook.if_decreased: (1) actual volumes falling below estimated thresholds reducing rebate obligations, (2) contract expirations or non-renewals, (3) improved estimation accuracy reducing true-up volatility, (4) renegotiated contracts with lower rebate rates

comparability.variations: Pharmaceutical companies have the most complex rebate true-up processes (Medicaid, Medicare, managed care). Technology companies accrue channel rebates with quarterly true-ups. CPG companies adjust trade promotion accruals at period end.

examples.treatment: Medicaid and Medicare rebate true-ups disclosed in gross-to-net bridge
Supplier rebate true-ups affecting quarterly revenue adjustments
Customer rebate accrual adjustments at contract measurement dates

nodes.label: SALES DISCOUNTS
nodes.formula_human: Volume/Quantity Discounts + Promotional Discounts + Early Payment/Cash Discounts
nodes.definition: Reductions in the invoice price offered to customers; contra-revenue under ASC 606.
nodes.example: A wholesale distributor with $200M in gross sales provides $8M in volume discounts, $3M in promotional discounts, and $2M in early payment discounts, totaling $13M in sales discounts.
nodes.classification_notes: Under ASC 606, discounts are treated as variable consideration and reduce the transaction price. Volume discounts that are contingent on future purchases require estimation using the most likely amount or expected value method. Trade discounts are typically netted against revenue at the time of sale, while cash discounts may be recorded when taken.

playbook.if_increased: (1) aggressive promotional campaigns to drive volume, (2) customers hitting higher volume discount tiers, (3) competitive pricing pressure requiring deeper discounts, (4) more customers taking early payment discounts due to low interest rates, (5) new customer acquisition incentives
playbook.if_decreased: (1) stronger brand positioning allowing reduced discounting, (2) tighter discount approval policies, (3) shift to value-based pricing, (4) fewer customers qualifying for volume tiers, (5) higher interest rates reducing early payment discount take-rates

comparability.variations: Most companies do not separately disclose discount amounts; they are netted into net revenue. CPG and pharmaceutical companies often have complex gross-to-net discount structures. Enterprise software companies may offer multi-year deal discounts.

examples.treatment: Trade promotions and discounts netted against net sales
Sales discounts deducted as part of gross-to-net adjustments
Product discounts included in net revenue presentation

nodes.label: Early Payment / Cash Discounts
nodes.definition: Discounts offered for early payment (e.g., "2/10 net 30" = 2% discount if paid in 10 days).
nodes.example: A building materials supplier offering '2/10 net 30' terms sees 40% of customers take the discount, resulting in $800K in cash discounts on $40M in qualifying invoices.
nodes.classification_notes: Under ASC 606, early payment discounts are variable consideration and should be estimated at contract inception using the expected value or most likely amount method. Historically (pre-ASC 606), some companies recorded cash discounts only when taken by the customer. The net method (reducing revenue at time of sale) is now preferred over the gross method. Cash discounts also impact working capital analysis as they accelerate cash collection.

playbook.if_increased: (1) more customers taking early payment discounts due to low borrowing costs, (2) increased discount terms offered to improve cash collections, (3) higher sales volumes generating more discount-eligible invoices, (4) seasonal patterns in customer payment behavior
playbook.if_decreased: (1) fewer customers able to pay early due to tight liquidity, (2) reduction or elimination of early payment discount programs, (3) higher interest rates making early payment less attractive for customers, (4) shift to prepaid or subscription billing models

comparability.variations: Early payment discounts are common in B2B manufacturing and distribution. Retail and SaaS companies rarely offer them. Some companies report cash discounts as a financing cost rather than contra-revenue, though ASC 606 favors contra-revenue treatment.

examples.treatment: Cash discounts offered on standard payment terms; netted against revenue
Early payment discounts included in net sales adjustments
Cash discounts reflected in machinery and equipment revenue

nodes.label: Promotional Discounts
nodes.definition: Temporary price reductions for marketing promotions or seasonal events.
nodes.example: A consumer electronics retailer running a Black Friday promotion offering 20% off TVs, resulting in $4.5M in promotional discounts on $22.5M in promotional sales during November.
nodes.classification_notes: Promotional discounts reduce the transaction price under ASC 606. When a promotion includes a coupon or rebate that the customer must redeem, judgment is needed on whether it represents a separate performance obligation (material right) or a price reduction. Cooperative advertising allowances paid to retailers may be classified as a reduction of revenue rather than a marketing expense if no distinct benefit is received.

playbook.if_increased: (1) more aggressive promotional calendar (holiday, back-to-school events), (2) inventory clearance promotions for excess or aging stock, (3) competitive response to rival promotions, (4) new product launch introductory pricing, (5) market share acquisition strategy
playbook.if_decreased: (1) reduced promotional activity due to strong demand, (2) brand strength allowing full-price selling, (3) shift to everyday-low-price strategy from high-low pricing, (4) supply constraints limiting need for promotions, (5) margin improvement initiatives restricting discounting

comparability.variations: Retail companies typically have the largest promotional discounts. CPG companies fund trade promotions through their trade spending budgets. Some companies classify promotional spend as a marketing expense rather than contra-revenue.

examples.treatment: Promotional markdowns reflected in net revenue
Promotional discounts netted against revenue; heavy coupon-driven model
Trade promotions classified as reduction of net sales

nodes.label: Volume / Quantity Discounts
nodes.definition: Price reductions given to customers who purchase above threshold quantities.
nodes.example: A chemical supplier offering 5% off for orders over 10,000 lbs, resulting in $1.2M in volume discounts on $24M in qualifying orders during the quarter.
nodes.classification_notes: Volume discounts are a form of variable consideration under ASC 606. When discounts depend on cumulative purchases over a period, the entity must estimate the most likely discount tier using either the expected value or most likely amount method. Retrospective volume discounts (applied retroactively when thresholds are met) create estimation complexity at interim periods.

playbook.if_increased: (1) customers ordering larger quantities to hit discount tiers, (2) new volume agreements with large enterprise customers, (3) market conditions encouraging bulk purchasing, (4) competitive dynamics requiring deeper volume incentives
playbook.if_decreased: (1) customers ordering below volume thresholds, (2) renegotiated contracts with tighter discount tiers, (3) shift to smaller, more frequent orders, (4) removal of volume discount programs

comparability.variations: Manufacturing, distribution, and CPG companies commonly use volume discounts. SaaS companies use tiered pricing but rarely call it a 'volume discount.' Most companies do not separately disclose volume discount amounts.

examples.treatment: Volume-based allowances netted in cost of goods sold or revenue
Volume discounts embedded in tiered pricing structures
Volume rebates to large customers based on annual purchase commitments

nodes.label: SALES RETURNS & ALLOWANCES
nodes.formula_human: Merchandise Returns + Allowances for Defective Goods + Reserve for Future Returns
nodes.definition: Reductions for goods returned by customers or credits granted for defective/damaged goods.
nodes.example: An online retailer with $500M in gross sales records $35M in merchandise returns, $5M in defective goods allowances, and a $10M reserve for future returns, totaling $50M in returns and allowances.
nodes.classification_notes: Under ASC 606, returns and allowances are treated as variable consideration and must be estimated at contract inception. A refund liability is recorded for expected returns, along with a right-of-return asset for the inventory expected to be recovered. E-commerce and retail companies typically have higher return rates (15-30%) than B2B companies (1-5%).

playbook.if_increased: (1) product quality issues driving higher defect-related returns, (2) more generous return policies (e.g., extended holiday return windows), (3) higher e-commerce mix with inherently higher return rates, (4) new product launches with higher trial-and-return behavior, (5) seasonal post-holiday return surge
playbook.if_decreased: (1) improved product quality and fewer defects, (2) better product descriptions/images reducing expectation mismatches, (3) tighter return policies, (4) shift to non-returnable product categories, (5) improved sizing/fit technology reducing apparel returns

comparability.variations: Most companies net returns against revenue and do not separately disclose the amount. E-commerce companies tend to have the highest return rates. Some companies disclose return reserves in balance sheet footnotes.

examples.treatment: Returns netted against net sales; return allowance on balance sheet
Liberal return policy; returns and allowances netted in net sales
High return rates for furniture; disclosed in revenue recognition notes

nodes.label: Allowances for Defective Goods
nodes.definition: Credits issued to customers who keep defective goods in lieu of returning them.
nodes.example: An electronics manufacturer issuing $500K in partial credits (30% of purchase price) to customers who received circuit boards with minor cosmetic defects, allowing customers to keep the goods rather than return them.
nodes.classification_notes: Allowances for defective goods are price concessions granted to customers who retain defective merchandise. Unlike returns, the goods are not sent back. Under ASC 606, these are treated as variable consideration reducing the transaction price. The allowance may be a partial or full credit depending on the severity of the defect. If defects are systematic, they may also trigger warranty expense accruals under ASC 460.

playbook.if_increased: (1) manufacturing quality control failures increasing defect rates, (2) raw material quality issues from suppliers, (3) new product launches with unresolved quality issues, (4) more generous allowance policies to preserve customer relationships, (5) supply chain disruptions causing shipping damage
playbook.if_decreased: (1) improved manufacturing processes and quality control, (2) better supplier quality management, (3) tighter allowance approval policies, (4) shift to higher-quality product lines, (5) improved packaging reducing transit damage

comparability.variations: Manufacturing and consumer goods companies typically have the highest defective goods allowances. These are rarely disclosed separately; they are combined with returns. Food and beverage companies may have spoilage-related allowances.

examples.treatment: Product allowances included in returns and allowances contra-revenue
Quality-related customer credits (Galaxy Note 7 recall was an extreme example)
Customer allowances for quality issues netted against automotive revenue

nodes.label: Merchandise Returns
nodes.definition: Physical goods returned by customers; reduces revenue and restores inventory.
nodes.example: A retailer processing holiday returns in January.
nodes.classification_notes: Merchandise returns reverse the original revenue transaction. Under ASC 606, the entity records a refund liability and a right-of-return asset for the cost of goods expected to be recovered. If returned goods cannot be resold (damaged, obsolete), the right-of-return asset is reduced. Returns differ from allowances in that the physical goods come back to the seller.

playbook.if_increased: (1) post-holiday return surge in Q1, (2) product quality issues driving higher defect-related returns, (3) increased e-commerce sales with higher inherent return rates, (4) new product launches with high trial-and-return behavior, (5) more liberal return policies to remain competitive
playbook.if_decreased: (1) improved product descriptions reducing buyer-expectation mismatch, (2) better sizing technology for apparel, (3) stricter return policies (restocking fees, shorter windows), (4) shift from physical goods to digital products, (5) improved quality control reducing defective merchandise

comparability.variations: Return rates vary dramatically by industry: apparel (20-40%), electronics (10-15%), furniture (5-10%), B2B industrial (<5%). E-commerce returns are typically 2-3x higher than in-store returns. Most companies net merchandise returns against revenue.

examples.treatment: Returns netted against net sales; free returns on most items
Generous no-questions-asked return policy; returns netted against net sales
High return rates (~25%) for online fashion; significant impact on net revenue

nodes.label: Reserve for Future Returns
nodes.definition: Estimated future returns accrued at time of revenue recognition per ASC 606.
nodes.example: An e-commerce company accruing a 3% return reserve on all holiday season sales.
nodes.classification_notes: Under ASC 606, the reserve for future returns consists of two components: (1) a refund liability (credit to revenue) for expected returns, and (2) a right-of-return asset (debit to inventory) for the expected recovery of returned goods. The reserve is based on historical return rates adjusted for current conditions. This is an estimate recorded at the time of sale, not when the return actually occurs.

playbook.if_increased: (1) higher sales volume requiring proportionally larger reserves, (2) increased return rate estimates based on recent trends, (3) extended return windows (e.g., holiday season policies), (4) new product categories with uncertain return profiles, (5) channel stuffing concerns requiring conservative reserves
playbook.if_decreased: (1) improved product quality reducing expected return rates, (2) better product-market fit lowering returns, (3) tighter return policies shortening return windows, (4) actual returns coming in below estimates (favorable true-ups), (5) shift to non-returnable product sales

comparability.variations: E-commerce and apparel companies carry the largest return reserves. Electronics and furniture companies have moderate reserves. SaaS and digital-only companies typically have minimal or no return reserves. The reserve amount is usually disclosed in the notes to the financial statements.

examples.treatment: Return provision of 50%+ of outstanding deliveries during peak season
Sales return allowance recorded as refund liability on balance sheet
Return reserve accrued at point of sale based on historical return rates

nodes.label: COST OF GOODS SOLD (COGS) / COST OF REVENUE
nodes.formula_human: Direct Materials + Direct Labor + Manufacturing Overhead + Inventory Adjustments + Service Delivery Costs
nodes.definition: The direct costs attributable to producing the goods sold or delivering the services rendered. Subtracted from Net Revenue to derive Gross Profit. The line that divides "how much it costs to make the product" from "how much it costs to run the business."
nodes.example: For a car manufacturer, COGS includes steel, assembly labor, and factory overhead. For a SaaS company, COGS includes hosting, infrastructure, and customer support labor.
nodes.classification_notes: In SaaS companies, COGS is often labeled "Cost of Revenue" and includes hosting costs, customer support, and amortization of capitalized software. In professional services, it includes billable labor and direct project costs. Manufacturing companies include raw materials, direct labor, and factory overhead. Retailers include purchase cost of merchandise plus freight-in.

playbook.if_increased: (1) Higher sales volume driving proportional cost increase, (2) raw material or input cost inflation, (3) supply chain disruptions increasing procurement costs, (4) unfavorable product mix shift toward lower-margin products, (5) manufacturing inefficiency or yield loss
playbook.if_decreased: (1) Lower sales volume reducing variable costs, (2) favorable input cost trends or renegotiated supplier contracts, (3) manufacturing efficiency gains or automation, (4) favorable product mix shift toward higher-margin products, (5) outsourcing or offshoring production to lower-cost regions

comparability.variations: Terminology varies significantly by industry: "Cost of Revenue" (tech/SaaS), "Cost of Goods Sold" (manufacturing/retail), "Cost of Services" (professional services). Some companies include D&A in COGS; others report it separately. Shipping costs may appear in COGS or selling expenses depending on ASC 606 election.

examples.treatment: Reports "Cost of sales" split between Products and Services segments
Reports "Cost of revenues" including subscription and professional services costs
Reports "Cost of sales" including purchase cost of merchandise, freight, and distribution center costs

nodes.label: DIRECT LABOR
nodes.formula_human: Production Wages + Payroll Taxes (Direct) + Benefits (Direct Labor)
nodes.definition: Compensation for employees whose time is directly and exclusively tied to production of the goods sold. Excludes supervisory, administrative, and indirect labor.
nodes.example: An auto assembly plant employs 2,000 production workers at an average total cost of $65K/year (wages + benefits + payroll taxes), totaling $130M in direct labor costs annually.
nodes.classification_notes: Direct labor includes only compensation for employees whose time is directly and exclusively traceable to production of goods sold. Supervisory, maintenance, and janitorial labor in the factory is indirect labor (Manufacturing Overhead). In professional services, direct labor is billable consultant time. The direct/indirect labor boundary is a key judgment area affecting COGS vs. overhead allocation.

playbook.if_increased: (1) Wage rate increases or union contract negotiations, (2) higher production volumes requiring more labor hours, (3) increased overtime to meet demand, (4) rising healthcare and benefits costs, (5) labor inefficiency from new product introductions or training
playbook.if_decreased: (1) Automation replacing manual labor, (2) lower production volumes reducing hours, (3) offshoring to lower-cost labor markets, (4) improved labor efficiency and learning curve gains, (5) headcount reductions or restructuring

comparability.variations: Labor-intensive manufacturers (apparel, food processing) have high direct labor as a percent of COGS. Capital-intensive manufacturers (semiconductors, chemicals) have low direct labor. Companies outsourcing production show lower direct labor but higher purchased component costs. Union vs. non-union labor affects cost structure.

examples.treatment: Reports production wages and benefits for assembly workers as direct labor; known for lean manufacturing efficiency
Reports massive direct labor costs for electronics assembly; labor is the primary value-add for contract manufacturer
Reports billable consultant compensation as direct labor (cost of services) in professional services model

nodes.label: BENEFITS — DIRECT LABOR
nodes.formula_human: Health Insurance (Direct) + Retirement Contributions (Direct) + Workers Compensation (Direct)
nodes.definition: Employee benefits costs attributable to direct production workforce.
nodes.example: A manufacturer with 1,000 production workers pays $8M in employer health insurance premiums, $2M in 401(k) matching contributions, and $1.5M in workers compensation insurance, for total direct labor benefits of $11.5M.
nodes.classification_notes: Benefits for direct labor employees are part of COGS, while benefits for SG&A employees are operating expenses. The allocation must be consistent and based on time tracking or headcount ratios. ASC 712 covers nonretirement postemployment benefits. Pension obligations (ASC 715) for production workers are also allocated to COGS. Benefits costs typically run 25-40% of base wages.

playbook.if_increased: (1) Healthcare premium increases (typically 5-8% annually), (2) higher headcount in production, (3) increased workers comp claims from workplace injuries, (4) richer benefit packages from union negotiations, (5) regulatory mandates (ACA compliance costs)
playbook.if_decreased: (1) Shift to high-deductible health plans reducing employer premiums, (2) lower headcount through automation, (3) improved workplace safety reducing workers comp rates, (4) switch from defined benefit to defined contribution retirement plans, (5) use of contract/temporary workers not receiving benefits

comparability.variations: US manufacturers have high benefits costs due to employer-provided healthcare. Companies in countries with universal healthcare (EU, Japan) have lower direct benefits costs but higher payroll taxes. Union manufacturers typically have richer benefit packages than non-union. Use of temporary or contract workers can reduce reported benefits costs.

examples.treatment: Reports significant retiree healthcare obligations (OPEB) for production workers under UAW contract; legacy costs are a major burden
Provides benefits to full-time warehouse workers; uses temp staffing agencies for seasonal workers to manage benefits costs
Reports production worker health insurance and pension contributions as direct labor benefits; transitioned from defined benefit to defined contribution plans

nodes.label: Health Insurance — Direct
nodes.definition: Employer-paid health insurance premiums for direct labor employees.
nodes.example: A manufacturer pays $650/month per employee in health insurance premiums for 200 direct labor workers, totaling $1.56M/year in employer-paid health benefits allocated to cost of goods sold.
nodes.classification_notes: Health insurance for direct labor employees is an inventoriable cost under ASC 330 for manufacturers. Distinguish from health insurance for SG&A or R&D employees which goes to those respective departments. Self-insured companies record claims expense rather than premiums. COBRA continuation costs for former employees are typically G&A.

playbook.if_increased:
1. Direct labor headcount growth adding more covered employees
2. Annual health insurance premium rate increases from carriers
3. Richer plan designs or expanded coverage options
4. Shift from contract workers to full-time employees with benefits
5. Higher claims experience in self-insured arrangements
playbook.if_decreased:
1. Reduction in direct labor headcount through automation
2. Migration to high-deductible health plans reducing employer premiums
3. Shift to self-insured model with favorable claims experience
4. Workforce reduction or plant closures

comparability.variations: Some companies combine all employee benefits into a single line by department. Others separate health insurance from other benefits. Self-insured companies report claims expense rather than premiums, creating different cost patterns. International operations have government-mandated health systems.

examples.treatment: Reports health care costs for production workers within cost of sales, with legacy retiree health care as a separate item
Includes health insurance for drivers and warehouse workers within compensation and benefits in cost of operations
Provides health benefits to part-time workers, included within store operating expenses

nodes.label: Retirement Contributions — Direct
nodes.definition: Employer 401(k) or pension contributions for direct labor employees.
nodes.example: A manufacturing company contributes $380K/year in 401(k) employer matches (4% of salary) for 120 direct production employees earning an average of $79K.
nodes.classification_notes: Includes employer 401(k) matching, profit-sharing contributions, and defined benefit pension costs for direct labor employees only. Classified under COGS because these employees are directly involved in production or service delivery. Defined benefit pension expense may include service cost, interest cost, and amortization components under ASC 715.

playbook.if_increased:
1. Increased employer match percentage to improve employee retention
2. Grew direct labor headcount expanding total contribution base
3. Salary increases raised the dollar amount of percentage-based matches
4. Higher employee participation rates in retirement plan
5. Added profit-sharing contributions on top of standard matching
playbook.if_decreased:
1. Reduced employer match percentage during cost-cutting measures
2. Direct labor headcount reductions through layoffs or automation
3. Suspended matching contributions temporarily (as during COVID)
4. Lower employee participation rates reducing required employer match

comparability.variations: Companies with defined benefit pension plans report significantly higher and more volatile retirement costs than those with 401(k) plans only. International companies face varying mandatory contribution requirements. Some companies report all retirement costs together; others split by function.

examples.treatment: Reports significant defined benefit pension costs within COGS for hourly production workers per union agreements
Allocates pension and 401(k) costs to COGS for manufacturing employees and to OpEx for salaried staff
Reports 401(k) matching within cost of sales for fulfillment center workers as part of total compensation costs

nodes.label: Workers' Compensation — Direct
nodes.definition: Workers' compensation insurance premium attributable to direct production employees.
nodes.example: A manufacturing company pays $275K/year in workers' compensation insurance premiums covering 200 production floor employees at a rate of $4.50 per $100 of payroll.
nodes.classification_notes: Workers' comp rates vary significantly by job classification code and state. Manufacturing and construction have much higher rates than office workers. Self-insured companies record estimated claims liability rather than insurance premiums. Experience modification rates (EMR) adjust premiums based on claims history. Only premiums for direct production employees belong here.

playbook.if_increased:
1. Grew direct labor headcount increasing total covered payroll
2. Higher claims experience raising the experience modification rate (EMR)
3. State regulatory increases in workers' comp premium rates
4. Expanded into higher-risk job classifications with costlier coverage
5. Salary increases raised the payroll base on which premiums are calculated
playbook.if_decreased:
1. Reduced direct labor headcount through automation
2. Improved workplace safety program lowered claims and EMR
3. Switched to self-insurance or high-deductible program
4. Negotiated better rates through safety certifications or carrier change

comparability.variations: Workers' comp costs vary dramatically by industry. Manufacturing and logistics companies have material costs while tech/SaaS companies have minimal workers' comp exposure. Self-insured companies report claims reserves rather than premiums, making comparison difficult.

examples.treatment: Reports significant workers' compensation expense within cost of operations, with self-insured retention and excess insurance layers
Allocates substantial workers' comp costs to cost of sales for processing plant workers, using actuarial estimates for self-insured claims
Reports workers' compensation within cost of automotive revenue for factory workers, with evolving safety record affecting premiums

nodes.label: PAYROLL TAXES — DIRECT
nodes.formula_human: Employer FICA / Payroll Tax (Direct)
nodes.definition: Employer-paid payroll taxes (FICA, FUTA, SUTA) attributable to direct labor employees.
nodes.example: A manufacturer with $20M in direct production wages pays approximately $1.53M in employer FICA (7.65% of wages up to Social Security wage base), $120K in FUTA, and $400K in state unemployment taxes.
nodes.classification_notes: Employer-paid payroll taxes for direct production workers are allocated to COGS. Includes FICA (Social Security 6.2% + Medicare 1.45%), FUTA (0.6% on first $7K), and SUTA (varies by state and experience rating). These taxes are computed on gross wages including overtime. The allocation between COGS and SG&A must match the employee allocation. Payroll taxes are capped at certain wage thresholds (Social Security cap) but Medicare has no cap.

playbook.if_increased: (1) Higher production headcount increasing taxable wages, (2) wage increases pushing more wages above previous tax thresholds, (3) legislative increases to payroll tax rates, (4) higher state unemployment tax rates due to layoff experience, (5) Social Security wage base increases
playbook.if_decreased: (1) Lower production headcount, (2) more employees hitting Social Security wage cap earlier in year, (3) improved unemployment experience rating, (4) shift to 1099 contractors not subject to employer payroll tax, (5) favorable state tax rate adjustments

comparability.variations: US payroll tax rates are relatively fixed (~7.65% FICA). International operations face very different employer tax rates — European social charges can be 20-40% of wages. Companies with high turnover face higher unemployment tax rates. Multinational companies must track payroll taxes by jurisdiction.

examples.treatment: Allocates employer FICA and state unemployment taxes to COGS based on direct labor hours in manufacturing
Reports employer payroll taxes on US production workers at ~8% of gross wages including FICA, FUTA, and SUTA
Reports significant payroll tax burden on UAW workforce; Social Security cap reached by many skilled trades workers mid-year

nodes.label: Employer FICA / Payroll Tax — Direct
nodes.definition: Employer's 7.65% FICA contribution on direct labor wages.
nodes.example: A manufacturer with $2M in direct labor wages pays 6.2% Social Security ($124K) and 1.45% Medicare ($29K) for a total employer FICA contribution of $153K on those wages.
nodes.classification_notes: FICA on direct labor is inventoriable under ASC 330 for manufacturers. Social Security tax has a wage base cap ($168,600 for 2024) above which it stops; Medicare has no cap and adds 0.9% surtax above $200K. Distinguish employer FICA on direct labor (COGS) from FICA on SG&A or R&D employees.

playbook.if_increased:
1. Direct labor headcount growth increasing total taxable wages
2. Wage increases pushing more employees above prior brackets
3. Federal FICA rate or wage base increases
4. Shift from contract labor (no FICA) to W-2 employees
playbook.if_decreased:
1. Reduction in direct labor headcount through automation
2. More employees reaching the Social Security wage base cap earlier in the year
3. Shift to contract/gig workers not subject to employer FICA
4. Workforce restructuring reducing direct labor roles

comparability.variations: All US employers pay the same FICA rates, but the allocation between COGS and OpEx varies. Manufacturers typically include FICA in inventoriable costs. Service companies may lump all payroll taxes into a single G&A line. International companies face different social contribution rates.

examples.treatment: Includes employer payroll taxes on production labor within cost of goods sold as an inventoriable cost
Reports payroll taxes on plant workers within cost of sales
Includes employer FICA on operations employees within operating expenses

nodes.label: PRODUCTION WAGES
nodes.formula_human: Regular Production Wages + Production Overtime Pay
nodes.definition: Gross wages paid to direct production workers.
nodes.example: A food processing plant pays $18M in regular wages to 500 production workers and $3M in overtime during peak season (holiday production ramp), for total production wages of $21M.
nodes.classification_notes: Production wages include only gross pay (regular and overtime) for workers directly involved in manufacturing. Excludes employer-paid payroll taxes (separate line item), benefits (separate), and supervisory salaries (indirect labor). In a standard cost system, wage rate variances and labor efficiency variances are tracked separately.

playbook.if_increased: (1) Hourly wage rate increases (minimum wage hikes, union contracts), (2) higher production volumes requiring more labor hours, (3) excessive overtime during peak demand, (4) new product launches with steep learning curves, (5) labor market tightness driving wage inflation
playbook.if_decreased: (1) Automation reducing labor hours per unit, (2) lower production volumes, (3) better production scheduling reducing overtime, (4) learning curve improvements on existing products, (5) outsourcing production to lower-cost facilities

comparability.variations: Union shops typically have higher wage rates but more predictable costs. Non-union manufacturers have more flexibility but may face higher turnover. Companies in high-cost regions (US, Western Europe) show higher wages than those in Asia or Latin America.

examples.treatment: Reports UAW-negotiated hourly wages for assembly workers; significant overtime during truck/SUV production peaks
Minimal direct production wages in-house; most production is outsourced to contract manufacturers
Reports production wages for meat processing workers; significant seasonal overtime during holiday periods

nodes.label: Production Overtime Pay
nodes.definition: Premium overtime pay (time-and-a-half) for direct production workers exceeding standard hours.
nodes.example: A plant running at 110% capacity during Q4 holiday season pays $2.5M in overtime premiums (1.5x rate) to production workers, compared to only $500K in Q1 overtime.
nodes.classification_notes: Overtime pay represents the premium portion (typically 1.5x base rate per FLSA) for hours worked beyond 40/week. Some cost systems record only the premium (0.5x) here, with the straight-time portion in regular wages. If overtime is caused by a specific customer order, it may be charged directly to that job. Abnormal overtime due to inefficiency may be expensed as period cost rather than inventoried per ASC 330.

playbook.if_increased: (1) Demand surge exceeding normal capacity, (2) labor shortages preventing adequate staffing, (3) poor production scheduling creating bottlenecks, (4) machine breakdowns requiring catch-up shifts, (5) new product ramp-up with steep learning curves
playbook.if_decreased: (1) Better production planning and scheduling, (2) additional shift or headcount added to reduce overtime, (3) demand normalization or decline, (4) automation reducing reliance on overtime labor, (5) improved equipment uptime reducing catch-up needs

comparability.variations: Seasonal businesses (food processing, toys) show significant Q3-Q4 overtime spikes. Continuous process industries (steel, chemicals) have built-in shift differentials rather than traditional overtime. Some companies report overtime separately; others combine with regular wages.

examples.treatment: Reports significant peak-season overtime for package handlers during November-December holiday surge
Reported heavy overtime during Model 3 production ramp ("production hell") before stabilizing
Reports seasonal overtime in meat processing plants during holiday production periods

nodes.label: Regular Production Wages
nodes.definition: Standard hourly or salary compensation for direct production employees.
nodes.example: Assembly line workers at an auto plant.
nodes.classification_notes: Regular production wages are the straight-time (non-overtime) gross pay for workers directly involved in manufacturing. Excludes overtime premium (separate line item), employer payroll taxes, and benefits. In standard costing, this creates the basis for labor rate and efficiency variances. Includes both hourly and salaried production workers during their standard work hours.

playbook.if_increased: (1) Annual wage rate increases or cost-of-living adjustments, (2) additional production headcount hired, (3) minimum wage legislation increases, (4) union contract wage escalators, (5) shift from contract to permanent employees
playbook.if_decreased: (1) Automation reducing required production headcount, (2) lean manufacturing reducing labor hours per unit, (3) attrition not replaced during demand downturn, (4) shift to lower-cost production facility, (5) increased use of temporary staffing

comparability.variations: Wage rates vary dramatically by geography: US average manufacturing wage ~$25/hr vs. China ~$6/hr vs. Vietnam ~$3/hr. Union vs. non-union wage differentials can be 20-40%. Some companies include regular wages and overtime in a single line.

examples.treatment: Reports regular hourly wages for non-union US assembly workers at ~$30/hr; competitive with UAW rates
Reports regular wages for assembly workers in China at approximately $3-5/hr; largest cost category
Reports UAW-negotiated hourly wages for production workers; includes skilled trades at higher rates

nodes.label: DIRECT MATERIALS
nodes.formula_human: Raw Materials + Purchased Components + Packaging Materials + Freight-In / Inbound Shipping
nodes.definition: Raw materials and components that physically become part of the finished product.
nodes.example: An auto manufacturer spends $25M on steel and aluminum, $12M on purchased electronic components, $3M on packaging, and $2M on inbound freight for total direct materials of $42M.
nodes.classification_notes: Direct materials must be physically traceable to the finished product. Indirect materials (cleaning supplies, lubricants not incorporated into product) belong in Manufacturing Overhead. Freight-in on materials is capitalized into inventory cost per ASC 330. For retailers, this is the purchase cost of merchandise for resale.

playbook.if_increased: (1) Commodity price inflation (steel, resin, cotton), (2) higher production volumes requiring more materials, (3) supply chain disruptions or tariffs increasing procurement costs, (4) unfavorable product mix shift to material-intensive products, (5) higher scrap/waste rates in production
playbook.if_decreased: (1) Commodity price deflation or favorable hedging, (2) renegotiated supplier contracts or volume discounts, (3) product redesign reducing material content, (4) improved yield rates and less scrap, (5) lower production volumes

comparability.variations: Vertically integrated manufacturers may have lower direct materials but higher labor/overhead. Companies using LIFO vs. FIFO will show different material costs during inflationary periods. Some companies capitalize freight-in; others expense it.

examples.treatment: Reports battery cells and raw materials as a major COGS component; vertically integrating lithium refining
Reports resin, pulp, and specialty chemicals as direct materials; uses commodity hedging
Reports fuselage, avionics, and engine components as direct materials under long-term program accounting

nodes.label: FREIGHT-IN / INBOUND SHIPPING
nodes.formula_human: Inbound Freight & Customs
nodes.definition: Transportation costs to bring raw materials and components to the manufacturing facility. COGS item (distinct from freight-out to customers, which is typically Selling Expense).
nodes.example: A furniture manufacturer pays $1.5M in trucking costs to transport lumber from suppliers to its factory, plus $400K in customs duties on imported hardware components, for total freight-in of $1.9M.
nodes.classification_notes: Freight-in (inbound shipping) is capitalized into inventory cost per ASC 330 and flows through COGS when goods are sold. Freight-out (outbound shipping to customers) is typically a selling expense or fulfillment cost. Under ASC 606, companies elect whether to treat outbound shipping as a separate performance obligation. Import duties and customs fees are part of the landed cost of inventory.

playbook.if_increased: (1) Rising fuel surcharges and transportation rates, (2) port congestion or shipping lane disruptions, (3) new tariffs or increased customs duties, (4) shift to air freight from ocean freight for faster delivery, (5) sourcing from more distant suppliers
playbook.if_decreased: (1) Favorable freight rate negotiations or long-term carrier contracts, (2) nearshoring supply chain reducing transit distances, (3) consolidation of shipments improving load utilization, (4) reduced tariff rates from trade agreements, (5) lower fuel costs

comparability.variations: Companies sourcing globally have higher freight-in than those sourcing domestically. Some companies report freight-in separately while others bundle it into material costs. Tariff exposure varies significantly by sourcing geography.

examples.treatment: Capitalizes inbound freight into inventory; operates own truck fleet to reduce costs
Includes ocean freight and customs duties in product cost; flat-pack design reduces shipping costs
Reports inbound freight on components from global suppliers as part of material cost

nodes.label: Inbound Freight & Customs
nodes.definition: Shipping, freight, and import duties on incoming materials.
nodes.example: A consumer electronics company pays $3M in ocean freight from Asia, $800K in customs brokerage fees, and $1.2M in import duties (e.g., Section 301 tariffs) on components shipped to its US assembly plant.
nodes.classification_notes: Inbound freight and customs duties are part of the landed cost of inventory per ASC 330 and must be capitalized into inventory value. This includes ocean/air/ground freight, customs brokerage fees, import duties, and tariffs. Customs duties can change significantly with trade policy (e.g., Section 301 tariffs, anti-dumping duties). Companies using bonded warehouses or foreign trade zones may defer or reduce duties.

playbook.if_increased: (1) New tariffs or increased duty rates on imports, (2) fuel surcharges driving up freight rates, (3) port congestion causing container demurrage fees, (4) shift from ocean to air freight for urgency, (5) sourcing from more distant or tariff-affected countries
