playbook.if_decreased: (1) Trade agreement reducing duty rates (e.g., USMCA, EU FTA), (2) use of foreign trade zones or duty drawback programs, (3) nearshoring supply chain to duty-free partners, (4) lower fuel costs reducing freight rates, (5) better load consolidation and logistics optimization

comparability.variations: Companies with global supply chains have significant customs exposure. Domestic-only manufacturers have zero customs costs. Tariff exposure varies by product category and country of origin. Some companies disclose tariff impacts separately in MD&A.

examples.treatment: Capitalizes import duties and ocean freight into merchandise inventory; significant exposure to China tariffs on consumer goods
Reports customs duties on imported battery cells and components; uses Shanghai Gigafactory to reduce tariff exposure for China market
Reports inbound freight and duties on apparel and footwear sourced from Vietnam, Indonesia, and China

nodes.label: PACKAGING MATERIALS
nodes.formula_human: Primary Packaging + Secondary / Shipping Packaging
nodes.definition: Materials used to package the final product for sale and delivery.
nodes.example: A beverage company spends $8M on bottles and labels (primary packaging) and $3M on corrugated cases and pallets (secondary packaging) for total packaging costs of $11M.
nodes.classification_notes: Packaging that is integral to the product (e.g., a beverage bottle) is a direct material. Packaging used solely for shipping may be classified as a selling expense under ASC 606 if the company elects that policy. Sustainability initiatives (recycled content, reduced packaging) can affect cost trends.

playbook.if_increased: (1) Resin or paperboard price increases, (2) shift to premium or sustainable packaging materials, (3) higher unit volumes, (4) regulatory requirements for packaging (e.g., recyclability mandates), (5) SKU proliferation requiring more packaging variants
playbook.if_decreased: (1) Packaging redesign reducing material usage (lightweighting), (2) lower resin or paperboard prices, (3) consolidation of packaging suppliers, (4) shift to bulk or concentrate formats, (5) lower production volumes

comparability.variations: CPG companies have significant packaging costs (5-15% of COGS). Industrial manufacturers may have minimal packaging. Some companies classify shipping packaging as a selling expense. Sustainability reporting is driving more detailed packaging cost disclosure.

examples.treatment: Reports PET bottles, aluminum cans, and glass as major packaging material costs; investing in recycled content
Reports shipping boxes, mailers, and void fill as packaging costs within fulfillment
Reports plastic bottles, tubes, and cartons as packaging; committed to reducing virgin plastic usage

nodes.label: Primary Packaging
nodes.definition: Packaging that directly contains the product (boxes, bottles, blister packs).
nodes.example: A pharmaceutical company spends $3M on blister packs and $2M on labeled pill bottles. A cosmetics brand spends $5M on glass perfume bottles and branded boxes.
nodes.classification_notes: Primary packaging directly contains and protects the product — it is what the consumer sees on the shelf. It is always a direct material cost capitalized into inventory. Distinguished from secondary/shipping packaging (outer boxes, pallets). For premium brands, primary packaging can be a significant percentage of COGS. Regulatory requirements (child-resistant, tamper-evident) affect costs.

playbook.if_increased: (1) Resin, glass, or aluminum price increases, (2) packaging redesign for premium look or regulatory compliance, (3) higher unit volumes, (4) shift to sustainable materials (recycled PET, bioplastics), (5) custom mold or printing costs for new SKUs
playbook.if_decreased: (1) Packaging lightweighting or material reduction, (2) standardization across SKUs reducing mold/die costs, (3) lower commodity input prices, (4) consolidated purchasing from fewer suppliers, (5) shift from glass to plastic or vice versa for cost savings

comparability.variations: CPG and beverage companies have high primary packaging costs (10-25% of COGS). Industrial and B2B companies have minimal primary packaging. Luxury brands may spend more on packaging than on product ingredients.

examples.treatment: Reports PET bottles, aluminum cans, and multi-pack cartons as primary packaging for beverages and snacks
Reports premium glass bottles, compacts, and branded boxes as primary packaging — a significant share of product cost
Reports child-resistant bottles, blister packs, and sterile pouches meeting FDA packaging requirements

nodes.label: Secondary / Shipping Packaging
nodes.definition: Outer packaging for shipping (corrugated boxes, pallets, shrink wrap).
nodes.example: An e-commerce retailer spends $4M on corrugated shipping boxes, $1M on bubble wrap and void fill, and $500K on stretch wrap and pallets for outbound shipments.
nodes.classification_notes: Secondary packaging protects the product during storage and transit but is not part of the consumer-facing product. Some companies classify shipping packaging as a selling expense or fulfillment cost rather than COGS — the classification depends on accounting policy election. Under ASC 606, shipping and handling can be treated as a fulfillment activity (COGS) or a separate performance obligation.

playbook.if_increased: (1) Corrugated paperboard price increases, (2) higher order volumes especially in e-commerce, (3) more protective packaging required for fragile products, (4) sustainability mandates requiring costlier materials, (5) smaller average order sizes requiring more boxes per unit
playbook.if_decreased: (1) Right-sizing packaging to reduce material waste, (2) lower paperboard prices, (3) reusable packaging programs, (4) bulk shipments reducing per-unit packaging, (5) supplier consolidation and volume discounts

comparability.variations: E-commerce companies have high secondary packaging costs. B2B industrial companies shipping in bulk have minimal secondary packaging. Some companies include secondary packaging in fulfillment or selling expenses rather than COGS.

examples.treatment: Reports shipping boxes and mailers as a major fulfillment cost; investing in frustration-free packaging to reduce waste
Minimal secondary packaging; products often sold on original pallets or in shelf-ready cases
Reports significant secondary packaging costs for large furniture items requiring custom crating

nodes.label: PURCHASED COMPONENTS
nodes.formula_human: OEM Components + Sub-Assemblies
nodes.definition: Pre-manufactured parts or sub-assemblies purchased from suppliers and incorporated into the final product.
nodes.example: Batteries purchased by an EV manufacturer; processors purchased by a laptop manufacturer.
nodes.classification_notes: Purchased components are pre-manufactured parts sourced externally and incorporated into the final product. Distinguished from raw materials (which require transformation) and from indirect supplies (which are consumed but not part of the product). Make-vs-buy decisions directly affect this line item. Long-term supply agreements may lock in pricing.

playbook.if_increased: (1) Supplier price increases on key components, (2) shift from in-house manufacturing to outsourced components, (3) product redesign requiring more purchased parts, (4) component shortages (e.g., semiconductor crisis) driving spot-market premiums, (5) higher production volumes
playbook.if_decreased: (1) Vertical integration replacing purchased components with in-house production, (2) renegotiated supplier contracts, (3) product simplification reducing component count, (4) economies of scale from volume commitments, (5) dual-sourcing strategy creating price competition

comparability.variations: Vertically integrated companies show lower purchased components but higher labor and overhead. Companies outsourcing more assembly will show higher purchased component costs. Transfer pricing in multinational companies can affect reported costs.

examples.treatment: Sources displays, chips (TSMC-fabricated), and camera modules as purchased components; designs in-house but outsources manufacturing
Reports purchased powertrain components, electronics modules, and brake systems from Tier 1 suppliers
Reports processors (Intel/AMD), memory, and storage as purchased components in configure-to-order model

nodes.label: OEM Components
nodes.definition: Parts sourced from original equipment manufacturers and used in final assembly.
nodes.example: A laptop manufacturer purchases $15M in Intel/AMD processors, $8M in Samsung display panels, and $5M in Realtek audio chips from OEM suppliers for integration into finished devices.
nodes.classification_notes: OEM components are branded parts from original equipment manufacturers used in final assembly. They are typically sole-sourced or limited-sourced, creating supplier concentration risk. Distinguished from generic commodity parts. Long-term supply agreements and minimum purchase commitments are common. Component obsolescence can trigger write-downs.

playbook.if_increased: (1) OEM supplier price increases due to technology upgrades, (2) component shortages requiring spot-market purchases, (3) single-source supplier leverage on pricing, (4) currency fluctuation on imported components, (5) end-of-life surcharges on legacy components
playbook.if_decreased: (1) Technology maturation driving component cost curves down, (2) qualifying second-source suppliers, (3) volume discount tiers achieved, (4) product redesign to use commodity alternatives, (5) favorable currency movements

comparability.variations: Electronics companies have high OEM component costs (50-70% of COGS). Companies designing custom ASICs may show lower OEM component costs but higher R&D. The boundary between OEM components and sub-assemblies can be blurry.

examples.treatment: Reports Intel/AMD processors and display panels as OEM components in PC segment
Reports engines, transmissions, and hydraulic systems from OEM suppliers for agricultural equipment
Reports specialized sensors, batteries, and microprocessors from OEM medical-grade suppliers

nodes.label: Sub-Assemblies
nodes.definition: Partially assembled components purchased externally and assembled into the final product.
nodes.example: An appliance manufacturer purchases $6M in pre-assembled compressor units for refrigerators and $4M in pre-wired control boards for washing machines from contract manufacturers.
nodes.classification_notes: Sub-assemblies are partially assembled units purchased from external contract manufacturers and integrated into the final product. They represent a make-vs-buy decision — higher sub-assembly costs typically mean lower direct labor and overhead. Quality defects in sub-assemblies create warranty and rework exposure. Distinguished from OEM components (which are individual parts, not assembled units).

playbook.if_increased: (1) Contract manufacturer price increases, (2) strategic decision to outsource more assembly steps, (3) higher production volumes, (4) quality issues requiring rework or premium suppliers, (5) supply chain disruptions forcing alternate sourcing
playbook.if_decreased: (1) Bringing assembly in-house (insourcing), (2) renegotiated contract manufacturing terms, (3) lower production volumes, (4) consolidating sub-assembly suppliers, (5) design-for-manufacturing improvements reducing assembly complexity

comparability.variations: Companies with high outsourcing show large sub-assembly costs but lower labor and overhead. Vertically integrated companies show minimal sub-assembly purchases. Contract electronics manufacturers (Foxconn model) make this the dominant COGS category for their customers.

examples.treatment: Purchases assembled iPhone sub-assemblies (display modules, camera modules) from Foxconn, LG, and Sony
Reports fuselage sections from Spirit AeroSystems and wing assemblies from Mitsubishi as sub-assemblies
Sources assembled bike frames and treadmill decks from contract manufacturers in Asia

nodes.label: RAW MATERIALS
nodes.formula_human: Primary Raw Material + Secondary Raw Materials + Raw Material Yield Losses
nodes.definition: Unprocessed inputs purchased to manufacture the product.
nodes.example: Steel coils for an auto manufacturer; cotton for an apparel company.
nodes.classification_notes: Raw materials are unprocessed inputs that undergo transformation during manufacturing. Distinguished from purchased components (which arrive pre-manufactured) and production supplies (which are consumed but not incorporated into the product). Under ASC 330, raw materials inventory is valued at lower of cost or net realizable value.

playbook.if_increased: (1) Commodity price spikes (oil, metals, agricultural inputs), (2) higher production volumes, (3) tariffs or trade restrictions on imported materials, (4) supplier consolidation reducing competitive pricing, (5) quality issues requiring premium-grade substitutes
playbook.if_decreased: (1) Commodity price drops or favorable long-term supply agreements, (2) lower production volumes, (3) material substitution with lower-cost alternatives, (4) improved purchasing leverage through volume commitments, (5) nearshoring reducing logistics costs

comparability.variations: LIFO companies (common in US) show higher raw material costs in inflation vs. FIFO companies. Vertically integrated companies may show transfer prices rather than market prices. Commodity hedging can smooth or defer material cost recognition.

examples.treatment: Reports scrap steel and iron ore as primary raw materials using LIFO; significant LIFO reserve
Reports hydrocarbon feedstocks as raw materials; uses commodity hedging extensively
Reports synthetic fabrics, rubber, and foam as raw materials sourced from contracted suppliers

nodes.label: Primary Raw Material
nodes.definition: The principal material input (e.g., steel in auto manufacturing, silicon in semiconductors).
nodes.example: A steel manufacturer purchases $50M of iron ore and coking coal as its primary raw materials. A semiconductor fab purchases $30M of silicon wafers.
nodes.classification_notes: The primary raw material is the highest-volume, highest-cost material input that defines the core product. It is the largest single driver of material cost variance. Companies often hedge primary raw material prices. Must be distinguished from secondary materials (additives, catalysts) which are used in smaller quantities.

playbook.if_increased: (1) Global commodity price spike for the primary input, (2) supply shortage or cartel pricing, (3) higher production volumes, (4) hedge positions expiring at unfavorable rates, (5) quality specification changes requiring premium-grade material
playbook.if_decreased: (1) Commodity price decline or favorable futures contracts, (2) new supply sources entering the market, (3) lower production volumes, (4) material substitution to a lower-cost alternative, (5) long-term supply agreement at below-market rates

comparability.variations: The identity of the primary raw material varies by industry: steel/aluminum (auto), silicon (semiconductor), crude oil (chemicals), cotton/polyester (apparel). Vertically integrated companies may extract their own primary material, showing lower costs here but higher operating costs.

examples.treatment: Reports alumina and bauxite as primary raw materials; vertically integrated from mining to smelting
Reports silicon wafers from Shin-Etsu and SUMCO as the principal raw material for chip fabrication
Reports live cattle, hogs, and poultry as primary raw material inputs for protein processing

nodes.label: Secondary Raw Materials
nodes.definition: Supporting material inputs used in smaller quantities (e.g., lubricants, adhesives).
nodes.example: An auto manufacturer spends $2M on adhesives, sealants, and lubricants used in assembly. A furniture maker spends $500K on wood stains, varnishes, and fasteners.
nodes.classification_notes: Secondary raw materials are consumed in production and become part of the finished product, but in smaller quantities than the primary material. Distinguish from production supplies (which do NOT become part of the product). If a secondary material cannot be economically traced to individual units, it may be allocated as part of manufacturing overhead instead.

playbook.if_increased: (1) Price increases on specialty chemicals or additives, (2) formula or specification changes requiring more secondary inputs, (3) higher production volumes, (4) supply shortages on specialty materials, (5) regulatory changes requiring new or more expensive additives
playbook.if_decreased: (1) Reformulation reducing secondary material usage, (2) bulk purchasing agreements, (3) lower production volumes, (4) substitution with cheaper alternatives, (5) process improvements reducing consumption rates

comparability.variations: Chemical and pharmaceutical companies may have many secondary materials. Simple assembly operations may have negligible secondary materials. Some companies combine primary and secondary materials into a single line item.

examples.treatment: Reports adhesives, abrasives, and specialty chemicals as secondary raw materials across diversified product lines
Reports pigments, solvents, and resins as secondary materials alongside primary titanium dioxide
Reports flavoring agents, preservatives, and vitamins as secondary materials added to cereal and snack products

nodes.label: Raw Material Yield Losses
nodes.definition: Waste or scrap from raw material processing that is a normal and expected part of manufacturing.
nodes.example: A semiconductor fab processes 10,000 silicon wafers but achieves only 85% yield, losing 1,500 wafers ($3M in material value) to defects. A lumber mill converts logs to boards at 55% yield, with 45% becoming chips, sawdust, and bark (some sold as byproducts).
nodes.classification_notes: Normal yield losses (expected scrap/waste from manufacturing processes) are absorbed into the cost of good units produced — they increase the per-unit material cost. Abnormal yield losses (above standard expectations) should be expensed as a period cost, not inventoried per ASC 330. Scrap with recovery value generates a credit against material cost. Yield improvement is a key manufacturing efficiency metric. In semiconductor and pharma manufacturing, yield is a critical financial driver.

playbook.if_increased: (1) Process instability causing higher defect rates, (2) new product introduction with immature manufacturing process, (3) raw material quality issues from suppliers, (4) equipment degradation affecting precision, (5) operator errors during production
playbook.if_decreased: (1) Process maturation and learning curve improvements, (2) statistical process control identifying and correcting drift, (3) higher-quality raw material inputs, (4) equipment upgrades improving precision, (5) scrap recovery or recycling programs converting waste to value

comparability.variations: Yield loss rates vary dramatically by industry: semiconductors (10-30% loss for advanced nodes), food processing (20-40% for meat cutting), chemicals (2-5% for continuous process). Companies may report yield losses as a variance from standard cost or embedded in total material cost. Revenue from scrap sales offsets yield losses.

examples.treatment: Yield improvement on new process nodes (e.g., 3nm) is a critical driver of COGS reduction; early yields of 50-60% improve to 90%+ at maturity
Reports normal yield losses in meat processing (bone, fat, trim); sells byproducts to offset raw material costs
Reports glass substrate yield losses in display manufacturing; yield improvement drives cost reduction on new glass compositions

nodes.label: INVENTORY ADJUSTMENTS
nodes.formula_human: Beginning Inventory + Net Purchases - Ending Inventory + Inventory Write-Downs & Obsolescence
nodes.definition: Adjustments to the value of inventory that flow through COGS, including the mechanical calculation of goods sold from the inventory account and any write-downs.
nodes.example: A retailer starts the year with $10M beginning inventory, purchases $50M in merchandise, and ends with $12M ending inventory, yielding COGS from inventory flow of $48M. An additional $500K inventory write-down for damaged goods brings total inventory adjustments to $48.5M.
nodes.classification_notes: Inventory adjustments capture the mechanical flow of inventory through COGS (beginning + purchases - ending) plus any write-downs. The periodic method uses this formula directly; perpetual systems record COGS at each sale but still reconcile. Under ASC 330, inventory is carried at lower of cost or NRV. Write-downs are recognized immediately when NRV drops below cost. LIFO vs. FIFO choice significantly impacts reported inventory adjustments during inflation.

playbook.if_increased: (1) Higher sales volume flowing more inventory through COGS, (2) inventory write-downs for obsolescence or damage, (3) LIFO layers liquidation during inventory reduction, (4) inventory shrinkage from theft or counting errors, (5) purchase price increases affecting cost of goods available for sale
playbook.if_decreased: (1) Lower sales volume, (2) inventory build-up (ending inventory exceeding beginning), (3) favorable purchase prices, (4) improved inventory management reducing write-downs, (5) FIFO in deflationary environment showing lower costs

comparability.variations: Retailers and distributors rely heavily on the periodic inventory formula. Manufacturers calculate COGS through work-in-process accounting. LIFO companies (common in US) show different inventory adjustments than FIFO companies. Write-down policies and thresholds vary by company.

examples.treatment: Uses retail inventory method; significant beginning/ending inventory flow drives COGS calculation
Reports periodic inventory write-downs for excess and obsolete networking equipment components
Reports inventory adjustments including shrinkage provisions and seasonal markdown write-downs

nodes.label: Beginning Inventory
nodes.definition: Value of inventory on hand at the start of the accounting period. A component of the COGS formula: COGS = Beginning Inventory + Net Purchases − Ending Inventory.
nodes.example: A retailer starts fiscal year 2024 with $15M in merchandise inventory on the balance sheet. This $15M becomes the beginning inventory input to the COGS calculation: $15M (BI) + $60M (Purchases) - $18M (EI) = $57M COGS.
nodes.classification_notes: Beginning inventory equals the prior period ending inventory. It is a balance sheet carryover, not a new expense. In the periodic COGS formula (BI + Purchases - EI = COGS), beginning inventory adds to cost of goods available for sale. Higher beginning inventory with constant purchases and ending inventory results in higher COGS. Beginning inventory is not an expense itself but a component of the COGS calculation.

playbook.if_increased: (1) Prior period inventory build-up in anticipation of demand, (2) prior period sales shortfall leaving excess inventory, (3) prior period purchase price increases raising carrying value, (4) seasonal build-up for holiday or peak season, (5) LIFO layer additions in prior period
playbook.if_decreased: (1) Prior period strong sales drawing down inventory, (2) prior period inventory write-downs reducing carrying value, (3) prior period destocking or lean inventory initiatives, (4) supply chain disruptions in prior period preventing inventory build, (5) seasonal low point at fiscal year start

comparability.variations: Beginning inventory is identical to prior-period ending inventory — differences indicate a restatement or accounting change. LIFO companies have structurally lower beginning inventory values than FIFO companies. Retailers with January fiscal year-end start with post-holiday low inventory; June year-end retailers start with mid-year inventory levels.

examples.treatment: Reports beginning inventory (January 31 balance) at approximately $56B; the largest single inventory balance globally
Reports beginning finished vehicles, work-in-process, and raw materials inventory by category
Reports beginning merchandise inventory at approximately $17B; high inventory turnover (~12x) keeps levels relatively low

nodes.label: Ending Inventory
nodes.definition: Value of inventory on hand at end of period. Subtracted in the COGS calculation.
nodes.example: A manufacturer counts $22M in raw materials, $8M in work-in-process, and $15M in finished goods at year-end, for total ending inventory of $45M. This $45M is subtracted in the COGS formula, reducing reported COGS.
nodes.classification_notes: Ending inventory is subtracted in the COGS formula (sign_convention: -1), so higher ending inventory reduces COGS and increases gross profit. This creates a potential for earnings manipulation — overvaluing ending inventory artificially reduces COGS. Ending inventory must be valued at lower of cost or NRV per ASC 330. Physical inventory counts or cycle counts are required to verify the balance. Ending inventory becomes next period beginning inventory.

playbook.if_increased: (1) Inventory build-up for anticipated demand, (2) sales shortfall leaving unsold inventory, (3) purchase price increases raising cost basis, (4) overproduction exceeding demand, (5) seasonal inventory build before peak selling season
playbook.if_decreased: (1) Strong sales drawing down inventory, (2) inventory write-downs to NRV, (3) lean or just-in-time inventory management, (4) supply chain disruptions preventing replenishment, (5) deliberate destocking strategy

comparability.variations: LIFO companies report lower ending inventory (and higher COGS) than FIFO companies in inflation. Retailers with post-holiday year-end have low ending inventory. Just-in-time companies maintain minimal ending inventory. The LIFO reserve disclosed in footnotes allows conversion between methods.

examples.treatment: Maintains very low ending inventory relative to revenue due to just-in-time production system
Reports ~$56B ending inventory; January year-end captures post-holiday drawdown
Uses LIFO; ending inventory reported at historical cost layers with significant LIFO reserve disclosed

nodes.label: INVENTORY WRITE-DOWNS & OBSOLESCENCE
nodes.formula_human: Inventory Obsolescence Write-down + Inventory Shrinkage & Spoilage
nodes.definition: Reductions in inventory value below cost, recognized when net realizable value (NRV) is below carrying cost (ASC 330).
nodes.example: A consumer electronics company writes down $5M of last-generation smartphones when the new model launches, plus $800K in shrinkage losses discovered during physical inventory count, for total write-downs of $5.8M.
nodes.classification_notes: Under ASC 330-10-35, inventory must be written down to NRV when cost exceeds NRV. Write-downs are generally recorded in COGS. Under US GAAP, write-downs are permanent (no reversal allowed), unlike IFRS which permits reversal. Large or unusual write-downs may be disclosed separately in footnotes. Companies must assess inventory for obsolescence at each reporting date. The estimation of obsolescence reserves is a significant accounting judgment.

playbook.if_increased: (1) Technology shifts making current inventory obsolete (e.g., new product generation), (2) market price declines below cost, (3) excess inventory from demand forecast errors, (4) product recalls or quality failures, (5) regulatory changes banning or restricting products
playbook.if_decreased: (1) Improved demand forecasting reducing excess inventory, (2) better inventory management and faster turnover, (3) product design stability reducing obsolescence risk, (4) secondary market or liquidation channels for slow-moving inventory, (5) tighter purchasing controls preventing overbuy

comparability.variations: Technology companies face rapid obsolescence (product lifecycles of 6-18 months). Fashion retailers face seasonal obsolescence. Pharmaceutical companies face expiration-based write-downs. Companies using LIFO may have ancient inventory layers that are rarely written down. Some companies use a reserve method (allowance); others write down specific items.

examples.treatment: Reports significant inventory write-downs for excess and obsolete networking components; maintains a reserve methodology
Reports write-downs for out-of-season athletic footwear and apparel; uses factory outlet stores to reduce write-down impact
Reports write-downs for expired pharmaceutical products and discontinued drug formulations

nodes.label: Inventory Obsolescence Write-down
nodes.definition: Write-down of slow-moving or obsolete inventory to estimated NRV.
nodes.example: A consumer electronics company writing down last-generation phones when new models launch.
nodes.classification_notes: Obsolescence write-downs reduce inventory to estimated net realizable value when products become slow-moving, technologically outdated, or discontinued. Under US GAAP (ASC 330), write-downs are permanent and cannot be reversed even if NRV recovers. Companies may use an aging-based reserve (e.g., 25% for 6-12 months old, 50% for 12-18 months, 100% for >18 months) or specific identification. Large obsolescence charges may be non-recurring and excluded from adjusted earnings.

playbook.if_increased: (1) New product generation making current inventory obsolete, (2) unexpected demand decline for existing products, (3) competitor launches rendering products uncompetitive, (4) engineering changes making existing components incompatible, (5) regulatory changes banning products or ingredients
playbook.if_decreased: (1) Better product lifecycle management and phase-out planning, (2) improved demand forecasting preventing overproduction, (3) secondary channels (outlet stores, liquidators) reducing write-down need, (4) modular design allowing component reuse across product generations, (5) build-to-order model reducing finished goods inventory risk

comparability.variations: Technology companies have the highest obsolescence risk (6-18 month product cycles). Fashion/apparel faces seasonal obsolescence. Pharmaceutical companies face expiration-date-based obsolescence. Companies vary in reserve methodology — some use aging schedules, others use specific identification. The reserve balance is typically disclosed in inventory footnotes.

examples.treatment: Manages obsolescence through tight supply chain; limits build-ahead of new products; writes down prior-generation components
Reports obsolescence reserves for printer cartridges and PC components as technology cycles shorten
Reports write-downs for out-of-season athletic apparel; uses markdown optimization and outlet stores to minimize losses

nodes.label: Inventory Shrinkage & Spoilage
nodes.definition: Reduction in inventory due to theft, damage, or (for perishables) spoilage.
nodes.example: A grocery chain discovers $3M in shrinkage during annual physical counts (theft, miscounting), plus $1.5M in spoiled perishable goods (expired dairy, damaged produce), for total shrinkage and spoilage of $4.5M.
nodes.classification_notes: Inventory shrinkage is the difference between book inventory and physical count, caused by theft, damage, administrative errors, or vendor fraud. Spoilage applies to perishable goods (food, pharmaceuticals, chemicals) that expire or degrade. Normal shrinkage and spoilage are absorbed into COGS; abnormal amounts may be classified as a separate expense line. Retailers typically accrue a shrinkage reserve based on historical rates and true up at physical count.

playbook.if_increased: (1) Increased retail theft (organized retail crime), (2) supply chain disruptions causing damage in transit, (3) poor temperature control causing spoilage of perishables, (4) expanded self-checkout reducing theft deterrence, (5) longer storage times increasing spoilage for perishable goods
playbook.if_decreased: (1) Enhanced loss prevention technology (RFID, video analytics, AI), (2) improved cold chain management for perishables, (3) better inventory management reducing dwell time, (4) employee training reducing handling damage, (5) faster inventory turnover reducing spoilage window

comparability.variations: Grocery retailers have the highest spoilage (2-5% of sales for perishables). General merchandise retailers have higher theft-based shrinkage (1-2% of sales). Manufacturers have lower shrinkage since products are in controlled environments. Some companies report shrinkage in SG&A rather than COGS.

examples.treatment: Reports significant shrinkage and spoilage in perishable departments (produce, dairy, meat); invested in AI demand forecasting to reduce waste
Cited organized retail crime as driver of increased inventory shrinkage; invested in loss prevention technology
Reports food spoilage losses in distribution; maintains strict cold chain management to minimize

nodes.label: Net Purchases
nodes.definition: Total purchases of inventory during the period, net of purchase returns and discounts.
nodes.example: A retailer purchases $5.2M of merchandise from suppliers during Q3, less $180K in purchase returns and $95K in early-payment discounts, for net purchases of $4.925M.
nodes.classification_notes: Net purchases equals gross purchases minus purchase returns and allowances minus purchase discounts. Only includes inventory for resale or raw materials for production. Capital equipment purchases are not included here. Freight-in may be included or reported separately depending on company policy.

playbook.if_increased:
1. Increased procurement to support higher anticipated sales volume
2. Supplier price increases passed through in purchase costs
3. Seasonal inventory buildup ahead of peak selling period
4. Stocked up on materials due to anticipated supply chain disruptions
5. Expanded product assortment requiring additional inventory categories
playbook.if_decreased:
1. Reduced order volume due to lower demand forecasts
2. Negotiated better supplier pricing or volume discounts
3. Destocking strategy to reduce excess inventory levels
4. Shifted to just-in-time procurement reducing purchase frequency
5. Supplier consolidation resulting in better terms and lower costs

comparability.variations: Retailers typically report net purchases as a major COGS component, while manufacturers may report raw materials purchases instead. Some companies include freight-in within net purchases; others report it separately.

examples.treatment: Reports purchases within cost of sales as part of its periodic inventory system, netting returns and allowances
Includes merchandise costs net of vendor rebates and allowances within cost of sales
Reports cost of sales inclusive of net purchases, freight, and distribution center costs combined

nodes.label: MANUFACTURING OVERHEAD
nodes.formula_human: Facility Costs + Equipment & Depreciation + Indirect Labor & Supervision + Production Supplies
nodes.definition: Indirect production costs that cannot be directly traced to a specific unit of output but are necessary for manufacturing operations. Allocated to products using a predetermined overhead rate.
nodes.example: Factory rent is the same regardless of units produced, but must be absorbed into product cost.
nodes.classification_notes: Manufacturing overhead includes all indirect production costs: facility costs, equipment depreciation, indirect labor, and production supplies. Under ASC 330, overhead must be allocated to inventory using a systematic and rational method (e.g., machine hours, labor hours, or activity-based costing). Unallocated overhead (idle capacity) should be expensed as a period cost. Fixed vs. variable overhead distinction drives cost behavior analysis.

playbook.if_increased: (1) New facility or capacity expansion adding fixed costs, (2) energy cost increases affecting utilities and operations, (3) equipment depreciation from capital investments, (4) lower production volume increasing per-unit overhead (under-absorption), (5) maintenance costs on aging equipment
playbook.if_decreased: (1) Higher production volume spreading fixed overhead over more units (over-absorption), (2) energy efficiency initiatives, (3) fully depreciated equipment reducing depreciation charges, (4) consolidation of production into fewer facilities, (5) outsourcing production eliminating factory overhead

comparability.variations: Capital-intensive industries (semiconductors, chemicals) have high manufacturing overhead relative to direct labor. Labor-intensive industries (apparel, food processing) have low overhead ratios. Companies using activity-based costing may report overhead differently than those using traditional volume-based allocation. Lease vs. own decisions affect whether costs appear as rent or depreciation.

examples.treatment: Reports very high manufacturing overhead due to multi-billion dollar fab facilities; depreciation is the largest overhead component
Reports moderate manufacturing overhead including factory utilities, equipment maintenance, and indirect labor in chocolate production
Reports manufacturing overhead across global facilities; overhead allocation is key to competitive pricing

nodes.label: EQUIPMENT & DEPRECIATION
nodes.formula_human: Production Equipment Depreciation
nodes.definition: Costs associated with production equipment and its depreciation over useful life.
nodes.example: An automotive manufacturer depreciates $800M in production line equipment over 10-15 years, recording $65M/year in production equipment depreciation within COGS.
nodes.classification_notes: Production equipment depreciation is typically included in COGS/manufacturing overhead, not in a separate D&A line. This is distinct from corporate/administrative equipment depreciation in SG&A. Units-of-production method may be used for equipment whose wear correlates with output volume. Idle equipment depreciation should be expensed in the period, not allocated to inventory.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new production equipment investments, (2) factory expansions with new machinery, (3) equipment acquired through business combinations, (4) change to shorter useful life estimates
playbook.if_decreased: (1) production equipment becoming fully depreciated, (2) equipment disposals or retirements, (3) extension of useful life estimates, (4) production line shutdowns

comparability.variations: Manufacturing companies embed equipment depreciation in COGS. Some companies using units-of-production method see depreciation fluctuate with volume. Capital-intensive industries (auto, steel, chemicals) have the highest amounts. Service companies have minimal production equipment.

examples.treatment: Heavy production equipment depreciation embedded in cost of goods sold
Massive production equipment depreciation using mix of straight-line and units-of-production
Semiconductor fab equipment depreciated over 3-5 years; significant COGS component

nodes.label: Equipment Maintenance & Service Contracts
nodes.definition: Preventive maintenance and service agreements for production equipment.
nodes.example: A semiconductor fab pays $2.1M/year for annual maintenance contracts on lithography equipment and $350K for quarterly calibration services on testing instruments.
nodes.classification_notes: Routine maintenance is expensed as incurred. Major overhauls that extend useful life may require capitalization under ASC 360. Multi-year service contracts should be expensed ratably over the contract term. Distinguish from repairs that restore function (expense) vs. improvements that add capability (capitalize).

playbook.if_increased:
1. Aging equipment requiring more frequent maintenance
2. New equipment purchases adding service contracts
3. Vendor price increases on maintenance agreements
4. Regulatory requirements mandating more frequent inspections
5. Shift from time-and-materials to full-service contracts
playbook.if_decreased:
1. Replacement of old equipment with new (under warranty)
2. Bringing maintenance in-house with hired technicians
3. Renegotiated service contracts at lower rates
4. Decommissioning of production lines reducing equipment base

comparability.variations: Some companies bundle maintenance costs with depreciation in a single line. Others separate them. Capital-intensive industries tend to disclose maintenance spending more prominently. Airlines have mandatory maintenance reserves.

examples.treatment: Includes equipment maintenance within cost of revenue as part of fab operating costs
Reports aircraft maintenance, materials, and outside repairs as a separate operating expense line
Includes maintenance and repair costs within cost of products sold for steel mill equipment

nodes.label: Equipment Rental / Leasing
nodes.definition: Lease payments on production equipment (operating lease treatment per ASC 842).
nodes.example: A food manufacturer leases packaging equipment for $8K/month under a 3-year operating lease and rents specialized mixing equipment for $3K/month on a short-term rental agreement.
nodes.classification_notes: Under ASC 842, most leases create a right-of-use asset and lease liability on the balance sheet. Operating leases recognize straight-line expense; finance leases split into depreciation and interest. Short-term leases (under 12 months) can use the practical expedient and expense as incurred. Distinguish from owned equipment depreciation.

playbook.if_increased:
1. New equipment leases to expand production capacity
2. Strategic shift from buying to leasing to preserve capital
3. Lease renewal at higher market rates
4. Short-term equipment rentals for project-based production
playbook.if_decreased:
1. Purchasing previously leased equipment at lease end
2. Lease expirations not renewed due to capacity reduction
3. Renegotiated lease terms at lower rates
4. Equipment returned as production lines are consolidated

comparability.variations: ASC 842 adoption made most leases visible on the balance sheet, but presentation of expense varies. Some companies show lease expense in a dedicated line; others embed it in depreciation or occupancy costs. Finance leases create depreciation plus interest, complicating comparisons with operating leases.

examples.treatment: As a lessor, discloses equipment rental revenue; as a lessee, reports fleet-related leases within cost of revenues
Reports production equipment leases within cost of products, with ASC 842 disclosures in notes
Includes equipment lease costs within manufacturing overhead allocated to cost of sales

nodes.label: Production Equipment Depreciation
nodes.definition: Straight-line or accelerated depreciation on production machinery and equipment (ASC 360).
nodes.example: A $500K CNC machine depreciated over 10 years = $50K/year in production overhead.
nodes.classification_notes: Production equipment depreciation flows into inventory cost and ultimately COGS when goods are sold. During periods of overproduction, some depreciation is capitalized into unsold inventory. Idle production equipment depreciation is expensed immediately rather than allocated to inventory. CNC machines, robotics, assembly line equipment, and testing rigs are typical items.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new production line investments, (2) capacity expansion with additional machinery, (3) equipment modernization replacing older assets, (4) acquisitions adding manufacturing facilities
playbook.if_decreased: (1) equipment reaching end of useful life, (2) production line retirements, (3) sale of manufacturing operations, (4) extended useful life estimates after equipment upgrades

comparability.variations: Heavy manufacturing (auto, steel, chemicals) has the highest production equipment depreciation. Companies using units-of-production method see depreciation vary with output. Semiconductor fabs have very short equipment lives (3-5 years) creating high annual charges.

examples.treatment: Production equipment depreciated over 10-15 years; significant COGS component
Fab equipment depreciated over 5 years; billions in annual production depreciation
Consumer goods production equipment depreciated using straight-line method

nodes.label: FACILITY COSTS
nodes.formula_human: Factory Rent/Lease + Factory Utilities + Facility Maintenance & Repairs
nodes.definition: Costs of operating the physical manufacturing facility.
nodes.example: A manufacturing plant incurs $2.8M in facility costs: $1.5M factory lease, $800K utilities (high electricity for machinery), $500K maintenance and repairs.
nodes.classification_notes: These are manufacturing facility costs — part of COGS via manufacturing overhead, not G&A. They are absorbed into inventory under ASC 330-10 and flow to COGS when inventory is sold. Corporate office facility costs belong under G&A Office & Facilities. Idle facility costs (excess capacity) should be expensed as period costs, not inventoried.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new manufacturing facility brought online, (2) utility rate increases (especially electricity for heavy manufacturing), (3) deferred maintenance catch-up on aging facilities, (4) lease renewals at higher market rates, (5) regulatory requirements for facility upgrades
playbook.if_decreased: (1) plant closure or consolidation, (2) energy efficiency improvements, (3) lease renegotiations, (4) outsourcing manufacturing to contract manufacturers, (5) reduced production shifting costs to idle capacity (period expense)

comparability.variations: Manufacturing companies absorb these costs into inventory; they appear in COGS when sold. Companies using contract manufacturers (asset-light model) show minimal facility costs. Facility costs as % of COGS vary by industry: heavy manufacturing 10-20%, light assembly 3-8%.

examples.treatment: Factory facility costs absorbed into vehicle inventory cost; large owned manufacturing footprint
Asset-light model; Foxconn/TSMC bear manufacturing facility costs; Apple shows minimal owned factory costs

nodes.label: Facility Maintenance & Repairs
nodes.definition: Ongoing maintenance and repair of the manufacturing facility (not capital improvements).
nodes.example: A manufacturing plant spends $480K on maintenance: $180K HVAC/electrical maintenance contracts, $120K roof and structural repairs, $100K plumbing and fire suppression servicing, $80K general upkeep.
nodes.classification_notes: Routine repairs and maintenance are expensed as incurred under ASC 360-10. Capital improvements that extend useful life or add functionality must be capitalized. The distinction between repair (expense) and improvement (capitalize) requires judgment. Planned shutdowns for maintenance may be accrued or expensed as incurred depending on policy. This is a manufacturing facility cost — corporate office maintenance is under G&A.

playbook.if_increased: (1) aging facility requiring more frequent repairs, (2) regulatory inspections requiring remediation, (3) deferred maintenance catch-up, (4) expansion or renovation of production areas, (5) inflation on contractor and materials costs
playbook.if_decreased: (1) new or recently renovated facility requiring minimal maintenance, (2) plant closure or consolidation, (3) outsourcing manufacturing to contract manufacturers, (4) preventive maintenance programs reducing reactive repair costs, (5) extended maintenance contract renegotiations

comparability.variations: Maintenance costs vary by facility age and type. Heavy manufacturing (chemicals, metals) requires more maintenance than light assembly. Companies that own facilities bear full maintenance; tenants under NNN leases share costs with landlords. Some companies capitalize major overhauls, reducing current-period expense.

examples.treatment: Significant turnaround and maintenance costs for chemical plants; some capitalized, others expensed
Newer facilities with lower maintenance; costs absorbed into vehicle inventory

nodes.label: Factory Rent / Lease
nodes.definition: Rent or lease payments for manufacturing plant and production facilities.
nodes.example: A contract electronics manufacturer leases a 200,000 sq ft factory at $12/sq ft/year for a total annual lease cost of $2.4M, allocated to manufacturing overhead and absorbed into product costs.
nodes.classification_notes: Factory rent or lease is a fixed manufacturing overhead cost absorbed into inventory. Under ASC 842, operating leases appear on the balance sheet as right-of-use assets. Only the manufacturing facility portion belongs in COGS; corporate office leases are SG&A. If a facility is partially used for production and partially for admin, the cost must be allocated. Idle facility space lease costs should be expensed as period cost, not inventoried.

playbook.if_increased: (1) Lease renewals at higher market rates, (2) expansion to additional leased manufacturing space, (3) real estate market appreciation in manufacturing regions, (4) new facility leases for capacity expansion, (5) CPI escalation clauses in existing leases
playbook.if_decreased: (1) Plant consolidation reducing leased space, (2) lease renegotiation at more favorable terms, (3) transition from leased to owned facilities, (4) subletting excess manufacturing space, (5) relocation to lower-cost industrial areas

comparability.variations: Companies owning their factories show depreciation instead of rent. Leasing companies show rent expense and right-of-use assets under ASC 842. Asset-light contract manufacturers may lease all facilities. Real estate costs vary dramatically by geography — a factory in coastal California costs far more than one in rural Tennessee.

examples.treatment: Leases manufacturing facilities globally; significant operating lease costs allocated to COGS
Owns most Gigafactories (depreciation, not rent); Fremont factory was initially leased from Toyota
Mix of owned and leased manufacturing facilities; lease costs allocated to COGS via overhead rates

nodes.label: Factory Utilities
nodes.definition: Electricity, gas, water, and other utilities consumed in manufacturing operations.
nodes.example: A steel mill pays $5M/year in electricity for arc furnaces, $1.2M for natural gas heating, and $300K for water used in cooling processes, totaling $6.5M in factory utilities.
nodes.classification_notes: Factory utilities are manufacturing overhead costs absorbed into inventory. They have both fixed (base load for lighting, HVAC) and variable (production-driven electricity for machinery) components. Only utilities consumed in manufacturing facilities belong in COGS; corporate office utilities are SG&A. Energy-intensive industries (aluminum smelting, glass, cement) have utilities as a major COGS driver. Companies with on-site power generation may show lower utility costs but higher depreciation.

playbook.if_increased: (1) Energy rate increases from utility providers, (2) higher production volumes increasing electricity and gas consumption, (3) extreme weather driving HVAC costs, (4) expansion to additional production shifts, (5) new energy-intensive equipment or processes
playbook.if_decreased: (1) Energy efficiency retrofits (LED lighting, VFDs, high-efficiency motors), (2) on-site solar or wind power generation, (3) favorable energy contract renegotiations, (4) lower production volumes, (5) process improvements reducing energy consumption per unit

comparability.variations: Energy-intensive industries (aluminum, steel, cement, glass) have utilities as 10-30% of COGS. Light assembly has utilities at 1-3% of COGS. Companies in regions with cheap energy (e.g., hydroelectric) have structural advantages. Some companies hedge energy costs with futures contracts.

examples.treatment: Electricity is the largest single factory utility cost in aluminum smelting; often co-locates near hydroelectric power
Reports significant electricity costs for semiconductor fabs (cleanroom HVAC, process equipment); investing in renewable energy
Reports natural gas for brewing and pasteurization plus electricity for refrigeration as major factory utilities

nodes.label: INDIRECT LABOR & SUPERVISION
nodes.definition: Labor costs for production support roles that cannot be directly traced to specific products.
nodes.example: A quality control manager who oversees the entire production line is indirect labor.
nodes.classification_notes: Indirect labor is inventoriable as manufacturing overhead under ASC 330. Includes production supervisors, quality inspectors, material handlers, and maintenance workers. Must be allocated to inventory using a systematic method (e.g., machine hours, labor hours). Under/over-applied overhead adjustments may be needed at period end.

playbook.if_increased:
1. New production lines requiring additional supervisors
2. Increased quality requirements adding inspection roles
3. Wage increases for supervisory and skilled support roles
4. Reduced span of control (fewer direct reports per supervisor)
5. Regulatory requirements adding safety or compliance oversight
playbook.if_decreased:
1. Consolidation of supervisory roles through lean manufacturing
2. Automation reducing need for material handling labor
3. Plant closures eliminating indirect labor positions
4. Outsourcing quality inspection to third parties

comparability.variations: Some companies combine all manufacturing labor (direct and indirect) in a single COGS line. Others separate direct from indirect. The boundary between indirect production labor and plant G&A varies. Some companies classify plant managers as G&A rather than overhead.

examples.treatment: Includes indirect labor and supervision within cost of sales as part of manufacturing overhead allocation
Reports indirect manufacturing labor within cost of products sold, allocated across product lines
Includes supervisory and quality labor within cost of sales for each operating segment

nodes.label: Indirect Production Labor
nodes.definition: Wages for production support roles (material handlers, janitors, forklift operators).
nodes.example: A manufacturing plant employs 20 material handlers at $40K/year, 10 janitors at $32K/year, and 8 forklift operators at $45K/year, totaling $1.48M in indirect production labor allocated to manufacturing overhead.
nodes.classification_notes: Indirect production labor includes factory workers who support production but do not directly manufacture the product — material handlers, janitors, maintenance workers, forklift operators, and setup crews. Their wages are part of manufacturing overhead, not direct labor. The boundary between direct and indirect labor is a key cost accounting judgment. In some lean operations, workers rotate between direct and indirect tasks, requiring time-based allocation.

playbook.if_increased: (1) Additional support staff for expanded production operations, (2) increased material handling from more complex product mix, (3) wage rate increases for support roles, (4) regulatory requirements mandating additional maintenance or cleaning staff, (5) poor layout design requiring more material movement
playbook.if_decreased: (1) Automated material handling (AGVs, conveyors) replacing manual labor, (2) lean manufacturing reducing non-value-add roles, (3) outsourcing janitorial or maintenance services, (4) plant layout optimization reducing material handling needs, (5) headcount reductions during demand downturn

comparability.variations: The boundary between direct and indirect labor varies by company and cost system. Some companies include setup time and material handling in direct labor. Automated factories have lower indirect labor. Outsourced janitorial or maintenance services may appear in purchased services rather than labor.

examples.treatment: Reports material handlers, maintenance techs, and custodial staff as indirect labor under UAW contract
Reports cleanroom technicians and facilities support as indirect labor in semiconductor fabrication
Reports warehouse operators and line setup crews as indirect production labor in consumer goods manufacturing

nodes.label: Production Supervisors & Managers
nodes.definition: Salaries of manufacturing supervisors and plant managers.
nodes.example: A factory with 3 production shifts employs 15 shift supervisors at $75K/year and 5 plant managers at $120K/year, totaling $1.725M in supervisory compensation allocated to manufacturing overhead.
nodes.classification_notes: Production supervisors and plant managers are indirect labor — they support production but do not directly manufacture the product. Their salaries are allocated to COGS through manufacturing overhead rates. If a supervisor splits time between production and non-production activities, only the production portion belongs in COGS. Plant manager salary above the shop floor level may be classified as SG&A depending on scope of responsibilities.

playbook.if_increased: (1) Additional supervisory headcount for new production lines or shifts, (2) salary increases for management retention, (3) plant expansion requiring more oversight, (4) regulatory requirements mandating additional supervision (e.g., FDA-regulated facilities), (5) reduced span of control increasing supervisor-to-worker ratio
playbook.if_decreased: (1) Consolidation of supervisory roles or layers, (2) lean management reducing spans of control, (3) plant closures eliminating management positions, (4) automation reducing need for shop floor oversight, (5) attrition not replaced during downturn

comparability.variations: Lean manufacturing companies have wider spans of control (1 supervisor per 20-30 workers vs. traditional 1 per 10-15). Self-directed work teams reduce supervisory needs. Companies vary on where plant manager compensation is classified — COGS or SG&A.

examples.treatment: Uses team leader model with wide spans of control; supervisory costs are relatively low per production worker
Reports program managers and production supervisors in COGS for defense manufacturing programs
Reports brewmaster and shift supervisor salaries as manufacturing overhead in beverage production

nodes.label: Quality Control Personnel
nodes.definition: Compensation for QC inspectors and quality assurance staff embedded in production.
nodes.example: A pharmaceutical manufacturer employs 25 QC inspectors at $55K/year and 5 QA managers at $85K/year, totaling $1.8M in quality control personnel costs allocated to manufacturing overhead.
nodes.classification_notes: QC personnel embedded in production are part of manufacturing overhead (COGS). QA staff in a corporate quality department may be classified as SG&A. In FDA-regulated industries (pharma, medical devices, food), QC staffing levels are driven by regulatory requirements and cannot be easily reduced. In-process inspection labor may be classified as direct labor if traced to specific production runs.

playbook.if_increased: (1) New regulatory requirements mandating additional testing or inspection, (2) quality problems requiring increased inspection frequency, (3) new product introductions requiring validation testing, (4) customer audit requirements driving additional QC staffing, (5) transition to higher-quality standards (ISO, GMP)
playbook.if_decreased: (1) Statistical process control reducing need for 100% inspection, (2) inline automated inspection systems, (3) supplier quality improvements reducing incoming inspection, (4) process maturity reducing defect rates, (5) consolidation of testing labs across facilities

comparability.variations: Regulated industries (pharma, aerospace, medical devices) have very high QC staffing as a percent of total labor. Consumer electronics companies may rely more on automated testing. Some companies report QC costs separately for transparency; others bundle with indirect labor.

examples.treatment: Reports significant QC personnel costs in pharmaceutical manufacturing; FDA cGMP requirements dictate staffing levels
Reports FAA-required quality inspectors as a major indirect labor category in aircraft manufacturing
Reports food safety and quality lab technicians as QC personnel in food and beverage production

nodes.label: PRODUCTION SUPPLIES
nodes.formula_human: Factory / Production Supplies
nodes.definition: Consumable materials used in manufacturing that are not incorporated into the final product.
nodes.example: Cutting tools, lubricants, safety equipment, cleaning supplies used on the factory floor.
nodes.classification_notes: Production supplies are indirect materials consumed during manufacturing but not incorporated into the finished product. Examples include cutting tools, drill bits, lubricants, cleaning agents, safety gloves, and protective equipment. Distinguished from direct materials (which become part of the product) and from office supplies (which are SG&A). Production supplies are part of manufacturing overhead and absorbed into inventory cost.

playbook.if_increased: (1) Higher production volumes consuming more supplies, (2) price increases on consumable materials, (3) equipment condition requiring more cutting tools or lubricants, (4) new safety requirements adding PPE costs, (5) less efficient processes consuming more supplies per unit
playbook.if_decreased: (1) Lower production volumes, (2) tool life improvements reducing replacement frequency, (3) bulk purchasing agreements, (4) process improvements reducing supply consumption, (5) preventive maintenance reducing consumable wear

comparability.variations: Machining-intensive manufacturers have high production supply costs (cutting tools, coolants). Assembly operations have lower supply costs. Chemical manufacturers may have significant catalyst costs. Some companies combine production supplies with maintenance supplies into a single MRO category.

examples.treatment: Reports cutting tools, welding consumables, and grinding wheels as production supplies in heavy machinery manufacturing
Reports lubricants, welding wire, and paint supplies as production consumables in vehicle assembly
Reports lab reagents, filters, and cleanroom consumables as production supplies in pharmaceutical manufacturing

nodes.label: Factory / Production Supplies
nodes.definition: All consumable supplies used in the manufacturing process that are not direct materials.
nodes.example: A machining shop spends $200K/year on drill bits and cutting inserts, $80K on coolants and lubricants, $50K on safety gloves and protective eyewear, and $30K on cleaning solvents.
nodes.classification_notes: Factory production supplies are consumables used on the shop floor that do not become part of the finished product. They are expensed as manufacturing overhead and absorbed into inventory cost. If supplies can be traced to specific products or jobs, they may be classified as direct materials instead. High-value tooling (e.g., molds, dies) above the capitalization threshold should be capitalized and depreciated, not expensed as supplies.

playbook.if_increased: (1) Higher production volumes increasing supply consumption, (2) price increases on consumable inputs, (3) older equipment requiring more frequent tool/consumable replacement, (4) new safety or environmental regulations adding required supplies, (5) shift to more supply-intensive manufacturing processes
playbook.if_decreased: (1) Lower production volumes, (2) longer-lasting tools or consumables (technology improvement), (3) bulk purchasing or vendor-managed inventory programs, (4) process optimization reducing waste, (5) standardization reducing variety of supplies stocked

comparability.variations: Metal fabrication and machining operations have high supply costs. Assembly-only operations have minimal supply costs. Companies may combine this with MRO (maintenance, repair, operations) supplies. Some firms use consignment or vendor-managed inventory programs that affect timing of cost recognition.

examples.treatment: Reports electrodes, refractories, and alloy additions as factory supplies in steel production
Reports sealants, fasteners below materiality threshold, and protective coatings as production supplies in aircraft assembly
Reports converting chemicals, adhesives, and process aids as factory supplies in tissue and diaper manufacturing

nodes.label: SERVICE DELIVERY COSTS
nodes.formula_human: Cloud Infrastructure & Hosting + Customer Support Labor + DevOps & Platform Engineering + Third-Party Data & Licensed Content + Payment Processing & Transaction Fees
nodes.definition: The direct costs of delivering the service to customers. Analogous to direct materials + manufacturing overhead for product companies, but specific to service/SaaS delivery.
nodes.example: For a SaaS company, service delivery costs are cloud hosting, support labor, and third-party data — not R&D, which belongs in Operating Expenses.
nodes.classification_notes: Service delivery costs are the SaaS/services equivalent of COGS for product companies. They include cloud hosting, customer support labor, DevOps, third-party data licensing, and payment processing fees — all costs directly tied to delivering the service to customers. R&D and sales/marketing are NOT included even though they support the service. The boundary between service delivery (COGS) and R&D is a key classification judgment for SaaS companies and affects gross margin comparability.

playbook.if_increased: (1) Customer growth driving higher cloud infrastructure consumption, (2) expansion of customer support team, (3) third-party data licensing cost increases, (4) higher transaction volumes increasing payment processing fees, (5) investment in reliability and uptime (more redundancy, multi-region deployment)
playbook.if_decreased: (1) Cloud cost optimization (reserved instances, spot instances, right-sizing), (2) automation reducing customer support headcount, (3) renegotiated data licensing agreements, (4) payment volume routing to lower-cost processors, (5) architecture improvements reducing per-user infrastructure costs

comparability.variations: SaaS companies report "Cost of Revenue" which is analogous to COGS. The line between Cost of Revenue and R&D varies — some companies include DevOps in COGS, others in R&D. Gross margins for SaaS (70-85%) are much higher than for professional services (25-40%). Companies hosting on own infrastructure vs. public cloud have different cost structures.

examples.treatment: Reports cost of revenues including data center operations, customer support, and amortization of acquired technology
Reports cost of revenue dominated by cloud infrastructure (AWS/Azure consumption) — largest single cost item
Reports cost of revenue including carrier network fees, cloud infrastructure, and customer support

nodes.label: CLOUD INFRASTRUCTURE & HOSTING
nodes.definition: Costs of cloud compute, storage, and networking directly tied to serving customers.
nodes.example: AWS, Azure, or GCP charges that scale with the number of active customers or data volume.
nodes.classification_notes: Only production infrastructure serving customers belongs in COGS. Dev/test environments and internal IT cloud costs belong in R&D or G&A respectively. Reserved instances may require upfront capitalization and amortization. Multi-cloud strategies split costs across vendors.

playbook.if_increased:
1. Rapid customer or usage growth increasing compute and storage demands
2. Migration from on-premise to cloud infrastructure
3. Cloud vendor price increases or expiration of committed-use discounts
4. Launch of new product features requiring additional infrastructure
5. Data residency requirements adding regional deployments
playbook.if_decreased:
1. Infrastructure optimization (right-sizing, auto-scaling, spot instances)
2. Negotiated enterprise discount programs or committed-use savings
3. Architecture redesign reducing resource consumption per customer
4. Customer churn reducing infrastructure load

comparability.variations: SaaS companies consistently report cloud hosting as cost of revenue, but the allocation between production vs. R&D environments varies. Some companies include CDN and bandwidth; others separate them. Non-tech companies may classify similar costs under G&A.

examples.treatment: Reports cloud hosting costs as a major component of cost of revenue, broken out in 10-K risk factors
Discloses cloud infrastructure costs on major public cloud providers as largest cost of revenue component
Reports co-location and public cloud hosting costs within cost of revenue, including data center leases

nodes.label: Compute / EC2 / Virtual Machines
nodes.definition: Cloud compute instance costs directly serving the production environment.
nodes.example: A SaaS company spends $45K/month on AWS EC2 reserved instances and $12K/month on on-demand instances to handle peak traffic for its production application.
nodes.classification_notes: Only production compute serving customers is COGS. Dev/staging compute belongs in R&D. Reserved instance prepayments may be capitalized as prepaid expenses and amortized. Spot/preemptible instances create cost variability. GPU instances for ML inference may be a separate sub-line.

playbook.if_increased:
1. Customer growth requiring more compute capacity
2. Migration to larger or GPU-heavy instance types
3. Expiration of reserved instance discounts reverting to on-demand pricing
4. New workloads (ML inference, real-time processing) requiring additional compute
5. Geographic expansion adding regional compute clusters
playbook.if_decreased:
1. Right-sizing instances to match actual utilization
2. Purchasing reserved instances or savings plans at discount
3. Containerization and serverless migration reducing idle capacity
4. Improved application efficiency reducing compute per request

comparability.variations: Most SaaS companies combine all cloud compute into a single hosting line. Some hyperscale users break out compute from storage and networking. Companies using co-location may report server depreciation instead.

examples.treatment: Reports cloud hosting (including compute) as a major cost of revenue component in its Atlas cloud product
Reports co-location and cloud compute costs within cost of revenue, including owned server depreciation
Includes AWS compute and hosting in cost of revenue with committed spend disclosures

nodes.label: Networking & CDN
nodes.definition: Data transfer, bandwidth, and content delivery network costs.
nodes.example: A video streaming SaaS company pays $340K/month to Cloudflare and AWS CloudFront for CDN bandwidth to deliver content to global users.
nodes.classification_notes: Includes data egress charges, CDN fees, and inter-region transfer costs. Only production-environment networking belongs in COGS; dev/test networking should be classified under R&D. Internal corporate network costs belong in G&A.

playbook.if_increased:
1. User traffic growth driving higher bandwidth consumption
2. Expanded to new geographic regions requiring additional CDN edge locations
3. Richer media content (video, images) increasing per-request data transfer
4. Cloud provider egress price increases
playbook.if_decreased:
1. Implemented caching optimizations reducing CDN traffic
2. Negotiated committed-use discounts with CDN provider
3. Migrated to a lower-cost CDN provider
4. Compressed assets and optimized delivery reducing bandwidth usage

comparability.variations: Most SaaS companies bundle networking and CDN costs within a broader cloud infrastructure or hosting line in COGS. Media and streaming companies often break out bandwidth costs separately due to their materiality.

examples.treatment: Reports CDN and bandwidth as a major component of cost of revenue including Open Connect infrastructure costs
Reports network costs including bandwidth, co-location, and transit within cost of revenue
Reports bandwidth and co-location costs as primary components of cost of revenue

nodes.label: Storage / S3 / Object Storage
nodes.definition: Cloud storage costs for customer data in the production environment.
nodes.example: A document management SaaS company pays $85K/month for AWS S3 storage hosting 450TB of customer files, plus $12K/month for S3 Glacier archival storage.
nodes.classification_notes: Only production-environment storage belongs in COGS. Dev/test storage should be classified under R&D. Includes S3, Azure Blob Storage, Google Cloud Storage, and equivalent services. Storage costs grow with customer data accumulation and rarely decrease, creating a ratcheting cost structure. Archival/cold storage tiers are significantly cheaper per GB.

playbook.if_increased:
1. Customer data growth increasing total stored volume
2. New product features generating more data per customer
3. Expanded customer base adding incremental storage needs
4. Regulatory retention requirements preventing data purging
playbook.if_decreased:
1. Implemented data lifecycle policies moving old data to cheaper tiers
2. Negotiated committed-use storage discounts or reserved capacity
3. Data compression and deduplication reduced stored volume
4. Migrated to lower-cost storage provider or self-hosted solution

comparability.variations: Most SaaS companies bundle storage within a single cloud hosting or infrastructure line in COGS. Companies with large media libraries (video, images) have disproportionately high storage costs. Some companies use reserved capacity pricing, making costs more predictable.

examples.treatment: Reports infrastructure costs including storage as the primary component of cost of revenue, with ongoing migration from AWS to own infrastructure
Includes cloud storage within cost of revenue as part of data center and infrastructure costs
Reports storage and transcoding costs within cost of revenue as a major component given video hosting model

nodes.label: Third-Party Infrastructure Services
nodes.definition: Managed services (databases, monitoring, security) that directly support production.
nodes.example: A SaaS company pays $55K/month for managed PostgreSQL (AWS RDS), $18K for Datadog monitoring, and $12K for Cloudflare WAF security services in production.
nodes.classification_notes: Includes managed databases (RDS, Cloud SQL), monitoring tools (Datadog, New Relic), managed Kubernetes, security services (WAF, DDoS protection), and similar production-support services. Only production-environment services belong in COGS; dev/test instances belong in R&D. Distinguish from cloud compute and storage which have their own line items.

playbook.if_increased:
1. Added new managed services to production stack (monitoring, security, caching)
2. Scaled managed database instances to handle growing data volumes
3. Vendor price increases at renewal or usage tier escalation
4. Migrated from self-managed to managed services increasing external costs
playbook.if_decreased:
1. Brought managed services in-house (self-managed databases, monitoring)
2. Negotiated enterprise discounts or committed-use agreements
3. Consolidated redundant services or vendors
4. Optimized resource utilization reducing overprovisionment

comparability.variations: The boundary between managed services and core compute/storage varies by company. Some include all cloud spending in a single hosting line; others separate managed services. Companies running their own data centers will not have these costs but will have equivalent depreciation and personnel expenses.

examples.treatment: Reports third-party infrastructure costs within cost of revenue, primarily AWS managed services
Includes managed cloud service costs within cost of revenue for its Elastic Cloud offering
Reports third-party hosting and infrastructure service costs within cost of revenue for its SaaS offering

nodes.label: CUSTOMER SUPPORT LABOR
nodes.definition: Compensation for support agents who directly resolve customer issues with the product. Post-sale technical support essential to service delivery.
nodes.example: A SaaS help desk team handling customer bugs and onboarding issues.
nodes.classification_notes: Post-sale technical support that is essential to delivering the service belongs in COGS. Pre-sale support engineers belong in Sales & Marketing. Customer success managers focused on retention/upsell may go in S&M. The line between support (COGS) and customer success (S&M) varies by company.

playbook.if_increased:
1. Customer base growth requiring more support headcount
2. Product complexity increases driving higher ticket volumes
3. Insourcing previously outsourced support operations
4. Wage inflation or geographic expansion to higher-cost support centers
5. New product launches creating onboarding demand
playbook.if_decreased:
1. AI chatbots and self-service tools reducing human ticket volume
2. Outsourcing support to lower-cost offshore centers
3. Product improvements reducing support contact rate
4. Customer churn reducing the support base

comparability.variations: SaaS companies generally classify support labor in cost of revenue. Some companies include customer success in this line while others separate it under S&M. Outsourced support may appear as professional services fees rather than labor.

examples.treatment: Includes customer support costs within cost of subscription and support revenue
Reports customer support and related overhead as part of cost of subscription revenues
Reported support team costs within cost of revenue, including outsourced agents

nodes.label: Payroll Taxes — Support
nodes.definition: Employer payroll taxes attributable to COGS-classified support staff.
nodes.example: A SaaS company pays $165K/year in employer FICA and state taxes on $2.1M in support staff salaries for its 35-person customer support team classified in COGS.
nodes.classification_notes: Only includes payroll taxes for support staff classified under COGS. If customer support is classified under G&A or S&M (less common), taxes follow the same functional allocation. Outsourced support (BPO) does not generate employer payroll taxes for the company.

playbook.if_increased:
1. Expanded in-house support team headcount
2. Salary increases for support staff raising payroll tax base
3. Brought previously outsourced support roles in-house
4. Hired support staff in higher-tax jurisdictions
playbook.if_decreased:
1. Outsourced support to BPO providers eliminating employer tax obligation
2. Reduced support headcount through AI/automation chatbots
3. Attrition without backfill in support organization
4. Reclassified support staff from COGS to G&A functional area

comparability.variations: The classification of support staff as COGS vs. G&A varies across companies. Companies with large outsourced support operations will show lower payroll taxes relative to total support costs. Some companies do not separately report support payroll taxes.

examples.treatment: Includes support personnel payroll taxes within cost of revenue for customer-facing support operations
Bundles support payroll taxes into cost of subscription and support revenue
Reports support staff costs including payroll taxes within cost of revenue, with significant offshore support reducing US tax burden

nodes.label: Support Staff Wages & Salary
nodes.definition: Gross compensation for customer support representatives in COGS.
nodes.example: A SaaS company pays $3.2M/year in salaries for its 50-person customer support team (Tier 1-3), classified as cost of revenue.
nodes.classification_notes: Includes base salary, overtime, and shift differentials for customer support staff classified in COGS. Some companies classify support under S&M or G&A rather than COGS, affecting gross margin comparability. Outsourced support (BPO) costs are not wages and belong in a separate line item.

playbook.if_increased:
1. Expanded support team to handle growing customer base
2. Annual salary increases or cost-of-living adjustments
3. Brought outsourced support roles in-house for quality control
