4. Added premium/enterprise support tier requiring specialized staff
5. Increased overtime due to higher support ticket volume
playbook.if_decreased:
1. Outsourced support to lower-cost BPO providers
2. Implemented AI chatbots and self-service reducing headcount needs
3. Support staff reductions through layoffs or attrition
4. Reclassified support staff from COGS to G&A or S&M

comparability.variations: The classification of customer support as COGS vs. OpEx significantly affects gross margin comparability. Companies with offshore support teams report lower per-head costs. BPO-heavy models show support costs as professional services expense rather than wages.

examples.treatment: Classifies customer success and support staff wages within cost of subscription and support revenue
Includes support team salaries within cost of revenue alongside infrastructure costs
Reports support staff wages in cost of revenue, emphasizing the direct connection between support delivery and service quality

nodes.label: Support Tools & Software
nodes.definition: Subscriptions to ticketing, CRM, and support tools used by the support team.
nodes.example: A SaaS company pays $145K/year for Zendesk ticketing, $60K for Intercom live chat, and $25K for Confluence knowledge base licenses used by the support team.
nodes.classification_notes: Includes per-seat or per-usage subscriptions for tools directly used by support teams. Classify under COGS only if support is COGS-classified. General CRM tools used by sales teams belong under S&M. Tools shared across departments should be allocated or classified based on primary use.

playbook.if_increased:
1. Added new support tools (chat, AI copilot, analytics) to tech stack
2. Vendor price increases at subscription renewal
3. Growing support team adding per-seat license costs
4. Upgraded to premium tiers for advanced features or SLAs
playbook.if_decreased:
1. Consolidated support tools reducing redundant subscriptions
2. Negotiated volume discounts or multi-year commitments
3. Migrated to lower-cost or open-source alternatives
4. Reduced support headcount lowering per-seat license needs

comparability.variations: Some companies bundle support tool costs within a general IT/software line rather than allocating to COGS. Companies building their own support platforms in-house report lower software costs but higher R&D capitalization. Per-seat pricing makes costs scale linearly with team size.

examples.treatment: Reports support tool costs within cost of revenue as part of technology and infrastructure costs
Includes internal tooling costs (including Jira Service Management) within cost of revenue for cloud products
As both a vendor and user of support tools, reports internal support tool costs within cost of revenue and R&D

nodes.label: DEVOPS / PLATFORM ENGINEERING
nodes.definition: Engineering labor costs for keeping the production platform running and reliable. Excludes R&D (new feature development).
nodes.example: Engineers maintaining uptime, resolving production incidents, and deploying patches.
nodes.classification_notes: Engineers maintaining production uptime belong in COGS. Engineers building new features or internal tools belong in R&D. The split between DevOps (COGS) and platform engineering (R&D) often requires time allocation estimates. On-call compensation and incident response are typically COGS.

playbook.if_increased:
1. Hiring additional SRE/DevOps engineers to improve uptime SLAs
2. Growing system complexity requiring more operational support
3. Post-incident investment in reliability after outages
4. Insourcing managed services previously handled by vendors
5. Wage inflation in competitive DevOps labor market
playbook.if_decreased:
1. Infrastructure automation reducing manual operations work
2. Migration to managed services (serverless, PaaS) reducing ops burden
3. Consolidation of engineering teams after platform stabilization
4. Outsourcing NOC/operations to managed service providers

comparability.variations: Most SaaS companies include DevOps labor in cost of revenue, but the boundary with R&D engineering varies. Some allocate a percentage of total engineering to COGS based on time studies. Others classify all infrastructure engineers as R&D.

examples.treatment: Allocates a portion of engineering costs to cost of revenue for production operations and support
Reports infrastructure and reliability engineering costs within cost of revenue
Includes network operations and platform engineering in cost of revenue

nodes.label: DevOps / SRE Wages & Salary
nodes.definition: Compensation for engineers whose primary role is production reliability and operations.
nodes.example: A SaaS company employs 8 SRE engineers at an average salary of $185K each, totaling $1.48M/year in base compensation allocated to cost of revenue.
nodes.classification_notes: Only base salary and wages belong here; stock-based compensation is typically a separate line. Engineers splitting time between production ops and new feature development require time-based allocation between COGS and R&D. On-call stipends and overtime premiums are included.

playbook.if_increased:
1. New SRE/DevOps hires to support scaling infrastructure
2. Annual merit increases and cost-of-living adjustments
3. Competitive market driving up DevOps salaries
4. Reclassification of engineers from R&D to production operations
playbook.if_decreased:
1. Layoffs or attrition in operations team
2. Offshoring operations roles to lower-cost regions
3. Automation reducing required headcount for production operations
4. Reclassification of time allocation shifting more hours to R&D

comparability.variations: Some companies combine all engineering wages and allocate a percentage to COGS. Others track DevOps/SRE as a distinct cost center. Stock-based compensation for these roles may or may not be included depending on company policy.

examples.treatment: Allocates a portion of engineering salaries to cost of revenue based on time spent on production infrastructure
Includes operations engineering salaries in cost of subscription revenue
Reports production operations team compensation within cost of subscription revenue

nodes.label: Payroll Taxes & Benefits — DevOps
nodes.definition: Employer payroll taxes and benefits for COGS-classified engineering staff.
nodes.example: A SaaS company pays $92K/quarter in FICA taxes and $48K in health insurance premiums for its 12-person DevOps team classified under COGS.
nodes.classification_notes: Only includes taxes and benefits for engineering staff whose work directly supports production infrastructure (DevOps, SRE, platform engineering). Engineers working on new features belong under R&D payroll taxes. The split between COGS and R&D engineering must follow consistent allocation methodology.

playbook.if_increased:
1. Expanded DevOps/SRE team headcount increasing tax and benefits burden
2. Healthcare premium renewal at higher rates
3. Reclassified engineers from R&D to COGS-DevOps increasing this line
4. Annual salary increases driving higher FICA/FUTA tax base
playbook.if_decreased:
1. Reduced DevOps headcount through automation or attrition
2. Shifted to contractor-based DevOps model (no employer taxes/benefits)
3. Migrated employees to lower-cost benefits plans
4. Reclassified staff from COGS-DevOps to R&D

comparability.variations: Many companies do not break out DevOps payroll taxes separately; they are bundled into total COGS personnel costs. The allocation of engineering staff between COGS and R&D varies significantly across SaaS companies.

examples.treatment: Includes DevOps-related personnel costs within cost of revenue without separately disclosing payroll taxes
Allocates engineering payroll taxes between cost of revenue and R&D based on time allocation
Reports personnel-related costs including benefits within cost of revenue for infrastructure-supporting staff

nodes.label: PAYMENT PROCESSING & TRANSACTION FEES
nodes.definition: Costs charged by payment processors directly tied to revenue transactions.
nodes.example: An e-commerce platform incurs $2.4M/quarter in combined payment processing fees across Stripe gateway fees and interchange costs on $85M in GMV.
nodes.classification_notes: This is a sub-category aggregating gateway fees and related transaction costs. Companies may report gross or net of these fees depending on whether they act as principal or agent in the transaction. Under ASC 606 principal vs. agent guidance, marketplace platforms often net these fees.

playbook.if_increased:
1. Revenue growth driving proportionally higher transaction volume
2. Shift toward higher-cost payment methods (credit cards vs. ACH)
3. International expansion with cross-border surcharges
4. Added new payment methods (BNPL, digital wallets) with incremental fees
5. Processor rate increases at contract renewal
playbook.if_decreased:
1. Negotiated lower blended rates through volume commitments
2. Shifted payment mix toward lower-cost methods (ACH, direct debit)
3. Consolidated payment processors to achieve volume discounts
4. Implemented surcharging or convenience fees offsetting costs

comparability.variations: Gross vs. net reporting creates significant comparability issues. Companies acting as principal report gross revenue and processing fees in COGS; agents report net revenue. Some companies report these fees as contra-revenue deductions.

examples.treatment: Reports transaction-based costs within cost of revenue including interchange, assessment, and processing fees
Reports transaction expense as the largest component of cost of revenue, including funding costs and processing fees
Reports payment processing fees within cost of revenue for its marketplace and payments segments

nodes.label: Credit Card Processing Fees
nodes.definition: Merchant fees (typically 1.5–3%) charged per customer payment transaction.
nodes.example: An e-commerce retailer processes $10M in credit card transactions monthly and pays 2.9% + $0.30 per transaction to Stripe, totaling approximately $295K/month in processing fees.
nodes.classification_notes: Always classified as cost of revenue when fees are transaction-based and tied to customer payments. Some companies net processing fees against revenue (agent model under ASC 606) rather than reporting gross. Distinguish from bank wire fees or ACH costs which may be lower-cost alternatives.

playbook.if_increased:
1. Revenue growth driving higher transaction volumes
2. Shift in payment mix toward higher-cost card types (rewards cards, international cards)
3. Processor rate increases or loss of volume discount tiers
4. Expansion into international markets with higher cross-border fees
playbook.if_decreased:
1. Negotiated lower processing rates with payment processor
2. Customer shift to ACH, wire, or direct debit reducing card usage
3. Volume discount tiers achieved through growth
4. Switching to lower-cost payment processors or interchange-plus pricing

comparability.variations: Companies acting as payment intermediaries (agent model) may net fees against revenue. Gross vs. net presentation significantly impacts reported revenue and COGS. Some companies bundle processing fees with other transaction costs.

examples.treatment: Reports merchant payment processing fees as cost of revenue under Merchant Solutions segment
Reports transaction-based costs including interchange as cost of revenue in its Seller ecosystem
Includes credit card processing fees within overall cost of sales, not separately disclosed

nodes.label: Payment Gateway Fees
nodes.definition: Fixed or variable fees charged by payment gateway providers (Stripe, Adyen, etc.).
nodes.example: A SaaS company pays Stripe 2.9% + $0.30 per transaction, totaling $185K/month on $6.4M in monthly recurring revenue processed.
nodes.classification_notes: Gateway fees are distinct from interchange fees paid to card networks. Some companies net gateway fees against revenue; others report them in COGS. If the company acts as a payment facilitator (PayFac), these become cost of revenue. Monthly platform/subscription fees from gateways may belong here or in G&A depending on materiality.

playbook.if_increased:
1. Revenue growth driving proportional increase in transaction volume
2. Higher share of credit card vs. ACH/wire payments increasing blended rate
3. Expanded into international markets with higher cross-border fees
4. Gateway provider raised per-transaction or percentage rates
playbook.if_decreased:
1. Negotiated lower rates based on increased transaction volume
2. Migrated to a lower-cost payment gateway provider
3. Shifted payment mix toward ACH or direct debit reducing per-transaction costs
4. Consolidated payment processors to leverage volume discounts

comparability.variations: Some companies report gateway fees as a contra-revenue deduction rather than COGS. E-commerce marketplaces often report these as cost of revenue, while SaaS companies may bundle them into a broader processing fees line.

examples.treatment: Reports payment processing fees within cost of Merchant Solutions revenue as a major cost component
Includes payment gateway fees within cost of revenue for its commerce segment
Reports payment processing costs as the primary component of cost of fintech solutions revenue

nodes.label: THIRD-PARTY DATA & LICENSED CONTENT
nodes.definition: Costs of data, APIs, or licensed content embedded in the delivered product.
nodes.example: A financial data platform paying Bloomberg for data incorporated into its product.
nodes.classification_notes: Only includes data and content that is directly incorporated into or delivered through the product. Data used for internal analytics or decision-making belongs in G&A or R&D. This sub-category aggregates API data feeds, licensed content libraries, and similar third-party inputs that are essential to the product offering.

playbook.if_increased:
1. Added new data sources or content providers to enrich the product
2. Usage-based data API costs grew with customer consumption
3. Vendor price increases at contract renewal
4. Expanded product functionality requiring additional third-party data
5. Entered new markets requiring region-specific data or content
playbook.if_decreased:
1. Built proprietary data pipelines replacing licensed feeds
2. Renegotiated vendor contracts at lower rates
3. Consolidated data providers reducing redundant costs
4. Customer usage decline reducing variable data consumption fees

comparability.variations: Financial data companies have very high third-party data costs as a percentage of revenue. Media and streaming companies report content costs as the dominant COGS component. Some companies capitalize content costs and amortize over the license period rather than expensing immediately.

examples.treatment: Licenses third-party data feeds as a component of its terminal product, embedded within cost of revenue
Reports music licensing and content costs as the primary component of cost of revenue at approximately 70% of revenue
Reports third-party data costs within cost of services as a major expense for data sourced from exchanges and providers

nodes.label: API / Integration Fees
nodes.definition: Per-call or subscription fees for third-party APIs essential to product functionality.
nodes.example: A fintech SaaS company pays Plaid $120K/year for bank account verification API calls and $85K/year for Twilio SMS verification APIs used in the product.
nodes.classification_notes: Classify as COGS when the API is essential to delivering the product to customers (e.g., mapping API in a logistics app). Classify as OpEx/R&D when used only in development or internal tooling. Volume-based contracts may have minimum commitments that require accrual even if usage is low.

playbook.if_increased:
1. Customer growth driving higher API call volumes
2. New third-party API integrations added to the product
3. Vendor price increases on per-call or tiered pricing
4. Migration to premium API tiers for better SLAs
playbook.if_decreased:
1. Building in-house replacements for third-party APIs
2. Renegotiated volume discounts with API vendors
3. Optimized code reducing unnecessary API calls
4. Sunset of product features that relied on external APIs

comparability.variations: Some companies bundle API fees into a general "third-party services" or "data processing" line. Others break out by vendor. SaaS companies increasingly disclose these as a component of cost of revenue.

examples.treatment: Reports third-party API and network fees as part of cost of revenue
Includes payment processing and third-party API costs within cost of revenue
Reports network carrier and third-party API costs as a key component of cost of revenue

nodes.label: Data Provider Fees
nodes.definition: Subscription or usage fees for third-party data incorporated into the product.
nodes.example: A fintech company pays $600K/year in data fees: $300K Bloomberg Terminal licenses, $150K S&P Capital IQ, $100K Refinitiv market data feeds, $50K alternative data providers.
nodes.classification_notes: Data feeds incorporated into the product are COGS, not G&A. Corporate-use data subscriptions (e.g., Bloomberg for internal investment decisions) are G&A. Classification depends on whether the data is resold/embedded in the product (COGS) or used internally (G&A). Usage-based pricing creates variable cost behavior.

playbook.if_increased: (1) adding new data providers to expand product coverage, (2) customer growth increasing usage-based data consumption, (3) vendor price increases on data licensing renewals, (4) expansion into new data categories (alternative data, ESG), (5) regulatory requirements for additional data sources
playbook.if_decreased: (1) renegotiated data licensing agreements, (2) building proprietary data collection reducing third-party dependency, (3) product pivots reducing data requirements, (4) consolidating data providers, (5) moving from premium to standard data tiers

comparability.variations: Financial services firms spend heavily on market data ($2K-$25K per user per year for Bloomberg). SaaS companies embedding third-party data may have it as largest COGS component. Some companies negotiate enterprise-wide licenses while others pay per-seat or per-query.

examples.treatment: Data licensing is revenue; internal data costs are minimal as a data provider itself
Third-party data content costs are a significant portion of COGS, disclosed in cost of services

nodes.label: Licensed Content Fees
nodes.definition: Royalties or licenses for content (images, media, text) delivered through the product.
nodes.example: A SaaS company pays Getty Images $120K/year for stock photo licenses embedded in its design platform.
nodes.classification_notes: Distinguish from software licenses (OpEx R&D) and from content created in-house. Only content licensed from third parties for delivery to customers belongs here. If content is used internally (e.g., training), classify under G&A.

playbook.if_increased:
1. Expanded content library with new licensing agreements
2. Renegotiated contracts at higher rates upon renewal
3. Usage-based royalties increased due to higher customer consumption
4. Shift from user-generated content to licensed premium content
playbook.if_decreased:
1. Consolidated content vendors or renegotiated volume discounts
2. Developed proprietary content to replace licensed material
3. Reduced scope of licensed content offerings
4. Shifted to royalty-free or open-source content

comparability.variations: Some companies bundle licensed content costs into a single COGS line; others split by content type (images, video, music). Streaming companies may report content amortization separately from content licensing fees.

examples.treatment: Reports licensed content costs as part of cost of revenue, driven by per-stream royalty payments to labels
Includes stock photo and media licensing fees within cost of revenue as content costs
Reports content licensing within cost of subscription revenue for Adobe Stock

nodes.label: Cost of Goods Sold
nodes.formula_human: Direct Materials + Direct Labor + Manufacturing Overhead + Inventory Adjustments + Service Delivery Costs
nodes.definition: The aggregate cost of goods produced and sold, and services rendered during the reporting period. Includes all direct costs attributable to the production of goods or delivery of services — materials, labor, and allocated overhead.
nodes.example: A manufacturer with $40M in raw materials, $15M direct labor, and $10M factory overhead reports $65M COGS against $100M revenue for a 35% gross margin.
nodes.classification_notes: In SaaS companies, COGS is often labeled 'Cost of Revenue' and includes hosting costs, customer support, and amortization of capitalized software. In professional services, it includes billable labor and direct project costs.

playbook.if_increased: (1) higher sales volume driving proportional cost increase, (2) raw material or input cost inflation, (3) supply chain disruptions increasing procurement costs, (4) unfavorable product mix shift toward lower-margin products, (5) manufacturing inefficiency or yield loss
playbook.if_decreased: (1) lower sales volume, (2) favorable input cost trends or renegotiated supplier contracts, (3) manufacturing efficiency gains or automation, (4) favorable product mix shift, (5) outsourcing or offshoring production

comparability.variations: Terminology varies significantly by industry: 'Cost of Revenue' (tech/SaaS), 'Cost of Goods Sold' (manufacturing/retail), 'Cost of Services' (professional services). Some companies include D&A in COGS; others report it separately.

examples.treatment: Cost of sales (products + services)
Cost of revenues (subscription + professional services)
Cost of sales
Not applicable — uses interest expense and provisions

nodes.label: Shipping & Handling — Classification Decision
nodes.formula_human: Route to COGS or Selling Expenses based on nature and timing of cost
nodes.definition: A decision node that routes shipping and handling costs to the appropriate parent based on whether the cost is incurred before or after transfer of control to the customer, and whether it represents a separate performance obligation.
nodes.example: An e-commerce company incurs $2M inbound freight (classified as COGS) and $5M outbound shipping to customers (could be COGS as fulfillment cost or Selling Expenses depending on policy election).
nodes.classification_notes: Under ASC 606, shipping and handling after control transfer may be treated as fulfillment cost (COGS) or separate performance obligation. If treated as fulfillment activity, the cost is accrued when revenue is recognized. Companies must elect and consistently apply a policy. Amazon classifies outbound shipping in COGS; many retailers classify it in Selling Expenses.

decision_criteria.condition: Cost incurred to bring goods to saleable condition (inbound freight, warehousing before sale)
Cost incurred to deliver goods to customers (outbound freight, last-mile delivery)
Shipping charged to customer and recognized as separate performance obligation

playbook.if_increased: (1) higher shipment volumes from revenue growth, (2) carrier rate increases, (3) shift toward faster/premium shipping, (4) fuel surcharges, (5) new geographic markets with higher logistics costs
playbook.if_decreased: (1) lower order volumes, (2) renegotiated carrier contracts, (3) logistics optimization (route consolidation), (4) shift toward customer pickup or digital delivery, (5) warehouse network optimization reducing shipping distances

comparability.variations: Classification of shipping costs varies significantly across companies. Some classify all shipping in COGS; others split between COGS (inbound) and Selling (outbound). This creates comparability challenges when analyzing gross margins across companies.

examples.treatment: Outbound shipping in Cost of Sales (COGS), also collects shipping revenue
Distribution costs in Operating, selling, general and administrative
Shipping and handling costs in SG&A
Shipping and handling in Merchandise costs (COGS)

nodes.label: Operating Expenses
nodes.formula_human: Selling Expenses + General & Administrative Expenses + Research & Development + Depreciation & Amortization
nodes.definition: The total of all expenses incurred in the ordinary course of business operations, excluding cost of goods sold. Encompasses selling, general & administrative, R&D, and other operating costs.
nodes.example: A SaaS company with $30M in sales & marketing, $20M G&A, and $25M R&D reports $75M total operating expenses.
nodes.classification_notes: The boundary between COGS and OpEx can be subjective. Companies may classify the same type of expense differently. For example, customer support costs may appear in COGS (Salesforce) or in OpEx (others). D&A may be embedded in COGS and OpEx or reported as a separate line.

playbook.if_increased: (1) headcount growth across sales, G&A, or R&D, (2) increased marketing/advertising spend, (3) new office/facility costs, (4) increased R&D investment for new products, (5) one-time restructuring or litigation charges
playbook.if_decreased: (1) workforce reductions or hiring freezes, (2) cost optimization programs, (3) reduced marketing spend, (4) office consolidation, (5) automation replacing manual processes

comparability.variations: Presentation varies: some companies show a single 'Operating Expenses' line; others break out S&M, G&A, R&D individually. Tech companies typically show more granular breakdowns. Some companies include D&A as a separate OpEx line; others embed it within functional categories.

examples.treatment: Research and development + Marketing and sales + General and administrative
Research and development + Selling, general and administrative
Operating, selling, general and administrative expenses
Research and development + Marketing and sales + General and administrative

nodes.label: Selling Expenses
nodes.formula_human: Sales Force Compensation + Advertising & Marketing + Shipping & Distribution
nodes.definition: All expenses directly related to the selling effort — compensation for sales teams, advertising, marketing campaigns, trade shows, shipping to customers, and related costs.
nodes.example: A consumer products company spending $15M on sales team compensation, $10M on advertising, and $3M on distribution reports $28M in selling expenses.
nodes.classification_notes: Many companies combine Selling and G&A into 'SG&A' as a single line item. Tech/SaaS companies often label this 'Sales and Marketing' or 'Marketing and Sales'. The split between selling vs. G&A can be discretionary.

playbook.if_increased: (1) sales team expansion or higher commissions from strong revenue, (2) increased marketing/advertising campaigns, (3) new market entry requiring go-to-market spend, (4) trade show or event-heavy quarter, (5) customer acquisition cost increases
playbook.if_decreased: (1) sales team reductions, (2) reduced advertising spend, (3) shift to lower-cost digital channels, (4) improved sales efficiency (higher revenue per rep), (5) market exit or product line discontinuation

comparability.variations: Reporting varies significantly: some companies present 'Sales and Marketing' as one line; others split selling from marketing; many combine into 'SG&A'. SaaS companies often have selling expenses as 40-60% of revenue in growth phase.

examples.treatment: Marketing and sales
Selling, general and administrative expenses (combined)
Selling, general and administrative
Selling, general and administrative expenses

nodes.label: ADVERTISING & MARKETING
nodes.formula_human: Digital Advertising + Content Marketing & SEO + Marketing Software & Tools + Marketing Agency Fees + Traditional / Offline Advertising + Brand Sponsorships & Events
nodes.formula_machine: fintree:DigitalAdvertising + fintree:ContentMarketingSeo + fintree:MarketingSoftwareTools + fintree:MarketingAgencyFees + fintree:TraditionalOfflineAdvertising + fintree:BrandSponsorshipsEvents
nodes.definition: Paid media and brand-building expenditures designed to generate demand.
nodes.example: A DTC e-commerce company spends $5M on digital ads (Google/Meta), $1.2M on content and SEO, $800K on marketing tools (HubSpot, Mixpanel), $600K on agency fees, $2M on TV/print, and $400K on sponsorships, totaling $10M in advertising and marketing.
nodes.classification_notes: Under ASC 720-35, advertising costs are generally expensed as incurred or when advertising first takes place. Direct-response advertising that meets specific criteria may be capitalized. Companies must disclose total advertising expense. Cooperative advertising arrangements with customers may be treated as revenue reductions rather than selling expenses. Internal marketing staff salaries are typically classified under sales compensation, not advertising.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new product launch requiring go-to-market campaign, (2) competitive pressure driving increased ad spend, (3) expansion into new markets or geographies, (4) shift from organic to paid acquisition channels, (5) seasonal campaigns (holiday, back-to-school)
playbook.if_decreased: (1) budget cuts during economic downturn, (2) improved marketing efficiency (lower CAC), (3) shift from paid to organic channels, (4) reduced campaign activity in off-peak periods, (5) consolidation of marketing tools and agency relationships

comparability.variations: Advertising expense disclosure is required by ASC 720-35 but the level of granularity varies. Consumer-facing companies (CPG, retail) typically spend 5-15% of revenue on advertising; B2B SaaS companies spend 15-40% of revenue on total sales & marketing. Some companies report advertising as a single number in footnotes; others provide detailed breakdowns by channel.

examples.treatment: Discloses advertising spend separately (~$7-8B annually); largest single ad spender globally
Reports Sales and marketing expense; relatively low as % of revenue (~10%) given inbound demand model
Reports Sales and marketing; advertising spend disclosed in footnotes as major component (~40% of S&M)

nodes.label: Brand Sponsorships & Events
nodes.definition: Sponsorship of events, conferences, or organizations for brand visibility.
nodes.example: A fintech company pays $250K to sponsor a major industry conference (keynote naming rights), $100K for a local tech meetup series sponsorship, and $50K for a charity gala presenting sponsorship, totaling $400K in brand sponsorships.
nodes.classification_notes: Sponsorship costs are expensed as incurred or over the sponsorship period. Multi-year sponsorship agreements should be expensed ratably. If the sponsorship includes tangible benefits (booth space, attendee lists), it is an advertising expense; if purely charitable with no benefit, it may be a charitable contribution. Sports stadium naming rights are typically amortized over the contract term. Distinguish from trade show costs — sponsorships are for brand visibility, not direct lead generation.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new multi-year sponsorship deal signed (stadium, conference series), (2) expansion into new markets requiring brand awareness investment, (3) competitive sponsorship escalation in key industry events, (4) IPO or public debut requiring brand visibility, (5) sponsoring major events in a given year (Olympics, World Cup cycles)
playbook.if_decreased: (1) exiting sponsorship agreements at renewal, (2) budget cuts reducing discretionary brand spend, (3) shift from event sponsorships to digital brand campaigns, (4) event cancellations or format changes, (5) renegotiating sponsorship terms at lower rates

comparability.variations: Sponsorship costs are rarely disclosed separately in public filings. Companies with major naming rights deals (stadiums, arenas) may disclose the total commitment in contractual obligations. B2B companies sponsor industry conferences; consumer brands sponsor sports and entertainment. Some companies classify sponsorships under advertising; others under general marketing or even G&A.

examples.treatment: Massive sponsorship spending (F1, extreme sports) embedded in marketing costs; core to brand identity
Major conference sponsor (Dreamforce own event + industry events); included in Marketing and Sales
Olympic and FIFA sponsor; multi-year commitments disclosed in contractual obligations; classified in SG&A

nodes.label: Content Marketing & SEO
nodes.definition: Production of content (blogs, videos, whitepapers) and SEO optimization spend.
nodes.example: A B2B SaaS company spends $300K on blog/whitepaper production, $150K on video content, $100K on SEO tools and consultants (Ahrefs, Moz), and $50K on podcast production, totaling $600K annually in content marketing and SEO.
nodes.classification_notes: Content production costs (freelance writers, video production, graphic design) are expensed as incurred under ASC 720-35. SEO tool subscriptions are period expenses. Internal content team salaries should be classified under sales compensation, not here. Content that is gated behind lead capture forms serves a demand-gen function. Educational content for existing customers may be classified under customer success/support rather than marketing.

playbook.if_increased: (1) strategic investment in inbound/organic demand generation, (2) hiring freelance writers or video producers, (3) new SEO tool subscriptions or agency retainers, (4) content refresh and optimization initiatives, (5) expansion into new content formats (podcasts, webinars, video)
playbook.if_decreased: (1) budget cuts reducing content production volume, (2) shift from outsourced to in-house content production, (3) consolidation of SEO tools, (4) pausing content programs during restructuring, (5) reliance on AI-generated content reducing production costs

comparability.variations: Content marketing and SEO are never separately disclosed in public filings; they are embedded in Sales & Marketing or advertising expense. B2B SaaS companies tend to invest more heavily in content/SEO (inbound model) while DTC companies lean toward paid digital. Content marketing ROI is difficult to attribute, making internal reporting granularity vary widely.

examples.treatment: Pioneer of inbound marketing; significant content/SEO investment embedded in Selling, general and administrative
Low sales & marketing spend (~20% of revenue); content and SEO-driven organic acquisition model
Sales and marketing; extensive educational content and SEO presence for merchant acquisition

nodes.label: Digital Advertising
nodes.definition: Paid search (Google Ads, Bing), social media ads (Meta, LinkedIn, Twitter/X), display, and programmatic advertising.
nodes.example: A DTC brand spending $2M/month on Meta and Google ads.
nodes.classification_notes: Digital advertising is expensed as incurred under ASC 720-35 (the first time the advertising takes place). Includes paid search (SEM), social media ads, display/programmatic, video ads, and retargeting. Excludes organic social media and SEO (those are content marketing). Cooperative advertising credits from vendors should reduce advertising expense, not increase revenue. Click fraud refunds reduce the expense.

playbook.if_increased: (1) increased budget allocation to paid channels for growth, (2) rising cost-per-click (CPC) due to competitive auction dynamics, (3) new product or market launch campaigns, (4) seasonal spending (holiday, back-to-school), (5) expansion to new ad platforms or channels
playbook.if_decreased: (1) budget cuts shifting spend to organic/earned channels, (2) improved targeting reducing wasted spend, (3) lower CPCs from reduced competitive bidding, (4) pausing campaigns during off-peak periods, (5) attribution analysis showing low ROI on certain channels

comparability.variations: Digital ad spend is rarely disclosed separately in 10-K filings; it is embedded in total advertising or S&M expense. DTC brands may spend 60-80% of marketing budget on digital; B2B enterprise companies typically spend 30-50%. Companies disclose total advertising expense in footnotes per ASC 720-35 but not the digital/traditional split.

examples.treatment: Advertising expense disclosed in footnotes; heavily weighted toward Google Shopping and Meta ads
Sales and marketing; famously cut digital brand ads in 2020 and shifted to organic/PR
Sales and marketing; digital performance marketing is the dominant component

nodes.label: Marketing Agency Fees
nodes.definition: Retainer or project fees paid to advertising and marketing agencies.
nodes.example: A consumer brand pays $15K/month retainer to a creative agency ($180K/year), $10K/month to a media buying agency ($120K/year), and $5K/month for a PR firm ($60K/year), totaling $360K in marketing agency fees.
nodes.classification_notes: Agency fees cover creative development, media buying, public relations, branding, and campaign execution. Retainer-based fees are expensed ratably over the service period. Project-based fees are expensed as services are delivered. The media spend managed by the agency (the actual ad dollars) is classified under Digital or Traditional Advertising, not here — only the agency service fee belongs in this account. PR agency costs may also be classified under G&A in some companies.

playbook.if_increased: (1) engaging new agencies for rebranding or campaign launches, (2) increasing retainer scope for additional services, (3) supplementing lean in-house team with agency support, (4) special projects (product launch, IPO communications), (5) expanding to agencies with international market expertise
playbook.if_decreased: (1) building in-house marketing team replacing agency work, (2) consolidating multiple agencies to reduce fees, (3) renegotiating retainer terms downward, (4) pausing discretionary creative projects, (5) shifting from full-service agency to specialized freelancers

comparability.variations: Not separately disclosed in public filings. Consumer brands and CPG companies typically rely heavily on agencies (WPP, Omnicom, Publicis); tech companies increasingly build in-house capabilities. Some companies are shifting from agency-of-record models to project-based engagements, reducing fixed retainer costs.

examples.treatment: Embedded in SG&A; one of the largest agency spenders globally, working with multiple agency networks
Part of Demand creation expense; uses Wieden+Kennedy and other agencies for iconic campaign creative
Included in Sales and marketing; primarily in-house marketing with selective agency use for creative campaigns

nodes.label: Marketing Software & Tools
nodes.definition: Subscriptions to marketing automation, analytics, and CRM platforms (HubSpot, Marketo, etc.).
nodes.example: A mid-market company pays $60K/year for HubSpot Marketing Hub, $24K/year for Mixpanel analytics, $18K/year for Hootsuite social management, and $12K/year for Canva Enterprise, totaling $114K in marketing software subscriptions.
nodes.classification_notes: SaaS subscriptions for marketing tools are expensed as incurred (period cost). Under ASC 350-40, implementation costs for cloud computing arrangements (CCA) may be capitalized if they meet internal-use software criteria. CRM platforms used by both sales and marketing (e.g., Salesforce) should be allocated between selling and G&A. Marketing automation tools used exclusively by marketing belong here; general analytics tools used company-wide may belong in G&A.

playbook.if_increased: (1) adding new marketing platforms or tools to the tech stack, (2) tier upgrades driven by contact/user growth, (3) price increases from SaaS vendors, (4) expanding to new marketing channels requiring dedicated tools, (5) adding AI/ML-powered marketing tools
playbook.if_decreased: (1) martech stack consolidation (reducing redundant tools), (2) vendor renegotiation or competitive switching, (3) downgrading tiers as team shrinks, (4) sunsetting underutilized tools, (5) bringing capabilities in-house with custom solutions

comparability.variations: Marketing software costs are not separately disclosed; they are embedded in Sales & Marketing or SG&A. Tech-forward companies may have martech stacks of 20-50+ tools; traditional companies may use fewer. The average company spends 25-30% of marketing budget on technology (Gartner). CRM costs are often shared between sales and marketing functions.

examples.treatment: Included in operating expenses; as a martech vendor, their own platform costs are minimal (dogfooding)
Embedded in SG&A; significant martech investment for global campaign management
Part of Sales and marketing; heavy use of marketing automation and ABM platforms for enterprise sales

nodes.label: Traditional / Offline Advertising
nodes.definition: TV, radio, print, billboard, and direct mail advertising.
nodes.example: An auto manufacturer spends $8M on national TV spots during NFL season, $2M on print ads in automotive magazines, $1.5M on billboard campaigns in major metro areas, and $500K on direct mail to prior customers, totaling $12M in traditional advertising.
nodes.classification_notes: Under ASC 720-35, broadcast advertising (TV, radio) is expensed when the advertising first takes place (when the commercial airs). Print advertising is expensed when published. Billboard costs are expensed over the display period. Production costs for commercials are expensed when the ad first airs, not when produced. Direct mail costs are expensed when mailed. Prepaid media buys are recorded as prepaid assets until the ads run.

playbook.if_increased: (1) brand awareness campaign with national TV placement, (2) seasonal heavy-up periods (Super Bowl, holiday), (3) new market entry requiring broad reach media, (4) competitive response requiring share-of-voice defense, (5) product launch supported by integrated offline campaign
playbook.if_decreased: (1) shift from traditional to digital channels for better measurability, (2) overall marketing budget cuts, (3) cord-cutting reducing TV advertising effectiveness, (4) move from national to local/regional targeting, (5) elimination of print advertising as readership declines

comparability.variations: Traditional advertising is declining as a share of total ad spend across most industries. CPG and automotive remain heavy users of TV/print. SaaS and tech companies spend minimally on traditional channels. Some companies (like Airbnb) have publicly shifted budgets away from traditional performance marketing to brand-oriented offline media. Total advertising expense is disclosed but not the traditional/digital split.

examples.treatment: Significant TV and print spend embedded in SG&A; disclosed total advertising ~$7.5B annually
Major TV advertiser; advertising costs disclosed as ~$2B+ in insurance segment
Substantial TV, print, and billboard spend embedded in SG&A for vehicle launches and brand campaigns

nodes.label: CUSTOMER ACQUISITION & DEMAND GEN
nodes.formula_human: Free Trial & Demo Costs + Referral & Affiliate Fees
nodes.definition: Direct costs of acquiring new customers outside of advertising (partnerships, trials, referrals).
nodes.example: A SaaS company spends $200K on free trial infrastructure costs for 50K trial users, $150K on referral bonuses ($50 per successful referral for 3,000 conversions), and $100K in affiliate partner payouts, totaling $450K in customer acquisition and demand generation costs.
nodes.classification_notes: Customer acquisition costs that are incremental to obtaining a contract may be capitalized under ASC 340-40 if the amortization period exceeds one year. Non-incremental costs (general marketing, brand advertising) must be expensed as incurred. Free trial costs (hosting, support) are period expenses. Referral fees that are contingent on a signed contract may qualify for capitalization. Affiliate commission structures should be evaluated for ASC 606 principal vs. agent considerations.

playbook.if_increased: (1) scaling free trial or freemium programs to drive top-of-funnel growth, (2) launching or expanding referral programs with higher payouts, (3) adding new affiliate partners or channels, (4) investing in demand-gen events (webinars, workshops), (5) entering new market segments requiring acquisition investment
playbook.if_decreased: (1) improved conversion rates reducing cost-per-acquisition, (2) sunsetting underperforming referral programs, (3) organic growth reducing reliance on paid acquisition, (4) tightening affiliate partner criteria, (5) shifting from acquisition to retention and expansion revenue focus

comparability.variations: Customer acquisition costs are embedded in Sales & Marketing. SaaS companies with freemium models have significant trial infrastructure costs that may appear in COGS (hosting) or Sales & Marketing. Companies report CAC as a non-GAAP KPI but the underlying cost components are not separately disclosed in GAAP financials. Affiliate and referral programs create variable selling costs that scale with revenue.

examples.treatment: Included in Sales and marketing; famous referral program (extra storage) reduced paid acquisition needs
Part of Sales and marketing; freemium-to-paid conversion model with low customer acquisition costs
Embedded in Sales and marketing; heavy rider/driver acquisition subsidies including referral bonuses

nodes.label: Free Trial / Demo Costs
nodes.definition: Costs of providing free trials or demos (infrastructure, support, sales engineering time).
nodes.example: A SaaS company offers 14-day free trials costing $180K/quarter in cloud infrastructure, $60K in sales engineering time for guided demos, and $25K in sandbox environment maintenance.
nodes.classification_notes: Free trial costs are typically classified as sales & marketing since they are customer acquisition costs. If the trial infrastructure is shared with production, allocation is required. Freemium models with perpetual free tiers may warrant COGS classification for the free user base. Sales engineering time for demos is S&M, not R&D.

playbook.if_increased:
1. Higher trial sign-up volumes from expanded marketing campaigns
2. Extended trial durations to improve conversion rates
3. Richer demo environments requiring more infrastructure
4. Hiring additional sales engineers for guided demos
5. Launch of product-led growth strategy with self-serve trials
playbook.if_decreased:
1. Shorter trial periods reducing infrastructure costs
2. Improved trial-to-paid conversion reducing cost per acquisition
3. Shift from resource-intensive guided demos to self-serve
4. Automation of demo environments reducing manual effort

comparability.variations: Most companies bury free trial costs within sales & marketing without separate disclosure. Product-led growth companies may break out trial infrastructure costs. Some companies classify freemium costs in COGS if the free tier is considered part of the service.

examples.treatment: Included free tier and trial infrastructure costs within sales and marketing expense
Reports product-led growth trial costs within sales and marketing, with minimal traditional sales headcount
Reported free-tier hosting costs within cost of revenue during rapid growth period

nodes.label: Referral & Affiliate Fees
nodes.definition: Fees paid to referral partners or affiliates for new customer introductions.
nodes.example: A fintech company pays $650K/quarter to affiliate partners who refer new customers, at $75 per qualified signup through tracked referral links.
nodes.classification_notes: Referral fees are typically classified under S&M as customer acquisition costs. If fees are revenue-sharing arrangements (ongoing % of revenue), they may be classified as cost of revenue instead. Distinguish from reseller discounts and channel partner margins. If paid as commission to employees, classify under sales compensation instead.

playbook.if_increased:
1. Expanded affiliate partner network driving more referral volume
2. Increased per-referral payout rates to attract higher-quality leads
3. Launched new affiliate programs in additional channels or markets
4. Shifted acquisition strategy from paid ads to affiliate/referral model
5. Seasonal campaigns driving higher affiliate-driven signups
playbook.if_decreased:
1. Reduced per-referral payout rates or tightened qualification criteria
2. Terminated underperforming affiliate partnerships
3. Shifted acquisition budget from affiliate to direct channels
4. Organic growth reduced reliance on paid referral programs

comparability.variations: Some companies report affiliate fees within a broader customer acquisition cost line; others separate them. Marketplace businesses may classify referral fees as cost of revenue rather than S&M. Revenue-sharing models create different cost structures than per-action fees.

examples.treatment: Reports referral incentives and affiliate costs within sales and marketing as part of performance marketing spend
Includes rider and driver referral bonuses within sales and marketing expense
Reports referral and affiliate revenue as primary income, with partner fees as cost of revenue on the flip side

nodes.label: SALES FORCE COMPENSATION
nodes.formula_human: Sales Salaries & Base Pay + Sales Bonuses & SPIFs + Sales Commissions + Sales Benefits + Payroll Taxes (Sales)
nodes.definition: All compensation for the sales team, including direct and indirect selling costs.
nodes.example: A mid-market SaaS company with 50 sales reps pays $5M in base salaries, $2M in commissions, $800K in bonuses/SPIFs, and $1.5M in benefits and payroll taxes, totaling $9.3M in sales force compensation.
nodes.classification_notes: Sales compensation may be classified under Selling Expenses or combined into SG&A. Commission costs may be capitalized under ASC 340-40 if the amortization period exceeds one year. Stock-based compensation for sales employees is sometimes carved out separately. The split between sales vs. non-sales compensation can be discretionary for hybrid roles (e.g., sales engineers).

playbook.if_increased: (1) sales team expansion with new hires, (2) higher commission payouts from strong bookings, (3) compensation plan changes (higher base or OTE), (4) increased SPIF programs to push specific products, (5) benefits cost inflation (healthcare premiums)
playbook.if_decreased: (1) sales team attrition or layoffs, (2) lower commissions from reduced bookings, (3) compensation restructuring (lower rates), (4) shift from direct sales to channel/partner model, (5) hiring freeze on open sales positions

comparability.variations: Most companies do not separately disclose sales force compensation as a line item; it is embedded in Sales & Marketing or SG&A. Companies with high variable compensation (SaaS, financial services) show more revenue-correlated patterns. Some companies capitalize commissions under ASC 340-40, creating timing differences vs. those that expense as incurred.

examples.treatment: Embedded in Marketing and Sales expense; commissions capitalized per ASC 340-40
Included in Cloud services and license support expenses and Sales and marketing
Included in Selling, general and administrative with commissions capitalized

nodes.label: Payroll Taxes — Sales
nodes.definition: Employer payroll taxes attributable to sales compensation.
nodes.example: A SaaS company pays $420K/year in employer FICA and state unemployment taxes on $5.5M in sales team base salaries and commissions.
nodes.classification_notes: Includes employer payroll taxes on both base salary and variable compensation (commissions, bonuses) for sales staff. Commissions subject to payroll tax create variability tied to sales performance. Does not include benefits or SBC, which are tracked in separate line items.

playbook.if_increased:
1. Sales team expansion increasing total payroll tax base
2. Higher commissions paid driving additional payroll tax on variable comp
3. Base salary increases for existing sales reps
4. Hired sales staff in higher-tax jurisdictions
playbook.if_decreased:
1. Sales force reductions or restructuring
2. Shifted to independent sales agents (1099) not subject to employer taxes
3. Lower commissions paid due to missed sales targets
4. Relocated sales operations to lower-tax states

comparability.variations: Most companies bundle sales payroll taxes within total S&M expense. The mix of base vs. variable compensation affects payroll tax variability. Companies with large international sales teams face different employer tax rates by country.

examples.treatment: Includes sales payroll taxes within total selling and marketing expense without separate line-item disclosure
Bundles sales team payroll taxes into sales and marketing personnel costs
Reports payroll taxes within S&M expense, with significant variability from commission-heavy sales compensation model

nodes.label: Sales Benefits
nodes.definition: Health insurance, retirement, and other benefits for sales employees.
nodes.example: A company with 40 sales employees pays $12K/year per employee in health insurance premiums ($480K), $4K/year in 401(k) matching ($160K), and $2K/year in other benefits ($80K), totaling $720K in sales benefits.
nodes.classification_notes: Benefits allocated to sales employees should be classified under selling expenses; benefits for G&A or R&D staff go to their respective categories. Includes health/dental/vision insurance, 401(k) matching, life insurance, disability, and other employer-paid benefits. Does not include stock-based compensation (reported separately under ASC 718). Post-retirement benefits for sales employees follow ASC 715.

playbook.if_increased: (1) sales headcount growth increasing total benefits cost, (2) healthcare premium inflation (typically 5-8% annually), (3) enhanced benefits package to attract sales talent, (4) higher 401(k) match rates, (5) geographic expansion into states/countries with higher mandated benefits
playbook.if_decreased: (1) sales team reductions lowering headcount, (2) shift to high-deductible health plans reducing employer premiums, (3) reduced 401(k) match or employer contributions, (4) transition of sales reps to contractor/1099 status, (5) benefits plan renegotiation with carriers

comparability.variations: Benefits costs are never separately disclosed for sales employees in public filings. They are embedded in total Sales & Marketing or SG&A. International companies face significantly different benefits cost structures (e.g., European social charges can be 30-45% of salary vs. US employer benefits at 15-25%). Companies using independent sales reps or channel partners have minimal benefits costs.

examples.treatment: Embedded in Marketing and Sales; significant benefits load for ~30K+ sales employees
Included in Sales and marketing; European social charges add significant per-head cost
Part of Sales and marketing; remote-first model with location-adjusted benefits

nodes.label: Sales Bonuses & SPIFs
nodes.definition: Non-commission variable pay (quotas bonuses, sales performance incentive funds for specific product pushes).
nodes.example: A SaaS company runs a Q4 SPIF paying $500 per new logo closed, costing $150K across 300 deals, plus $600K in quarterly quota attainment bonuses for reps exceeding 100% of target.
nodes.classification_notes: Bonuses and SPIFs are distinct from commissions — commissions are tied to specific deal revenue, while bonuses/SPIFs reward specific behaviors or threshold attainment. SPIFs are typically short-term (days to weeks) and targeted at specific products or activities. Unlike commissions, bonuses/SPIFs are generally not subject to ASC 340-40 capitalization because they are not incremental costs of obtaining a specific contract. Accrue ratably when probable and estimable under ASC 710-10.

playbook.if_increased: (1) strong quota attainment triggering more bonus payouts, (2) new SPIF programs launched to drive specific product adoption, (3) bonus plan changes with higher payout thresholds, (4) Q4 accelerators kicking in for over-quota performance, (5) management adding retention bonuses for top performers
playbook.if_decreased: (1) weak sales performance reducing bonus pool payouts, (2) SPIF programs discontinued or reduced, (3) restructured bonus plans with higher thresholds, (4) shift from bonus-heavy to commission-heavy compensation, (5) cost-cutting measures eliminating discretionary incentives

comparability.variations: Not separately disclosed by public companies; embedded in total sales compensation within Sales & Marketing or SG&A. Companies vary widely in their use of bonuses vs. commissions vs. SPIFs. Hardware companies tend to use more SPIFs; SaaS companies lean toward commission-heavy plans with fewer discretionary bonuses.

examples.treatment: Embedded in Sales and marketing; uses quota bonuses and product-specific SPIFs for Azure push
Included in Sales and marketing; known for aggressive SPIF programs on new product launches
Part of Sales and marketing expense; bonus accelerators for above-quota performance

nodes.label: Sales Commissions
nodes.formula_human: Commission rate × qualifying sales or bookings
nodes.definition: Variable compensation paid to sales personnel based on closed deals, bookings, or revenue targets. Under ASC 340-40, incremental costs of obtaining a contract (including commissions) may be capitalized and amortized over the expected customer benefit period if the amortization period exceeds one year.
nodes.example: A SaaS company paying 10% first-year commission on a $500K ACV deal recognizes $50K commission expense (or capitalizes and amortizes over 3-year expected customer life at ~$16.7K/year).
nodes.classification_notes: Under ASC 340-40, commissions that are incremental costs of obtaining a contract must be capitalized if the expected amortization period exceeds one year. Companies may use a practical expedient to expense commissions as incurred if the amortization period is one year or less. Capitalized commissions are amortized on a systematic basis consistent with the pattern of transfer of goods/services. Renewal commissions at lower rates may be treated differently from new-deal commissions.

playbook.if_increased: (1) higher bookings/revenue driving proportional commission payouts, (2) sales team expansion, (3) commission plan changes (higher rates or accelerators), (4) large enterprise deal closings with premium commission rates, (5) shift in mix toward new business vs. renewals (new typically pays higher)
playbook.if_decreased: (1) lower bookings volume, (2) sales team attrition not backfilled, (3) commission plan restructuring (lower rates), (4) shift toward renewal-heavy mix (lower commission rates), (5) increased use of channel partners (partner margins vs. direct commissions)

comparability.variations: Some companies report commissions within Sales & Marketing; others embed them in SG&A. ASC 340-40 capitalization creates timing differences — a company capitalizing commissions shows lower current-period expense but carries a deferred asset on the balance sheet.

examples.treatment: Capitalized as 'Deferred commissions' on balance sheet, amortized over 4 years for new contracts and 2 years for renewals in Marketing and Sales
Not separately disclosed — embedded in SG&A (primarily retail and online sales, minimal traditional commission structure)
Capitalized per ASC 340-40, amortized in Selling, general and administrative over estimated customer benefit period

nodes.label: Sales Salaries & Base Pay
nodes.definition: Fixed salary component for sales representatives and account executives.
nodes.example: A SaaS company pays 30 account executives an average base salary of $85K each, totaling $2.55M annually in sales base pay before variable compensation.
nodes.classification_notes: Base salary for sales roles is a fixed cost regardless of sales performance. Classify under selling expenses only for roles primarily dedicated to selling (AEs, SDRs, sales managers). Hybrid roles (sales engineers, customer success with upsell responsibilities) may require allocation between selling and G&A or COGS. Stock-based compensation is typically reported separately.

playbook.if_increased: (1) net new sales hires added to the team, (2) annual merit increases or cost-of-living adjustments, (3) market-rate adjustments to remain competitive, (4) promotion of SDRs to AE roles at higher base, (5) geographic expansion into higher-cost markets
playbook.if_decreased: (1) sales team layoffs or attrition not backfilled, (2) shift to more variable-heavy compensation plans (lower base, higher commission), (3) offshoring or nearshoring SDR roles, (4) hiring freeze on open positions, (5) organizational restructuring reducing sales headcount

comparability.variations: Base salary as a percentage of on-target earnings (OTE) varies significantly. Enterprise SaaS typically uses 50/50 base-to-variable split; transactional sales may be 30/70. Not separately disclosed by public companies — embedded in total sales & marketing or SG&A compensation.

examples.treatment: Embedded in Marketing and Sales; enterprise reps with ~50/50 base/variable OTE
Included in Sales and marketing expense; not separately disclosed
Part of Sales and marketing; direct sales model with significant base pay component

nodes.label: SHIPPING & DISTRIBUTION
nodes.formula_human: Outbound Freight & Shipping + Distribution Center Costs
nodes.definition: Costs of delivering goods to customers (freight-out). SELLING expense — distinct from freight-in on materials, which is COGS.
nodes.example: An e-commerce company spends $3M on UPS/FedEx outbound parcel shipping, $1.5M on distribution center lease and staffing, and $500K on last-mile delivery services, totaling $5M in shipping and distribution costs.
nodes.classification_notes: Under ASC 606-10-25-18B, shipping and handling after control transfers to the customer may be treated as a fulfillment cost (expense) rather than a separate performance obligation. Companies can elect to classify shipping costs in COGS or in selling expenses — this is a significant comparability issue. Freight-OUT (to customers) is a selling expense; freight-IN (from suppliers) is COGS. Companies must disclose their shipping and handling cost policy. Free shipping offers increase this cost line.

playbook.if_increased: (1) higher order volume driving more shipments, (2) carrier rate increases (fuel surcharges, peak-season pricing), (3) shift to faster shipping methods (next-day, same-day), (4) expansion to new geographies with higher shipping costs, (5) free shipping promotions increasing company-borne costs
playbook.if_decreased: (1) lower order volume, (2) negotiated carrier rate reductions from volume commitments, (3) shift from individual shipments to consolidated freight, (4) opening distribution centers closer to customers, (5) passing shipping costs to customers (charging for shipping)

comparability.variations: Major comparability issue: some companies classify outbound shipping in COGS, others in selling expenses. Amazon classifies shipping costs in COGS; many manufacturers include it in selling expenses. ASC 606 allows companies to elect either treatment. When comparing companies, always check the shipping cost classification policy disclosed in the accounting policies footnote.

examples.treatment: Shipping costs included in Cost of Sales (~$90B+); separate line item in income statement
Customer service and merchant fees (includes shipping) shown separately; also significant costs in COGS
Shipping and handling costs included in SG&A, not COGS; disclosed in accounting policies

nodes.label: Distribution Center Costs
nodes.definition: Operating costs of distribution centers handling finished goods awaiting delivery.
nodes.example: A consumer goods company operates 5 distribution centers with combined annual costs of $18M including warehouse labor, utilities, equipment, and facility leases.
nodes.classification_notes: Some companies classify distribution costs in COGS (product companies) while others put them in SG&A (when viewed as selling costs). Under ASC 330, distribution costs after production are period costs unless the company elects to include them in inventory. Third-party logistics (3PL) fees are a common alternative to owned distribution centers.

playbook.if_increased:
1. Opening new distribution centers to expand geographic coverage
2. Volume growth requiring additional warehouse labor and shifts
3. Rising real estate and lease costs in distribution markets
4. Investment in warehouse automation (robotics, conveyors)
5. Seasonal peak staffing for holiday fulfillment
playbook.if_decreased:
1. Consolidation of distribution centers for efficiency
2. Outsourcing to third-party logistics (3PL) providers
3. Automation reducing warehouse labor requirements
4. Renegotiated facility leases at lower rates

comparability.variations: Retailers and manufacturers differ on whether distribution costs sit in COGS or SG&A. Some companies operate their own facilities while others use 3PL exclusively. E-commerce companies may show fulfillment as a separate line item.

examples.treatment: Reports fulfillment costs as a separate operating expense line, including distribution center labor, facilities, and equipment
Includes distribution center costs within cost of sales
Reports distribution costs within SG&A, separately disclosing the logistics and warehousing component

nodes.label: Outbound Freight & Shipping
nodes.definition: Third-party shipping costs to deliver products to customers.
nodes.example: A manufacturer ships 10,000 orders per month via UPS Ground at an average cost of $12 per shipment, plus 500 expedited shipments at $35 each, totaling $137.5K monthly ($1.65M annually) in outbound freight costs.
nodes.classification_notes: Outbound freight (freight-out) is the cost of shipping finished goods to customers. This is a selling expense, distinct from freight-in (inbound shipping of materials from suppliers, which is COGS). Under ASC 606-10-25-18B, shipping occurring after control transfers to the customer is a fulfillment cost. Companies may include or exclude fuel surcharges, insurance, and handling fees. If the company charges customers for shipping, the revenue is reported in Net Revenue and the cost here.

playbook.if_increased: (1) higher order volume driving proportional shipping cost increase, (2) carrier rate increases including fuel surcharges, (3) customers requesting expedited or premium shipping, (4) heavier/bulkier product mix increasing per-unit shipping costs, (5) international shipping expansion with higher rates
playbook.if_decreased: (1) lower order volume reducing total shipping costs, (2) negotiated volume discounts with carriers, (3) shift to slower/cheaper shipping methods, (4) optimized packaging reducing dimensional weight charges, (5) regional distribution reducing average shipping distance

comparability.variations: Classification of outbound freight varies significantly between companies. Some include it in COGS, others in selling expenses, and some report it as a separate line item. This is one of the most important comparability adjustments when benchmarking companies. Check the accounting policy note for classification. Companies offering free shipping absorb this entirely; those charging for shipping offset it partially with shipping revenue.

examples.treatment: Outbound shipping included in Cost of Sales; reported shipping costs of ~$90B in 2023
As a carrier, outbound shipping is COGS (purchased transportation); own delivery is operating cost
Shipping costs included in SG&A; significant cost given heavy pet food/supplies shipments

nodes.label: TRADE SHOWS & SALES EVENTS
nodes.formula_human: Trade Show Materials & Setup + Booth / Exhibit Space + Event Travel & Entertainment
nodes.definition: Costs of exhibiting at or hosting trade shows, industry conferences, and sales events.
nodes.example: A B2B software company spending $300K on a booth at Dreamforce.
nodes.classification_notes: Trade show costs are expensed when incurred (booth rental, setup, travel). Prepaid booth deposits are recorded as prepaid assets until the event occurs. If an event is canceled, deposits that are nonrefundable should be expensed immediately. Company-hosted events (user conferences, SKOs) are also classified here. Distinguish from brand sponsorships — trade shows involve direct exhibiting and lead capture, while sponsorships are for brand visibility.

playbook.if_increased: (1) attending more industry conferences for pipeline generation, (2) upgrading booth size or placement (island vs. inline booth), (3) hosting proprietary user conferences or roadshows, (4) new market entry requiring conference presence, (5) larger event investments with speaking slots and after-parties
playbook.if_decreased: (1) reducing conference attendance to cut costs, (2) shifting to virtual or hybrid events, (3) downgrading booth presence or sharing booths with partners, (4) event cancellations, (5) analysis showing low ROI from specific trade shows

comparability.variations: Trade show costs are embedded in Sales & Marketing or SG&A and not separately disclosed. B2B companies (industrial, enterprise software) invest heavily in trade shows; DTC and consumer companies invest more in advertising. Some companies host their own major user conferences (Salesforce Dreamforce, AWS re:Invent) which represent significant event costs. Trade show spending is highly seasonal, concentrated in Q1 and Q3.

examples.treatment: Hosts Dreamforce ($30M+ annual cost); trade show costs embedded in Marketing and Sales
Major trade show presence at ConExpo and bauma; included in SG&A
Active at RSA Conference and Black Hat; trade show costs in Sales and marketing

nodes.label: Booth / Exhibit Space
nodes.definition: Rental fees for trade show floor space.
nodes.example: A cybersecurity company rents a 20x30 island booth at RSA Conference for $85K, a 10x10 inline booth at Black Hat for $12K, and a corner booth at Gartner Security Summit for $25K, totaling $122K in booth and exhibit space rental fees.
nodes.classification_notes: Booth rental fees are expensed when the event takes place, not when the deposit is paid. Prepaid booth deposits are recorded as prepaid assets. Booth types vary significantly in cost: inline (10x10, $3-15K), peninsula (20x20, $20-50K), island ($50-200K+). Fees typically include floor space, basic carpet, and exhibitor badges; electricity, internet, and other services are additional. If the event is canceled and the deposit is nonrefundable, expense the deposit when cancellation is confirmed.

playbook.if_increased: (1) attending more conferences and trade shows, (2) upgrading booth size for greater visibility, (3) venue price increases from event organizers, (4) premium placement fees (near entrance, high-traffic areas), (5) expansion into international trade shows
playbook.if_decreased: (1) reducing the number of events attended, (2) downgrading booth size to smaller footprint, (3) sharing exhibit space with partners, (4) shifting to virtual-only attendance (speaking slots without booth), (5) negotiating multi-event packages with show organizers

comparability.variations: Not separately disclosed in public filings; embedded in total Sales & Marketing or SG&A. Major industry conferences (CES, RSA, NRF, HIMSS) charge premium rates for floor space. Island booths at major conferences can cost $100K+ for space alone. B2B and industrial companies typically spend more on booth space than consumer brands.

examples.treatment: Major CES presence with large island booths; exhibit costs included in SG&A
Large presence at RSA and .conf user conference; booth costs in Sales and marketing
Significant ag and construction trade show booths; embedded in SG&A

nodes.label: Event Travel & Entertainment
nodes.definition: Travel, lodging, and entertainment for sales staff attending events.
nodes.example: A SaaS company sends 15 sales reps to AWS re:Invent at $4,500 per person ($67.5K total): $15K flights, $22.5K hotel (5 nights), $15K meals, $15K event dinners and entertainment with prospects.
nodes.classification_notes: This is a selling expense (under Trade Shows & Sales Events), not G&A. Includes airfare, hotel, ground transportation, meals, and client entertainment associated with trade shows, conferences, and sales events. Travel for G&A staff (executives, HR, finance) should be classified under General Corporate Overhead travel. Entertainment expenses are generally non-deductible for tax (post-TCJA 2017).

playbook.if_increased: (1) expanded trade show and conference participation, (2) larger sales team attending more events, (3) travel cost inflation (flights, hotels), (4) hosting proprietary events (user conferences, customer summits), (5) international events requiring long-haul travel
playbook.if_decreased: (1) shift to virtual events reducing travel, (2) budget cuts pulling back on event attendance, (3) smaller sales team, (4) selective event participation focusing on highest-ROI events, (5) co-locating events to reduce separate travel

comparability.variations: Enterprise SaaS and tech companies spend heavily on events (AWS re:Invent, Dreamforce, CES). Manufacturing companies attend industry trade shows (IMTS, FABTECH). Some companies classify all event costs together (booth + travel + entertainment); others split by type. Virtual event shift during COVID reduced this cost significantly; it has partially recovered.

examples.treatment: Dreamforce is both revenue (sponsorships) and a major sales/marketing expense; event travel in selling expenses
Conference attendance (AMA, specialty medical conferences) is critical for sales; classified in selling expenses

nodes.label: Trade Show Materials & Setup
nodes.definition: Display materials, signage, collateral, and setup/teardown costs.
nodes.example: A B2B software company spends $25K on banner displays and signage, $15K on printed brochures and data sheets, $10K on promotional swag (t-shirts, pens), and $8K on booth setup/teardown labor, totaling $58K for a major conference.
nodes.classification_notes: Materials and setup costs are expensed when incurred or at the time of the event. Reusable booth structures and displays may be capitalized as fixed assets and depreciated if they have a useful life exceeding one year and meet the capitalization threshold. Printed materials (brochures, data sheets) are expensed when distributed. Promotional items (swag, giveaways) are advertising costs expensed when distributed. Setup and teardown labor from event services companies is a period expense.

playbook.if_increased: (1) upgraded booth design with custom fabrication, (2) more events on the calendar requiring new materials, (3) rebranding necessitating new signage and collateral, (4) higher-quality promotional items, (5) adding interactive technology (demo stations, LED walls) to booth
playbook.if_decreased: (1) reusing existing booth materials across multiple events, (2) shifting to digital collateral (QR codes, tablets) instead of print, (3) attending fewer events, (4) simplifying booth design, (5) reducing promotional item quantity or quality

comparability.variations: Not separately disclosed in public filings; embedded in Sales & Marketing or SG&A. Companies with heavy trade show presence (industrial, medical devices, enterprise tech) have higher material costs. Companies increasingly shifting to digital/virtual booth experiences, reducing physical material costs but increasing technology costs.

examples.treatment: Significant trade show material costs for Hannover Messe and other industrial fairs; included in SG&A
Cybersecurity conference materials (RSA, Black Hat); embedded in Sales and marketing
Medical device trade show displays and demo equipment; included in SG&A

nodes.label: General & Administrative Expenses (G&A)
nodes.formula_human: Executive Compensation + HR + Finance & Accounting + Legal + Office & Facilities + IT + General Corporate Overhead
nodes.formula_machine: fintree:ExecutiveManagementCompensation + fintree:HumanResources + fintree:FinanceAccounting + fintree:LegalCompliance + fintree:OfficeFacilitiesCorporate + fintree:InformationTechnology + fintree:GeneralCorporateOverhead
nodes.definition: The overhead costs of running the corporate organization — all costs not directly attributable to selling or producing. Sometimes called 'corporate overhead.' Includes executive management, finance, legal, HR, IT, and office operations.
nodes.example: Amazon describes G&A as 'payroll and related expenses; facilities and equipment; professional fees; and other general corporate costs for accounting, finance, tax, legal, and HR.'
nodes.classification_notes: Many companies combine G&A with Selling Expenses into 'SG&A' (Selling, General and Administrative). The split between selling and G&A is discretionary. Stock-based compensation for G&A employees is typically included here.

playbook.if_increased: (1) executive hiring or compensation increases, (2) office space expansion, (3) increased legal/compliance costs, (4) new ERP or IT system implementations, (5) audit fee increases for public company requirements
playbook.if_decreased: (1) headcount reductions in corporate functions, (2) office consolidation or shift to remote work, (3) renegotiated vendor contracts, (4) automation of back-office processes, (5) outsourcing of functions

comparability.variations: Reporting of G&A varies significantly. Some companies report SG&A combined; others break out S&M and G&A separately. Tech companies often have high G&A due to stock-based compensation.

examples.treatment: General and administrative
Selling, general and administrative expenses (combined)
Noninterest expense (includes all operating costs)

nodes.label: EXECUTIVE & MANAGEMENT COMPENSATION
nodes.formula_human: Executive Salaries + Executive Bonuses & Incentive Pay + Executive Benefits & Perquisites + Stock-Based Compensation (G&A)
nodes.definition: Compensation for C-suite executives and senior management whose roles span the entire business rather than a single function.
nodes.example: A public tech company pays its CEO $1.2M salary, $2.5M bonus, $800K benefits/perks, and $8M in stock-based compensation, totaling $12.5M in executive comp.
nodes.classification_notes: Proxy statement (DEF 14A) provides detailed named executive officer (NEO) compensation. Stock-based compensation is often the largest component for tech companies. Some companies allocate a portion of exec comp to functional areas (R&D, Sales) based on time spent.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new C-suite hires or expanded executive team, (2) stock price appreciation increasing SBC expense, (3) above-target bonus payouts due to strong performance, (4) retention packages or sign-on bonuses, (5) increased perquisites or benefits
playbook.if_decreased: (1) executive departures not replaced, (2) stock price decline reducing SBC mark-to-market, (3) below-target bonus payouts, (4) salary freezes or voluntary pay cuts, (5) forfeiture of unvested equity upon departure

comparability.variations: Tech companies have much higher SBC component. Financial services firms pay large cash bonuses. Some companies allocate executive comp across functions rather than all to G&A. Proxy disclosures provide standardized NEO compensation tables.

examples.treatment: CEO Tim Cook comp primarily stock-based; disclosed in proxy; allocated to G&A
CEO compensation heavily cash/bonus-weighted; reported within compensation and benefits
CEO comp primarily performance-based stock options; significant SBC charges in G&A

nodes.label: Executive Benefits & Perquisites
nodes.definition: Benefits specific to executive roles (supplemental insurance, car allowances, housing, etc.).
