nodes.example: A CEO receives $150K in perquisites including $60K personal security, $40K car allowance, $30K supplemental life insurance, and $20K financial planning services.
nodes.classification_notes: Perquisites exceeding $10K per item for NEOs must be disclosed individually in proxy statement per SEC rules. Common perks include personal security, company aircraft use, car allowances, housing allowances, financial planning, supplemental insurance, and club memberships. Relocation packages for new executives are also classified here.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new executive hires with relocation packages, (2) enhanced security requirements for executives, (3) board approval of new perquisite programs, (4) increased personal use of company aircraft, (5) supplemental retirement plan contributions
playbook.if_decreased: (1) elimination of perquisite programs to improve optics, (2) executive departures, (3) policy changes restricting personal aircraft use, (4) industry trend toward reducing disclosed perquisites

comparability.variations: Perquisite levels vary significantly by industry and company size. Financial services and energy companies tend to offer more perks. Tech companies increasingly minimize disclosed perquisites. SEC requires itemized disclosure in proxy for NEOs above $10K thresholds.

examples.treatment: CEO perquisites include personal security, personal use of company aircraft; disclosed in proxy All Other Compensation column
Minimal executive perquisites; CEO famously takes $100K salary with minimal additional benefits

nodes.label: Executive Bonuses & Incentive Pay
nodes.definition: Annual performance bonuses for executives tied to company-wide metrics.
nodes.example: A CFO earns a $500K annual cash bonus (target 75% of base salary) after the company hits 110% of its revenue target and 105% of EBITDA target.
nodes.classification_notes: Bonuses are accrued when probable and estimable (ASC 710-10-25). Short-term incentive plans (STIPs) are typically annual cash bonuses. Long-term incentive plans (LTIPs) may be cash or equity. Distinguish from stock-based compensation which is a separate line. Sign-on bonuses for new executives should be amortized over the expected service period.

playbook.if_increased: (1) company exceeding performance targets triggering above-target payouts, (2) new executive hires with sign-on bonuses, (3) special retention bonuses during M&A, (4) expansion of incentive plan metrics or participation, (5) catch-up accruals for updated performance estimates
playbook.if_decreased: (1) company missing performance targets resulting in zero or below-target payouts, (2) restructuring or elimination of bonus programs, (3) shift from cash bonuses to equity compensation, (4) executive departures forfeiting bonus eligibility, (5) tightening of bonus criteria by compensation committee

comparability.variations: Financial services firms pay significantly higher bonuses (often multiples of base salary). Tech companies tend to weight equity over cash bonuses. Bonus structures disclosed in proxy statement under Non-Equity Incentive Plan Compensation.

examples.treatment: Compensation and benefits includes large discretionary bonuses; dominant comp component for senior bankers
CEO historically declined cash bonus; other executives receive modest bonuses relative to equity awards

nodes.label: Executive Salaries (CEO, CFO, COO, etc.)
nodes.definition: Base salary for top executive officers.
nodes.example: A mid-cap company pays its CEO $950K, CFO $650K, COO $600K, and CTO $625K in base salaries, totaling $2.825M in executive salaries.
nodes.classification_notes: Base salary is the fixed component of executive pay. Disclosed in the proxy statement Summary Compensation Table. Salary alone is usually a small fraction of total comp for public company executives. Includes employer payroll taxes attributable to executive salaries.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new C-suite hires expanding the executive team, (2) annual merit increases approved by compensation committee, (3) promotions to executive level, (4) cost-of-living adjustments in high-cost markets
playbook.if_decreased: (1) executive departures not backfilled, (2) voluntary salary reductions (e.g., during downturns), (3) consolidation of executive roles, (4) shift to lower-cost geographies

comparability.variations: Base salaries are relatively comparable across industries for similar-sized companies. Tech companies often set lower base salaries offset by larger equity grants. Financial services and healthcare tend to have higher base salaries.

examples.treatment: CEO base salary $2.5M; disclosed in proxy Summary Compensation Table; classified in G&A
CEO base salary $1.3M; retail executives have moderate base salaries with large bonus potential

nodes.label: Stock-Based Compensation — G&A
nodes.definition: Expense recognized for equity awards (RSUs, stock options) granted to G&A employees (ASC 718).
nodes.example: A $1M RSU grant vesting over 4 years = $250K/year SBC expense in G&A.
nodes.classification_notes: Non-cash expense recognized under ASC 718 for equity awards granted to G&A employees (executives, finance, HR, legal). Many analysts add SBC back when calculating non-GAAP operating income. CEO and executive RSU grants are typically the largest component. Acceleration of vesting upon M&A or executive departure can cause one-time spikes.

playbook.if_increased:
1. Large new equity grants to executives or new senior hires
2. Rising stock price increasing fair value of new grants
3. Accelerated vesting due to M&A change-of-control provisions
4. Catch-up expense from modified performance-based awards meeting targets
5. Expanded equity compensation to broader G&A employee base
playbook.if_decreased:
1. Prior large grants fully vested reducing ongoing amortization
2. Executive departures causing forfeiture of unvested awards
3. Lower stock price reducing fair value of new option grants
4. Shifted from equity to cash compensation for G&A staff

comparability.variations: SBC is a major non-GAAP adjustment, making GAAP vs. non-GAAP comparisons critical. Tech companies have significantly higher SBC as a percentage of revenue than traditional industries. Some companies allocate SBC across functions; others report a single total SBC line.

examples.treatment: Allocates SBC to G&A and other functions, disclosing total SBC in notes with functional breakdown
Reports SBC within each operating expense category including G&A, with total disclosed in cash flow statement
Reports very high G&A SBC relative to revenue, particularly for executive grants, as a frequent investor concern

nodes.label: FINANCE & ACCOUNTING
nodes.formula_human: Finance & Accounting Staff Compensation + Accounting Software & ERP + External Audit Fees + Tax Advisory & Compliance Fees + Financial Reporting Costs
nodes.definition: Costs of the finance and accounting function, including internal staff and external professional services.
nodes.example: A public company spends $4.2M on its finance function: $2.5M staff compensation, $400K ERP subscriptions, $800K audit fees, $300K tax advisory, and $200K reporting costs.
nodes.classification_notes: Includes both internal finance staff and external professional fees. Audit and tax fees are typically disclosed in the proxy statement under Audit Committee. SEC registrants must disclose audit, audit-related, tax, and all other fees paid to the principal auditor.

playbook.if_increased: (1) IPO or new SEC reporting requirements adding compliance burden, (2) hiring of additional finance staff for SOX compliance, (3) ERP implementation or upgrade, (4) increased audit fees from scope expansion, (5) international tax complexity from global expansion
playbook.if_decreased: (1) automation of accounting processes reducing headcount, (2) renegotiated audit firm fees, (3) simplification of legal entity structure, (4) outsourcing of bookkeeping or tax preparation, (5) consolidation of ERP systems

comparability.variations: Public companies have significantly higher finance costs than private due to SOX compliance, SEC reporting, and audit requirements. Financial services companies have the largest finance departments. Audit fees scale with company complexity, not just size.

examples.treatment: Finance and accounting costs included in General and administrative; audit fees disclosed in proxy
Decentralized finance function; each subsidiary maintains its own accounting with minimal corporate finance staff
Large internal finance and controllers function; included in noninterest expense

nodes.label: Accounting Software & ERP
nodes.definition: Subscriptions to ERP and accounting platforms (SAP, Oracle, NetSuite, QuickBooks).
nodes.example: A mid-market company pays $350K/year for NetSuite ERP ($200K base license + $100K additional modules + $50K annual support), plus $15K for Avalara tax automation.
nodes.classification_notes: Cloud/SaaS ERP subscriptions are operating expenses per ASC 350-40. On-premise ERP license fees may be capitalized. Implementation and customization costs for cloud ERP have specific capitalization rules — internal-use software development costs in the application development stage can be capitalized. Annual maintenance and support fees are expensed as incurred.

playbook.if_increased: (1) ERP migration (e.g., QuickBooks to NetSuite or NetSuite to SAP), (2) adding new ERP modules (inventory, project accounting), (3) multi-entity or multi-currency expansion, (4) implementation consulting fees during ERP projects, (5) vendor price increases on contract renewals
playbook.if_decreased: (1) completing ERP implementation (one-time costs normalize), (2) consolidating multiple accounting systems into one, (3) downgrading from enterprise to mid-market ERP, (4) renegotiated licensing terms, (5) elimination of unused modules

comparability.variations: ERP costs range from $500/month (QuickBooks) to millions/year (SAP S/4HANA). Implementation costs can be 2-5x the annual license cost. Companies using on-premise ERP will show this as depreciation/amortization rather than subscription expense. Some companies classify ERP under IT rather than Finance.

examples.treatment: QuickBooks Online at $1K-$3K/year; minimal ERP costs
SAP S/4HANA or Oracle Cloud at $1M-$10M/year; multi-year implementation projects capitalized

nodes.label: External Audit Fees
nodes.definition: Fees paid to public accounting firms for the annual financial statement audit.
nodes.example: A mid-cap public company paying $1.5M/year to a Big 4 firm for its annual audit.
nodes.classification_notes: SEC registrants must disclose audit fees, audit-related fees, tax fees, and all other fees paid to the principal auditor in the proxy statement. SOX Section 404 internal control audits significantly increase audit costs for public companies. First-year audit fees are typically higher due to transition work. Audit committee pre-approval is required for all services from the auditor.

playbook.if_increased: (1) IPO creating new SEC audit requirements, (2) acquisition adding entities to audit scope, (3) material weakness remediation requiring additional audit procedures, (4) first-year auditor change with transition costs, (5) new accounting standard implementation requiring additional audit work
playbook.if_decreased: (1) auditor rotation leveraging competitive bidding, (2) simplified entity structure reducing audit scope, (3) improved internal controls reducing substantive testing, (4) going private eliminating SEC audit requirements, (5) mature audit relationship reducing new-client premiums

comparability.variations: Audit fees for public companies range from $200K (small-cap) to $100M+ (large complex financial institutions). Big 4 firms charge premiums over mid-tier firms. Financial services and multi-national companies have the highest fees. Private companies pay significantly less. Proxy statement disclosure enables direct comparability.

examples.treatment: Audit fees of approximately $60M+; disclosed in proxy; large scope due to regulatory complexity
Audit fees of $300K-$800K; often uses mid-tier firm; SOX 404(b) exemption for smaller filers

nodes.label: Finance & Accounting Staff Compensation
nodes.definition: Salaries, payroll taxes, and benefits for CFO, controllers, accountants, FP&A staff.
nodes.example: A 500-employee company has a 12-person finance team costing $1.8M in total compensation: $1.4M salaries, $200K benefits, $200K payroll taxes.
nodes.classification_notes: Includes salaries for controllers, staff accountants, FP&A analysts, accounts payable/receivable clerks, and payroll specialists. CFO salary may be included here or under Executive Compensation depending on company policy. Temporary accounting staff during close periods should also be captured here.

playbook.if_increased: (1) hiring additional accountants for SOX compliance or IPO readiness, (2) annual merit increases, (3) adding FP&A headcount for improved business partnering, (4) market salary adjustments for in-demand accounting talent, (5) internalization of previously outsourced bookkeeping
playbook.if_decreased: (1) automation of AP/AR reducing headcount needs, (2) outsourcing bookkeeping to third-party providers, (3) offshoring accounting functions to lower-cost centers, (4) natural attrition not backfilled, (5) consolidation of accounting roles across business units

comparability.variations: Finance team size varies by complexity. Public companies require more staff for SEC reporting and SOX compliance. Companies using outsourced accounting (e.g., fractional CFO services) will show lower staff comp but higher professional fees.

examples.treatment: Finance and accounting staff costs included within General and administrative line
May use fractional CFO and outsourced bookkeeper, showing minimal staff comp

nodes.label: Financial Reporting Costs
nodes.definition: Costs of external financial reporting, XBRL tagging, and SEC filing services.
nodes.example: A public company pays $280K/year for reporting services: $120K financial printer (10-K, 10-Q, proxy), $80K XBRL/iXBRL tagging, $50K transfer agent fees, $30K annual report design and production.
nodes.classification_notes: Includes financial printing services (Donnelley, Merrill), XBRL/iXBRL tagging services, transfer agent fees, annual report production, and SEC EDGAR filing services. IPO-related printing and filing costs are typically capitalized as deferred offering costs. Ongoing reporting costs are expensed as incurred. Private companies have minimal financial reporting costs since they do not file with the SEC.

playbook.if_increased: (1) IPO creating new SEC reporting requirements, (2) new reporting mandates (climate disclosure, cybersecurity disclosure), (3) increased complexity of disclosures, (4) vendor price increases from reporting service providers, (5) special reports or filings (restatements, S-1 amendments)
playbook.if_decreased: (1) going private eliminating SEC filing requirements, (2) in-house XBRL tagging replacing outsourced services, (3) reduced filing complexity, (4) competitive bidding among financial printing vendors, (5) shift to digital-first annual reports reducing print costs

comparability.variations: Only public companies (SEC registrants) incur significant financial reporting costs. Large accelerated filers have more extensive reporting requirements. Foreign private issuers may have different reporting schedules. iXBRL (inline XBRL) is now required for most SEC filers. Private companies typically have near-zero costs in this category.

examples.treatment: Financial reporting costs are immaterial relative to G&A; uses Donnelley for SEC filings
Elevated reporting costs in first year due to complex accounting and frequent filings (S-1, Super 8-K)

nodes.label: Tax Advisory & Compliance Fees
nodes.definition: Fees for external tax preparation, planning, and compliance services.
nodes.example: A multinational company pays $650K/year in tax fees: $250K federal and state tax return preparation, $200K international tax advisory, $120K transfer pricing study, $80K sales tax compliance.
nodes.classification_notes: Tax advisory fees are G&A operating expenses (not income tax expense). These are the cost of preparing and planning taxes, not the taxes themselves. SEC requires disclosure of tax fees paid to the auditor in the proxy. Tax fees related to M&A transactions may be capitalized as transaction costs. Transfer pricing studies for multinational companies are a significant component.

playbook.if_increased: (1) international expansion adding foreign tax jurisdictions, (2) M&A transactions requiring tax structuring, (3) new tax legislation requiring compliance changes (e.g., GILTI, BEAT), (4) IRS audit defense, (5) transfer pricing documentation for new intercompany arrangements
playbook.if_decreased: (1) building internal tax team reducing outside advisory needs, (2) simplification of legal entity structure, (3) tax technology automation reducing preparation costs, (4) resolved IRS audits, (5) consolidated return filing reducing separate entity work

comparability.variations: Tax fees scale with complexity, not just company size. Multinational companies with 50+ jurisdictions pay significantly more. Private companies may outsource all tax work. Tax fees paid to the audit firm are disclosed in the proxy, but fees to other tax advisors are not separately disclosed.

examples.treatment: Complex international tax structure; significant tax advisory fees disclosed in proxy; classified in G&A
Tax return preparation $5K-$20K/year from local CPA firm; minimal advisory fees

nodes.label: GENERAL CORPORATE OVERHEAD
nodes.formula_human: Business Travel & Entertainment + Meals & Entertainment + Subscriptions & Publications + Miscellaneous G&A
nodes.definition: Miscellaneous G&A costs not classified into the above sub-categories.
nodes.example: A mid-size SaaS company incurs $1.2M in general corporate overhead including $450K travel, $180K meals, $70K subscriptions, and $500K miscellaneous.
nodes.classification_notes: Catch-all for G&A costs that do not fit neatly into executive comp, HR, finance, legal, IT, or office/facilities. Companies vary widely in what they classify here vs. in other sub-categories.

playbook.if_increased: (1) loosened travel and entertainment policies, (2) return-to-office or increased in-person meetings, (3) new subscriptions or publications, (4) one-time corporate events or retreats, (5) catch-all reclassifications from other categories
playbook.if_decreased: (1) travel freezes or remote-first policies, (2) corporate expense austerity measures, (3) consolidation of subscriptions and vendor contracts, (4) reclassification of items to more specific G&A sub-categories

comparability.variations: Highly variable across companies. Some lump nearly all non-compensation G&A here; others distribute items to specific functional categories. Travel may appear here or under selling expenses depending on the traveler.

examples.treatment: General corporate overhead included in General and administrative line; travel allocated by function
General and administrative includes miscellaneous corporate costs not allocated to R&D or sales

nodes.label: Business Travel & Entertainment
nodes.definition: Corporate travel, lodging, and business entertainment for non-sales employees.
nodes.example: A consulting firm spends $150K on airfare, $100K on hotel accommodations, $40K on rental cars and rideshares, $30K on client meals and entertainment, and $20K on per diem allowances, totaling $340K annually in business travel and entertainment.
nodes.classification_notes: Travel for non-sales corporate employees (executives, finance, HR, operations) belongs under G&A. Sales-specific travel should be classified under selling expenses instead. Entertainment expenses have limited tax deductibility (50% for meals, 0% for entertainment under IRC Section 274 post-TCJA). Distinguish from trade show travel (which goes under Trade Shows). Company-wide retreats and team-building events may be classified here or under employee benefits depending on nature.

playbook.if_increased: (1) return-to-travel after remote work period, (2) expansion requiring cross-office or cross-region travel, (3) increased client-facing meetings for deal pursuit, (4) inflation in airfare, hotel, and meal costs, (5) company events or all-hands meetings requiring employee travel
playbook.if_decreased: (1) travel restrictions or policy tightening, (2) shift to virtual meetings (Zoom, Teams), (3) headcount reductions, (4) stricter expense approval processes, (5) renegotiated corporate travel rates or preferred vendor discounts

comparability.variations: Travel and entertainment costs are typically embedded in G&A or SG&A and not separately disclosed. Consulting and professional services firms have the highest T&E as a percentage of revenue (5-10%). Remote-first companies have structurally lower T&E. Some companies allocate T&E across functional categories (sales travel to S&M, executive travel to G&A) while others consolidate into a single T&E line within G&A.

examples.treatment: Significant T&E for client site travel; would be a major G&A/SGA component
Major travel costs for consulting engagements; embedded in operating costs
All-remote company with minimal recurring T&E but periodic team offsites; included in G&A

nodes.label: Meals & Entertainment
nodes.definition: Business meals with clients, staff meals, and entertainment (subject to IRS 50% deductibility limit).
nodes.example: A consulting firm spends $220K/year on meals and entertainment: $100K client business meals, $60K team meals and celebrations, $35K entertainment events, $25K holiday parties.
nodes.classification_notes: Business meals are 50% deductible for federal tax (IRC Section 274). Entertainment expenses are generally non-deductible after 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act. Companies often maintain separate GL accounts for meals vs. entertainment for tax reporting purposes. Client-facing meals and entertainment may be classified under Selling Expenses rather than G&A. Company-wide parties and events are typically 100% deductible.

playbook.if_increased: (1) return-to-office increasing in-person meal occasions, (2) increased client entertainment for business development, (3) company events and team-building activities, (4) loosened expense policies, (5) food price inflation
playbook.if_decreased: (1) remote work reducing in-person meals, (2) expense policy tightening during austerity, (3) reduction in client entertainment, (4) cultural shift away from entertainment-heavy business relationships, (5) elimination of company-sponsored meals

comparability.variations: Professional services and financial services firms spend heavily on client meals and entertainment. Tech companies may provide free meals to employees (classified here or as employee benefits). Some companies combine meals & entertainment with travel in a single line. Tax treatment differences (50% meals vs. 0% entertainment deduction) drive separate tracking.

examples.treatment: Significant entertainment and client dining; included in noninterest expense
Free employee meals in cafeterias; classified as employee benefits within G&A

nodes.label: Miscellaneous G&A
nodes.definition: Catch-all for minor G&A costs not warranting a separate line item.
nodes.example: A company records $85K in miscellaneous G&A including $25K bank service charges, $15K postage/courier, $20K charitable donations, and $25K sundry office costs.
nodes.classification_notes: Should be reviewed periodically — if any single item grows material, it should be reclassified to a named line item. Bank fees, postage, charitable contributions, and minor penalties often land here. Tax penalties and fines may require separate disclosure.

playbook.if_increased: (1) growth in sundry costs as company scales, (2) reclassification of items from other categories, (3) one-time penalties or fees, (4) increased charitable contributions
playbook.if_decreased: (1) tighter expense controls and approval processes, (2) reclassification of items to specific G&A sub-categories, (3) elimination of discretionary spend, (4) automation reducing manual processes (e.g., postage)

comparability.variations: Varies widely. Some companies keep this line minimal; others use it as a dumping ground for hard-to-classify costs. Materiality threshold determines what warrants its own line.

examples.treatment: Other costs within Corporate Items and Eliminations
Other (income) expense includes miscellaneous items not classified elsewhere

nodes.label: Subscriptions & Publications
nodes.definition: Industry publications, research subscriptions, and news services for corporate management.
nodes.example: A company pays $95K/year in subscriptions: $30K Wall Street Journal and Financial Times, $25K Gartner research, $20K industry trade publications, $20K professional association memberships (AICPA, bar associations).
nodes.classification_notes: Includes news services (WSJ, Bloomberg News), industry research (Gartner, Forrester), professional memberships and dues (AICPA, bar associations, trade groups), and trade publications. Distinguish from data provider fees (product-embedded data, which is COGS) and software subscriptions (IT). Lobbying-related memberships may be non-deductible for tax purposes.

playbook.if_increased: (1) adding new research services (Gartner, CB Insights), (2) expanding access to more employees, (3) vendor price increases on subscription renewals, (4) joining new industry associations, (5) upgrading from basic to premium research tiers
playbook.if_decreased: (1) budget cuts eliminating discretionary subscriptions, (2) consolidating overlapping research services, (3) reducing seat count for expensive per-user subscriptions, (4) switching to free or lower-cost alternatives, (5) dropping professional association memberships

comparability.variations: Financial services firms have the highest research subscription costs (Bloomberg, S&P, Moody's). Consulting firms invest heavily in research (Gartner, Forrester). Manufacturing and retail companies spend relatively little. Some companies classify research subscriptions under the functional department that uses them.

examples.treatment: Significant research subscription costs (Bloomberg at $24K/user/year); classified as a core business expense
Minimal subscriptions; maybe $500-$2,000/year for trade publications and local business news

nodes.label: HUMAN RESOURCES
nodes.formula_human: HR Staff Compensation + HRIS & HR Software + Employee Training & Development + Recruiting & Hiring Costs
nodes.definition: Costs of the HR function — recruiting, training, employee relations, and HR administration.
nodes.example: A 1,000-employee company spends $2.1M on HR: $1.2M HR staff comp, $250K HRIS software, $350K training programs, and $300K recruiting fees.
nodes.classification_notes: HR costs are driven by total company headcount, not just HR department headcount. Recruiting costs are highly variable — spikes during growth phases. Some companies classify employee training under the functional department rather than centralized HR.

playbook.if_increased: (1) aggressive hiring campaigns requiring more recruiters and fees, (2) implementation of new HRIS platform, (3) expanded training programs for compliance or upskilling, (4) growing company headcount requiring additional HR support, (5) labor law changes requiring new compliance programs
playbook.if_decreased: (1) hiring freezes reducing recruiting costs, (2) layoffs reducing overall HR workload, (3) consolidation of HRIS vendors, (4) shift to self-service HR portals, (5) outsourcing of HR functions (PEO/ASO models)

comparability.variations: Some companies outsource HR entirely through PEOs (Professional Employer Organizations). Tech companies invest heavily in recruiting. Retail/hospitality have high HR costs per dollar of revenue due to turnover. Some companies report HR costs within functional departments rather than centrally.

examples.treatment: People Operations costs included in General and administrative; heavy investment in recruiting and culture
As an HR services provider, distinguishes between HR costs serving clients (COGS) and internal HR (G&A)

nodes.label: Employee Training & Development
nodes.definition: Costs of training programs, workshops, online learning platforms (LinkedIn Learning, Udemy), and conferences for professional development.
nodes.example: A tech company spends $500K on training: $150K LinkedIn Learning licenses, $120K external instructor-led workshops, $80K conference attendance, $100K certification reimbursements, $50K internal LMS platform.
nodes.classification_notes: Training costs are expensed as incurred — they cannot be capitalized as an intangible asset. Some companies allocate training costs to functional departments (R&D training under R&D) rather than centralizing under HR. Mandatory compliance training (safety, harassment prevention) is typically here; sales training may be under S&M.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new compliance training mandates (cybersecurity, DEI), (2) upskilling programs for technology transitions, (3) onboarding surge from rapid hiring, (4) expanded tuition reimbursement program, (5) leadership development programs for high-potentials
playbook.if_decreased: (1) budget cuts during economic downturns (training is often first cut), (2) headcount reductions reducing training volume, (3) shift from paid external training to free internal content, (4) hiring freeze reducing onboarding training needs, (5) consolidation of learning platforms

comparability.variations: Training spend per employee varies widely: $500-$2,000 per year is typical. Highly regulated industries (financial services, healthcare) spend more on mandatory compliance training. Tech companies often offer generous tuition reimbursement. Some companies classify training under the functional department.

examples.treatment: Significant investment in Deloitte University and professional development; classified as a strategic expense
Career Choice program provides tuition for warehouse workers; included in fulfillment and G&A costs

nodes.label: HR Staff Compensation
nodes.definition: Salaries, payroll taxes, and benefits for the HR department.
nodes.example: A 2,000-employee company has an 8-person HR team costing $960K: CHRO $200K, 3 HR business partners at $120K each, 2 recruiters at $100K each, 2 coordinators at $70K each.
nodes.classification_notes: Includes CHRO/VP of HR salary, HR business partners, recruiters, benefits administrators, and HR coordinators. CHRO comp may be in Executive Compensation instead if they are a named executive officer. Internal recruiters are included here; external agency fees go to Recruiting & Hiring Costs.

playbook.if_increased: (1) scaling HR team to support rapid company growth, (2) adding specialized HR roles (DEI, people analytics), (3) hiring internal recruiters to reduce agency dependency, (4) market salary adjustments for HR talent, (5) bringing HR functions in-house from a PEO
playbook.if_decreased: (1) outsourcing HR to a PEO or ASO provider, (2) automating HR processes with self-service tools, (3) layoffs reducing HR team proportionally, (4) attrition not replaced due to improved HR tech efficiency, (5) shared services model consolidating HR across business units

comparability.variations: HR-to-employee ratio varies: typically 1:100 to 1:250. Tech companies often invest more in recruiting staff. Companies using PEOs may show near-zero internal HR staff comp. Ratio is higher in heavily regulated industries requiring more compliance oversight.

examples.treatment: Lean HR team relative to 300K+ employees; focused on compensation and benefits administration
Heavy investment in HR/people ops relative to headcount; classified within G&A

nodes.label: HRIS & HR Software
nodes.definition: Subscriptions to HR information systems, payroll software, and benefits administration platforms (Workday, ADP, Rippling).
nodes.example: A 500-employee company pays $180K/year for Workday HCM ($120K), ADP payroll processing ($35K), and Greenhouse ATS ($25K).
nodes.classification_notes: SaaS HRIS subscriptions are expensed as incurred (ASC 350-40 for cloud computing arrangements). Implementation costs may be capitalized if they meet the criteria. Payroll processing fees (per-employee-per-month) are included here. Distinguish from IT software subscriptions — HRIS is classified under HR, not IT.

playbook.if_increased: (1) company headcount growth increasing per-employee license fees, (2) migration to a more expensive HRIS platform, (3) adding new HR modules (learning management, performance reviews), (4) implementation costs for new system, (5) price increases on multi-year contract renewals
playbook.if_decreased: (1) headcount reductions lowering per-employee costs, (2) vendor consolidation replacing multiple point solutions, (3) renegotiated contract rates, (4) downgrading to a less expensive HRIS tier, (5) shifting payroll processing in-house

comparability.variations: HRIS costs are typically $10-50 per employee per month depending on platform and modules. Enterprise companies using Workday or SAP SuccessFactors pay significantly more than SMBs using Gusto or Rippling. Some companies classify all software under IT rather than functional departments.

examples.treatment: Workday HCM at $30-50 PEPM; costs classified within G&A
Gusto or Rippling at $10-15 PEPM; often combined with IT software subscriptions

nodes.label: Recruiting & Hiring Costs
nodes.definition: External recruiter fees (typically 15–25% of first-year salary), job board postings, background checks.
nodes.example: A company paying a $30K recruiter fee to fill a $120K engineering role.
nodes.classification_notes: External recruiter contingency fees (15-25% of first-year salary) and retained search fees ($100K+ for executives) are expensed when incurred. Job board subscriptions (LinkedIn Recruiter, Indeed) are recurring costs. Background check and drug screening fees are per-hire costs. Relocation costs for new hires may be classified here or under a separate relocation line.

playbook.if_increased: (1) aggressive hiring ramp-up requiring external agency support, (2) executive searches using retained search firms, (3) expanding into new markets requiring local talent acquisition, (4) high turnover driving replacement hiring, (5) competitive labor market increasing agency fees
playbook.if_decreased: (1) hiring freeze eliminating recruiting spend, (2) building internal recruiting team replacing agencies, (3) employee referral programs reducing need for job boards, (4) lower turnover reducing replacement hiring, (5) brand-driven inbound applicant flow reducing sourcing costs

comparability.variations: Recruiting costs are highly variable and cyclical. Hyper-growth companies may spend 15-25% of new-hire first-year comp on recruiting. Mature companies with strong employer brands spend far less. Tech companies in competitive markets have the highest per-hire costs. Some companies capitalize certain onboarding costs.

examples.treatment: Significant recruiting investment during growth phases; sharp reduction during 2023 efficiency year
Extensive campus recruiting programs; high per-hire investment for selective hiring

nodes.label: INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY (IT)
nodes.formula_human: IT Staff Compensation + Software Subscriptions (Corporate) + Hardware & Equipment (Corporate) + Cybersecurity & Compliance Software + IT Infrastructure & Networking
nodes.definition: Costs of corporate IT infrastructure and systems, excluding software used in the production environment (which is COGS for SaaS).
nodes.example: A company's internal email servers, corporate laptops, and business intelligence tools are G&A IT.
nodes.classification_notes: Critical to distinguish corporate IT (G&A) from production IT (COGS). For SaaS companies, hosting and infrastructure serving the product is COGS, while internal corporate tools are G&A. For manufacturing, production floor automation and SCADA systems are manufacturing overhead, not G&A IT.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new ERP or enterprise system implementation, (2) cybersecurity investments post-breach or for compliance, (3) laptop refresh cycle for employees, (4) expansion of corporate software licenses with headcount growth, (5) migration to new IT infrastructure
playbook.if_decreased: (1) vendor consolidation reducing software sprawl, (2) renegotiated multi-year enterprise agreements, (3) headcount reductions lowering license counts, (4) cloud migration eliminating on-premise hardware costs, (5) outsourcing IT support to managed service providers

comparability.variations: IT spend as % of revenue varies by industry: financial services 7-10%, tech companies 5-8%, manufacturing 2-4%. Some companies report IT costs under each functional department rather than centrally. Cloud-first companies have higher opex but lower capex for IT.

examples.treatment: Significant IT investment classified in G&A; distinguishes from client-facing technology services (revenue)
Technology is a core strategic investment; IT costs are a large portion of noninterest expense
Corporate IT in G&A; production floor technology in COGS/manufacturing overhead

nodes.label: Cybersecurity & Compliance Software
nodes.definition: Security software, penetration testing, and compliance tooling for corporate systems.
nodes.example: A mid-size company pays $95K/year for CrowdStrike endpoint protection, $40K/year for Vanta SOC 2 compliance automation, and $25K/year for Tenable vulnerability scanning.
nodes.classification_notes: Corporate security tools belong in G&A. Product-embedded security (e.g., WAF protecting customer-facing app) may belong in COGS. Penetration testing by external firms is a professional services expense. Multi-year licenses may require prepaid treatment. Compliance audit fees (SOC 2, PCI-DSS) are distinct from the software cost.

playbook.if_increased:
1. New regulatory requirements (GDPR, CCPA, PCI-DSS) requiring additional tooling
2. Security incident response triggering investment in additional defenses
3. Expansion of compliance frameworks (adding SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, HIPAA)
4. Vendor price increases on annual renewals
5. Growth in endpoints and users increasing per-seat license costs
playbook.if_decreased:
1. Vendor consolidation reducing overlapping security tools
2. Migration to bundled security platforms from point solutions
3. Negotiated multi-year discount agreements

comparability.variations: Companies vary widely in how they categorize security spend. Some include it in IT infrastructure, others in compliance/legal, and some in a dedicated security line. Financial services firms tend to have dedicated disclosures.

examples.treatment: Reports cybersecurity spending as part of technology expense, disclosed as $15B+ annual technology budget
Reports its own internal security costs within G&A, while being a cybersecurity vendor itself
Increased cybersecurity disclosures post-2013 breach, reports within SG&A technology costs

nodes.label: Hardware & Equipment — Corporate
nodes.definition: Corporate laptops, servers, networking equipment (either expensed if below capitalization threshold or depreciated).
nodes.example: A company provisions 100 new employee laptops at $1,500 each ($150K total), expensed immediately under a $5K capitalization threshold, plus $30K in monitors, docking stations, and peripherals.
nodes.classification_notes: Items below the capitalization threshold (typically $1K-$5K) are expensed immediately. Items above threshold are capitalized as PP&E and depreciated (typically 3-5 years for IT equipment). Depreciation of capitalized IT equipment flows through a separate depreciation line. This line captures items expensed below threshold plus minor peripherals and accessories.

playbook.if_increased: (1) laptop/desktop refresh cycle (typically every 3-4 years), (2) rapid headcount growth requiring new equipment, (3) return-to-office requiring monitor and desk setup, (4) technology upgrade (e.g., M1 to M4 Mac migration), (5) raising the capitalization threshold causing more items to be expensed
playbook.if_decreased: (1) hiring freeze reducing new equipment needs, (2) extending equipment refresh cycles, (3) BYOD (bring your own device) policies, (4) lowering capitalization threshold causing more items to be capitalized, (5) shift to virtual desktop infrastructure reducing physical hardware

comparability.variations: Hardware spend per employee is typically $500-$2,000/year including refresh amortization. Companies with higher capitalization thresholds will show more here and less depreciation. Tech companies tend to provide more expensive equipment. Some companies lease equipment (operating lease expense) rather than purchase.

examples.treatment: Provides high-end equipment to all employees; classified within General and administrative
Strict security requirements drive specialized (more expensive) hardware; often leased rather than purchased

nodes.label: IT Infrastructure & Networking
nodes.definition: Corporate network infrastructure, VPN, cybersecurity tools, and cloud services for internal operations.
nodes.example: A mid-size company spends $120K/year on corporate network switches and routers, $45K on VPN services for remote employees, and $60K on firewall and Wi-Fi access point maintenance across 3 office locations.
nodes.classification_notes: Corporate IT infrastructure is a G&A cost, not COGS. Distinguish from production infrastructure (which is COGS for SaaS companies). Hardware purchases above capitalization thresholds should be capitalized and depreciated under ASC 360. Cloud-based networking (SD-WAN, SASE) is expensed as a subscription. Shared infrastructure supporting both corporate and production may require allocation.

playbook.if_increased:
1. Office expansion or new location buildouts requiring network infrastructure
2. Technology refresh cycles replacing aging network equipment
3. Migration to zero-trust security architecture adding tooling
4. Growth in remote workforce requiring VPN and SD-WAN investment
5. Bandwidth upgrades for video conferencing and cloud app usage
playbook.if_decreased:
1. Office consolidation reducing networking footprint
2. Migration from on-premise to cloud-based networking (SASE)
3. Shift to fully remote work eliminating office network costs
4. Vendor consolidation reducing overlapping tools

comparability.variations: Companies vary in whether IT infrastructure is a standalone line or bundled into general technology or occupancy costs. Some allocate networking costs across departments; others centralize in IT. Cloud-first companies may have minimal physical networking costs.

examples.treatment: Reports IT infrastructure and networking within technology spending, part of its multi-billion dollar annual tech budget
Includes corporate IT costs within general and administrative expense, separate from cloud production infrastructure
Reported networking and IT infrastructure as part of building operations costs for its co-working spaces

nodes.label: IT Staff Compensation
nodes.definition: Salaries and benefits for internal IT support and systems staff.
nodes.example: A 1,000-employee company has a 15-person IT team costing $2.1M: CIO $250K, 4 systems admins at $130K, 3 helpdesk at $75K, 3 network engineers at $140K, 2 security analysts at $145K, 2 IT project managers at $135K.
nodes.classification_notes: Includes IT helpdesk, systems administrators, network engineers, security analysts, and IT management. CIO/CTO salary may be under Executive Compensation if they are a named executive officer. Software developers building internal tools (not product) are here. Developers working on the product are in R&D, not G&A IT.

playbook.if_increased: (1) expanding IT team for cybersecurity or infrastructure modernization, (2) salary inflation in competitive IT labor market, (3) insourcing previously outsourced IT support, (4) adding specialized roles (cloud architects, security engineers), (5) increased IT headcount to support company growth
playbook.if_decreased: (1) outsourcing IT helpdesk or managed services, (2) cloud migration reducing on-premise administration needs, (3) consolidation of IT roles across business units, (4) automation reducing manual IT tasks, (5) offshoring IT support functions

comparability.variations: IT-to-employee ratio varies: typically 1:50 to 1:150 depending on industry. Financial services and tech companies have higher ratios. Companies heavily using managed service providers show lower IT staff comp but higher vendor costs. Some companies classify IT staff under each department rather than centrally.

examples.treatment: Large internal IT workforce; technology staff costs are a major component of noninterest expense
May have 1-2 IT staff supplemented by outsourced managed IT services

nodes.label: Software Subscriptions — Corporate
nodes.definition: Business software subscriptions for productivity, communication, and corporate operations (Microsoft 365, Slack, Zoom, Salesforce for internal use).
nodes.example: A 300-employee company pays $540K/year in corporate SaaS: $108K Microsoft 365 ($30/user/mo), $72K Slack ($20/user/mo), $54K Zoom ($15/user/mo), $180K Salesforce CRM, $126K various other tools.
nodes.classification_notes: SaaS subscriptions are expensed as incurred per ASC 350-40 (hosting arrangements that are service contracts). Implementation costs of cloud-hosted software may be capitalized if meeting criteria under ASC 350-40. Distinguish from production/product software (COGS) and R&D tools (R&D expense). Software sprawl is a common audit finding — companies may have 50-200+ SaaS subscriptions.

playbook.if_increased: (1) headcount growth adding per-seat license costs, (2) adoption of new SaaS tools across the organization, (3) vendor price increases on contract renewals, (4) upgrade to premium software tiers, (5) shadow IT — departments purchasing unauthorized subscriptions
playbook.if_decreased: (1) software rationalization eliminating redundant tools, (2) headcount reductions reducing license counts, (3) renegotiated enterprise agreements, (4) consolidation to platform vendors (e.g., Microsoft suite replacing multiple point solutions), (5) open-source alternatives replacing paid software

comparability.variations: SaaS spend per employee ranges from $1,000-$5,000/year. Tech companies and financial services firms spend more per employee. Some companies classify software by function (HR software under HR, etc.) rather than centralizing under IT. SaaS spend has grown rapidly as companies shift from on-premise to cloud.

examples.treatment: Uses its own CRM; other corporate SaaS costs in General and administrative
Lower SaaS spend; more investment in on-premise production software classified as manufacturing overhead

nodes.label: LEGAL & COMPLIANCE
nodes.formula_human: External Legal Fees (General Corporate) + External Legal Fees (Litigation) + Regulatory & Compliance Fees + D&O and Other Corporate Insurance + Intellectual Property
nodes.definition: Costs of legal counsel, regulatory compliance, and corporate governance.
nodes.example: A public company spends $3.8M on legal and compliance: $1.2M corporate legal fees, $800K litigation defense, $600K regulatory fees, $700K D&O insurance, $500K IP protection.
nodes.classification_notes: Legal costs are expensed as incurred. Litigation losses require accrual when probable and estimable (ASC 450-20). Contingent gains are not recognized until realized. Settlement costs may be reported separately if material. IP-related legal fees (patent prosecution) may be capitalized as part of the intangible asset under ASC 350.

playbook.if_increased: (1) major litigation or regulatory investigation, (2) new regulatory requirements (GDPR, SOX compliance), (3) increased M&A activity requiring legal due diligence, (4) IP litigation in competitive industries, (5) D&O insurance premium increases post-IPO or securities litigation
playbook.if_decreased: (1) settlement of major litigation, (2) bringing legal work in-house reducing outside counsel fees, (3) favorable regulatory environment reducing compliance burden, (4) reduced D&O premiums after claims-free period, (5) simplified corporate structure reducing governance costs

comparability.variations: Heavily regulated industries (financial services, healthcare, pharma) have significantly higher legal/compliance costs. Tech companies face IP litigation risk. Some companies report litigation settlements as a separate line below operating income. D&O insurance costs spiked post-2020 and have since moderated.

examples.treatment: Significant litigation costs (talc lawsuits); disclosed as litigation expense and accruals
Legal and compliance is a major cost center; provisions for litigation within noninterest expense
Antitrust and regulatory costs; European Commission fines separately disclosed

nodes.label: D&O and Other Corporate Insurance
nodes.definition: Directors & Officers liability insurance and other corporate insurance policies.
nodes.example: A newly public company pays $800K/year in corporate insurance: $500K D&O liability, $120K errors & omissions (E&O), $100K employment practices liability (EPL), $80K cyber liability insurance.
nodes.classification_notes: General liability and property insurance specific to production facilities is Manufacturing Overhead; this is corporate-level insurance. D&O insurance is essential for public companies to attract board members. Premiums are prepaid and amortized over the policy period. Claims-made vs. occurrence policies affect timing of expense recognition. Side-A, B, and C D&O coverage serve different purposes.

playbook.if_increased: (1) IPO dramatically increasing D&O premiums, (2) securities litigation or SEC investigation driving rate increases, (3) hard insurance market with rising premiums industry-wide, (4) adding new coverage lines (cyber liability, EPL), (5) increased limits of liability requested by board
playbook.if_decreased: (1) claims-free history earning premium reductions, (2) soft insurance market with competitive pricing, (3) higher retention/deductible levels to reduce premiums, (4) going private reducing D&O exposure, (5) forming a captive insurance subsidiary

comparability.variations: D&O premiums vary enormously: $50K-$100K for private companies, $200K-$5M+ for public companies. Post-IPO companies and companies in litigation-prone industries pay the highest rates. D&O pricing is cyclical — premiums spiked 200-300% in 2020-2021, then moderated. Cyber insurance has become a significant new cost category.

examples.treatment: D&O premium $30K-$80K; increases 5-10x upon IPO
D&O tower of $100M+ in coverage with $1-3M annual premium; disclosed in proxy as director compensation

nodes.label: External Legal Fees — General Corporate
nodes.definition: Retainer and hourly fees for corporate legal counsel (contracts, corporate governance, employment law).
nodes.example: A mid-size company pays $450K/year to outside counsel: $180K corporate governance and board matters, $120K commercial contract review, $90K employment law advisory, $60K regulatory advisory.
nodes.classification_notes: General corporate legal fees are routine operating expenses — contract negotiation, employment matters, governance advice, and regulatory guidance. Distinguish from litigation fees (separate line) and M&A transaction costs (may be capitalized or expensed depending on deal type per ASC 805). Legal fees for patent prosecution may be capitalized as part of the intangible asset.

playbook.if_increased: (1) M&A activity requiring legal due diligence, (2) new market entry requiring regulatory legal advice, (3) increased contract volume requiring more outside review, (4) complex employment matters (executive terminations, investigations), (5) corporate restructuring or reorganization
playbook.if_decreased: (1) building internal legal team reducing outside counsel dependency, (2) legal technology (contract automation) reducing attorney hours, (3) reduced M&A or deal activity, (4) fixed-fee arrangements replacing hourly billing, (5) simplified corporate structure

comparability.variations: Companies with large in-house legal teams spend less on outside counsel. Startup and early-stage companies rely more on external firms. Big Law hourly rates ($500-$2,000/hour) drive significant spend for complex matters. Some companies use alternative legal service providers (ALSPs) for routine work.

examples.treatment: Large in-house legal team with selective use of outside counsel for specialized matters; classified in G&A
Heavy reliance on outside counsel for all legal matters; may defer or minimize legal spend to conserve cash

nodes.label: External Legal Fees — Litigation
nodes.definition: Fees for defending or prosecuting lawsuits (disclosed separately if material per Reg S-X).
nodes.example: A company defending a patent infringement lawsuit pays $2.1M in litigation fees: $1.5M to lead litigation counsel, $400K expert witnesses and discovery, $200K e-discovery and document review.
nodes.classification_notes: Litigation fees are expensed as incurred. Separate from settlement accruals — settlements are accrued when probable and estimable per ASC 450-20. Material litigation should be disclosed in footnotes (ASC 450-20-50). Companies often add back litigation costs in non-GAAP metrics. Insurance recoveries should be recorded separately, not netted against litigation costs, unless virtually certain.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new lawsuits filed against the company, (2) existing litigation moving to trial phase (more expensive), (3) class action certification increasing defense costs, (4) government investigation or enforcement action, (5) IP litigation in competitive markets
playbook.if_decreased: (1) settlement of major litigation, (2) cases dismissed or resolved favorably, (3) insurance coverage offsetting defense costs, (4) strategic decision to settle early rather than litigate, (5) fewer new claims filed

comparability.variations: Litigation costs are inherently lumpy and unpredictable. Some companies report them as a separate line item when material; others bury them in G&A. Pharma (product liability), tech (patent trolls), and financial services (regulatory) face the highest litigation costs. Non-GAAP metrics often exclude litigation charges.

examples.treatment: FTC privacy litigation and antitrust cases; legal fees within G&A; settlement accruals separately disclosed
Massive Roundup litigation reserves; disclosed as significant items outside normal G&A

nodes.label: Intellectual Property (Patent / Trademark)
nodes.definition: Patent filing, maintenance, and trademark registration fees.
nodes.example: A pharmaceutical company spends $350K/year on patent filings and prosecution costs across 45 active patents, plus $80K on trademark registrations in 12 international jurisdictions.
nodes.classification_notes: Patent filing and prosecution costs for internally developed IP are expensed as incurred under US GAAP. Patents acquired in a business combination are capitalized as intangible assets and amortized. Trademark registration fees are typically expensed. Patent defense litigation costs are expensed, while successful patent enforcement costs may be capitalized in some cases. Distinguish from R&D costs and from acquired IP amortization.

playbook.if_increased:
1. Increased patent filing activity from new product innovations
2. International trademark expansion into new jurisdictions
3. Patent prosecution costs rising due to examiner rejections
4. Defensive patent strategy against competitor filings
5. Outside counsel rate increases for IP law firms
playbook.if_decreased:
1. Reduced innovation pipeline leading to fewer patent filings
2. Consolidation of trademark portfolio dropping unused marks
3. Shift to trade secret strategy over patent filings
4. Bringing IP legal work in-house from outside counsel

comparability.variations: Tech and pharma companies typically have large IP budgets; consumer goods companies focus more on trademarks. Some companies capitalize certain IP costs (especially acquired patents) while others expense all. Patent amortization of acquired IP is a separate line from filing costs.

examples.treatment: Reports significant patent-related legal costs within G&A, with licensing revenue as a separate segment
Expenses patent filing costs within G&A while amortizing acquired pharmaceutical IP over patent life
Reports trademark registration and maintenance costs within SG&A, with brand intangibles on the balance sheet

nodes.label: Regulatory & Compliance Fees
nodes.definition: Costs of regulatory filings, compliance programs, and government fees.
nodes.example: A public company pays $320K/year in regulatory fees: $150K SEC filing fees, $80K stock exchange listing fees (NYSE/NASDAQ), $50K state registration fees, $40K compliance consulting.
nodes.classification_notes: Includes SEC filing fees, stock exchange listing fees, state corporation fees, industry-specific licensing fees, and compliance consulting. Financial services firms pay significant regulatory fees to FINRA, OCC, FDIC, and state regulators. GDPR, HIPAA, and SOX compliance consulting fees belong here. Regulatory fines and penalties should be disclosed separately and may not be tax-deductible.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new regulatory requirements (GDPR, CCPA, AI regulations), (2) IPO creating SEC and exchange listing fees, (3) expansion into regulated industries or markets, (4) increased compliance consulting for new mandates, (5) government fee increases
playbook.if_decreased: (1) deregistration from SEC reporting, (2) regulatory simplification, (3) bringing compliance expertise in-house, (4) delisting from a stock exchange, (5) exiting regulated business lines

comparability.variations: Financial services and healthcare companies face the highest regulatory costs (FDIC assessments, OCC fees, HIPAA compliance). Tech companies face increasing regulatory scrutiny (privacy, AI, antitrust). SEC filing fees are based on aggregate offering amount. Stock exchange listing fees are based on shares outstanding.

examples.treatment: FDIC insurance assessments and OCC fees are significant regulatory costs within noninterest expense
FDA regulatory compliance costs (clinical trial oversight, drug safety reporting) embedded in G&A and R&D

nodes.label: OFFICE & FACILITIES — CORPORATE
nodes.formula_human: Office Rent/Lease + Office Utilities + Office Equipment & Supplies + Office Maintenance & Janitorial + Corporate Depreciation (Buildings & Fixtures)
nodes.definition: Costs of maintaining corporate office space and facilities (excludes manufacturing/production facilities, which are Manufacturing Overhead).
nodes.example: A company with 50,000 sq ft of office space in Manhattan spends $3.5M: $2.4M rent, $180K utilities, $120K supplies, $200K maintenance, $600K depreciation on leasehold improvements.
nodes.classification_notes: Strictly corporate/administrative office facilities — manufacturing plants are manufacturing overhead, retail stores are selling expenses, and warehouses may be COGS or selling. Under ASC 842, operating leases create a right-of-use asset and lease liability on the balance sheet, but the P&L expense is presented as a single lease cost.

playbook.if_increased: (1) office expansion or relocation to more expensive space, (2) return-to-office requiring additional capacity, (3) rent escalation clauses in existing leases, (4) opening offices in new geographic markets, (5) leasehold improvement amortization from build-outs
playbook.if_decreased: (1) shift to remote/hybrid work reducing office footprint, (2) subleasing excess office space, (3) consolidating multiple offices into one, (4) lease renegotiations at renewal, (5) relocating from high-cost to low-cost markets

comparability.variations: Varies enormously by location (Manhattan vs. suburban), industry, and remote work policies. Under ASC 842, all operating leases are now on balance sheet. Some companies report occupancy as a separate line; others embed it in G&A. Financial services firms (banking branches) have very high occupancy costs.

examples.treatment: Occupancy is a core cost; office lease expense reported under cost of revenue and operating expenses
Went digital by default in 2020; significantly reduced office footprint and associated G&A costs
Massive real estate portfolio; occupancy expense reported as a separate line within noninterest expense

nodes.label: Corporate Depreciation — Buildings & Fixtures
nodes.definition: Depreciation on owned corporate buildings, leasehold improvements, and office fixtures (ASC 360).
nodes.example: A financial services company records $8M/year in corporate depreciation: $5M on owned headquarters (39-year life) and $3M on office fixtures and tenant improvements.
nodes.classification_notes: This captures depreciation on corporate and administrative properties, distinct from production facilities (in COGS) and R&D facilities (in R&D). Includes headquarter buildings, regional offices, and associated permanent fixtures (built-in shelving, lighting systems, plumbing upgrades). Often embedded within SG&A rather than shown as a separate D&A line item.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new corporate office acquisitions or buildouts, (2) major office renovations, (3) acquisitions adding corporate properties, (4) new regional office openings
playbook.if_decreased: (1) office consolidation and property sales, (2) assets becoming fully depreciated, (3) shift to leased vs owned offices, (4) remote work reducing need for corporate space

comparability.variations: Banks and financial institutions often own significant corporate real estate. Tech companies typically lease, minimizing this line. Post-COVID office consolidation has led to impairments and reduced depreciation for many companies.

examples.treatment: Significant owned corporate real estate depreciation across branches and HQ
Corporate building depreciation on owned properties including 200 West Street HQ
Primarily leasehold improvement depreciation; most offices leased

nodes.label: Office Equipment & Supplies
nodes.definition: Consumable office supplies, furniture, and minor equipment not capitalized.
nodes.example: A 200-person office spends $85K/year on supplies: $25K paper and printing supplies, $20K kitchen supplies and snacks, $30K furniture replacements, $10K miscellaneous office supplies.
nodes.classification_notes: Includes paper, toner, pens, kitchen supplies, breakroom snacks, furniture below capitalization threshold, and minor office equipment. Standing desk purchases above $1K-$5K capitalization threshold should be capitalized as PP&E. Office supplies for manufacturing areas are manufacturing overhead. Distinguish from IT hardware (computers, monitors) which go under IT.

playbook.if_increased: (1) headcount growth increasing consumable usage, (2) office build-out for new or renovated space, (3) return-to-office increasing in-office supply consumption, (4) enhanced kitchen/snack programs for employee retention, (5) inflation on paper and supply costs
playbook.if_decreased: (1) remote work reducing in-office supply needs, (2) going paperless reducing print supplies, (3) budget austerity cutting snack and kitchen programs, (4) bulk purchasing agreements reducing unit costs, (5) headcount reductions

comparability.variations: Tech companies tend to spend more per employee on office amenities (snacks, beverages, ergonomic furniture). Traditional offices spend more on paper and printing. This line item has declined industry-wide as offices go paperless and hybrid. Some companies combine this with office maintenance into a single facilities line.

examples.treatment: Generous office amenities (micro-kitchens, snacks) included in G&A; higher per-employee spend
Higher paper and printing costs; premium office furniture capitalized and depreciated

nodes.label: Office Maintenance & Janitorial
nodes.definition: Ongoing maintenance, cleaning, and facility management for corporate offices.
nodes.example: A corporate office pays $144K/year for maintenance: $84K janitorial services (3x/week cleaning), $36K HVAC maintenance contract, $24K miscellaneous repairs (plumbing, electrical).
nodes.classification_notes: Includes janitorial/cleaning services, minor plumbing/electrical repairs, HVAC servicing, pest control, landscaping, and security services. Capital improvements (new HVAC system, roof replacement) should be capitalized under ASC 360, not expensed here. Manufacturing facility maintenance is under manufacturing overhead, not G&A.

playbook.if_increased: (1) aging building requiring more frequent repairs, (2) enhanced cleaning protocols (post-COVID), (3) office expansion increasing square footage, (4) vendor price increases on service contracts, (5) adding new services (security, concierge)
playbook.if_decreased: (1) office downsizing reducing maintained square footage, (2) renegotiated cleaning and maintenance contracts, (3) reduced cleaning frequency for hybrid offices, (4) newer building requiring less maintenance, (5) bringing janitorial services in-house

comparability.variations: Gross lease tenants may have maintenance included in rent (showing $0 here). NNN lease tenants pay all maintenance directly. Typical office maintenance is $3-8/sq ft/year depending on building class and services. Some companies combine this with office supplies into a single occupancy line.

examples.treatment: Maintenance included in WeWork membership fee; shows $0 in this line
Full maintenance budget managed internally; includes landscaping, security, cleaning

nodes.label: Office Rent / Lease
nodes.definition: Lease payments for corporate office space (operating lease per ASC 842).
nodes.example: A company leases 25,000 sq ft of Class A office space in San Francisco at $72/sq ft/year, resulting in $1.8M annual lease expense recognized straight-line under ASC 842.
nodes.classification_notes: Under ASC 842, operating leases are recognized straight-line over the lease term even if cash payments escalate. Finance leases split into depreciation of the ROU asset and interest on the lease liability. Lease incentives (tenant improvement allowances) reduce the ROU asset and are amortized over the lease term. Short-term leases (under 12 months) may be expensed as incurred without balance sheet recognition.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new office leases for expansion, (2) rent escalation clauses in existing leases (typically 2-3%/year), (3) relocation to higher-cost market, (4) converting co-working/flex space to dedicated leases, (5) lease modification extending term or adding space
playbook.if_decreased: (1) office consolidation or downsizing post-remote work, (2) subleasing excess space (sublease income offsets), (3) lease expirations not renewed, (4) relocation to lower-cost market, (5) negotiating lower rates at renewal in soft real estate markets

comparability.variations: Office rent per employee ranges from $3K/year (low-cost suburban) to $20K+/year (Manhattan, San Francisco). Under ASC 842, the P&L shows a single operating lease cost, but the balance sheet now shows a right-of-use asset and lease liability. Some companies own rather than lease, showing depreciation instead.

examples.treatment: Significant lease liabilities in San Francisco; attempted to sublease excess space post-acquisition
Mix of owned (HQ2) and leased office space; leases disclosed in ASC 842 footnotes

nodes.label: Office Utilities
nodes.definition: Electricity, HVAC, water, and other utilities for corporate offices.
nodes.example: A 40,000 sq ft corporate office in Chicago pays $96K/year in utilities: $60K electricity, $18K natural gas (heating), $12K water/sewer, $6K trash removal.
nodes.classification_notes: Office utilities are G&A; manufacturing plant utilities are manufacturing overhead (COGS). In multi-use facilities, utilities should be allocated between production and corporate use. Gross leases often include utilities in the rent; net leases require separate utility payments. Internet and phone service may be classified here or under IT depending on company policy.

playbook.if_increased: (1) energy rate increases, (2) office expansion increasing square footage, (3) return-to-office increasing occupancy and usage, (4) extreme weather driving HVAC costs, (5) adding energy-intensive equipment (server rooms, EV charging stations)
playbook.if_decreased: (1) reduced office occupancy from hybrid work, (2) energy efficiency improvements (LED lighting, smart HVAC), (3) solar panel installations reducing grid electricity costs, (4) office downsizing, (5) utility rate negotiations or switching providers

comparability.variations: Utilities per sq ft vary by climate, building age, and energy efficiency. Gross lease tenants show zero utility expense (included in rent). Net lease tenants show full utility costs. Companies with on-site data centers will have significantly higher electricity costs classified under IT rather than office utilities.

examples.treatment: 100% renewable energy campus; low utility costs relative to building size
Utilities paid separately under NNN lease; typically $2-4/sq ft/year

nodes.label: Research & Development (R&D)
nodes.formula_human: R&D Personnel + R&D Materials & Supplies + R&D Equipment & Facilities + External/Contract Research
nodes.definition: Costs incurred to discover new knowledge or create new products, processes, or technologies. Expensed as incurred under ASC 730 (with certain software development costs capitalized under ASC 350-40). Note: As of 2022, IRC Section 174 requires R&D to be capitalized and amortized for TAX purposes, but it continues to be expensed for GAAP purposes.
nodes.example: Google's 'Other Bets' research projects and core search algorithm development both flow through R&D.
nodes.classification_notes: R&D is expensed as incurred for GAAP (ASC 730). Software development costs may be capitalized once technological feasibility is established (ASC 985-20) or during application development stage for internal-use software (ASC 350-40). Stock-based compensation for R&D employees is included here.

playbook.if_increased: (1) engineering hiring for new product development, (2) increased cloud compute for ML/AI training, (3) new R&D facility or lab investment, (4) clinical trial costs (pharma), (5) strategic pivot requiring new technology
playbook.if_decreased: (1) R&D headcount reductions, (2) project completions or cancellations, (3) shift from internal to acquired technology, (4) R&D tax credit offset (if shown as reduction), (5) capitalization of software development costs

comparability.variations: Tech companies typically report R&D as a separate line item and it represents 15-25% of revenue. Pharma companies may have R&D exceeding revenue for pre-commercial-stage companies. Manufacturing companies may embed R&D within SG&A.

examples.treatment: Research and development
Research and development
Research and development expenses
Research and development

nodes.label: EXTERNAL / CONTRACT RESEARCH
nodes.formula_human: Contract Research Organizations + University Research Grants & Partnerships + R&D Tax Credit Offset
nodes.definition: Payments to third parties for research conducted on the company's behalf.
nodes.example: A pharma company spends $25M on external R&D: $18M to CROs for Phase II clinical trials, $5M in university partnerships, and $2M in grants.
nodes.classification_notes: Payments to third parties for R&D performed on the company's behalf are expensed as incurred under ASC 730. Funded R&D arrangements (ASC 730-20) require careful analysis of who bears the risk. If the company bears the risk, costs are expensed; if a third party bears the risk, the arrangement may be treated as a contract. Milestone-based contracts require judgment on when to recognize expense.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new clinical trials initiated with CROs, (2) outsourcing of development tasks previously done in-house, (3) expansion of university research partnerships, (4) new contract research programs
playbook.if_decreased: (1) clinical trial completions, (2) insourcing of previously outsourced R&D, (3) contract research program cancellations, (4) shift from external to internal capabilities

comparability.variations: Pharma companies heavily rely on CROs and external research (40-60% of R&D). Biotech startups may outsource nearly all R&D. Tech companies use external research less frequently. Some companies classify consulting and professional services for R&D here.

examples.treatment: Major CRO contracts for global clinical trial management
Significant external research collaborations and CRO partnerships
External research partnerships for autonomous vehicle development

nodes.label: Contract Research Organizations (CRO)
nodes.definition: Fees for external research firms or CROs conducting qualifying research.
nodes.example: A pharma company paying a CRO for clinical trial management.
nodes.classification_notes: CRO fees are expensed as incurred under ASC 730. For milestone-based contracts, judgment is required on expense timing -- typically recognized proportionally as services are rendered. Upfront payments may be prepaid and amortized over the contract period. Includes both full-service CROs (managing entire trials) and functional service providers (specific tasks like data management or biostatistics).

playbook.if_increased: (1) new clinical trials initiated, (2) trials advancing to later (more expensive) phases, (3) geographic expansion of clinical trials, (4) outsourcing of previously in-house clinical operations
playbook.if_decreased: (1) trial completions or FDA approvals, (2) trial failures leading to program cancellations, (3) insourcing clinical operations, (4) regulatory holds pausing trials

comparability.variations: Pharma companies are the primary users of CROs. Biotech startups may outsource 80-100% of clinical development. Medical device companies use CROs for regulatory studies. Non-pharma companies rarely have CRO costs.

examples.treatment: Major CRO contracts with IQVIA and PPD for oncology clinical trials
CRO partnerships for vaccine clinical trial management globally
Mix of in-house and CRO-managed clinical trials for biologics

nodes.label: University Research Grants & Partnerships
nodes.definition: Funding provided to academic institutions for collaborative R&D.
nodes.example: A tech company funds $3M in AI research at MIT and $2M at Stanford for natural language processing research, with IP licensing rights to resulting discoveries.
nodes.classification_notes: Grants and sponsored research payments to universities are expensed as incurred if the company bears the research risk. If the arrangement grants the company IP rights, analyze whether it is a funded R&D arrangement under ASC 730-20. Charitable research donations may be classified as G&A rather than R&D. Joint research ventures may require equity method or consolidation analysis.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new academic research partnerships established, (2) expanded funding for existing collaborations, (3) strategic pivot requiring fundamental research capabilities, (4) industry consortium participation
playbook.if_decreased: (1) partnership completions or expirations, (2) budget cuts reducing discretionary research spending, (3) shift to in-house research capabilities, (4) strategic reprioritization away from basic research

comparability.variations: Large tech and pharma companies are the heaviest funders of university research. Some arrangements include student placement programs. IP ownership terms vary -- some companies retain full rights, others share with the university. Government-funded joint programs may offset company costs.

examples.treatment: Extensive university AI research partnerships with major institutions globally
Multi-year research collaborations with universities for drug discovery
Long-standing university research programs including quantum computing partnerships

nodes.label: R&D Tax Credit Offset
nodes.definition: Where companies offset R&D expense with R&D tax credits on the P&L. Less common; credit usually flows through tax expense, but some companies show it as an R&D offset.
nodes.example: A company with $50M in qualifying R&D expenses claims a $3.5M R&D tax credit (IRC Section 41), shown as a contra-R&D expense on the income statement, reducing reported R&D to $46.5M.
nodes.classification_notes: Most companies record R&D tax credits as a reduction of income tax expense (ASC 740), NOT as an R&D offset. Some companies choose to present the credit as a reduction of R&D expense, which is less common but acceptable. This line item captures the latter presentation. International R&D incentives (UK RDEC, Australia R&D Tax Incentive) may be presented differently. Always verify the company's accounting policy.

playbook.if_increased: (1) increased qualifying R&D expenditures, (2) improved R&D tax credit study identifying more qualifying activities, (3) new state or international R&D tax incentives, (4) change in presentation from tax line to R&D offset
playbook.if_decreased: (1) reduced qualifying R&D spend, (2) legislative changes reducing R&D credit rates, (3) change in presentation to record credit in tax expense instead, (4) loss of qualifying status for certain activities

comparability.variations: Most US companies record R&D credits as tax benefit (not R&D offset). UK companies using RDEC must present the credit as an above-the-line item. Some companies show the credit in other income. Presentation choice is a significant comparability issue.

examples.treatment: UK RDEC credit shown as above-the-line income, offsetting R&D costs
R&D tax credits reflected in income tax provision, not as R&D offset
UK R&D expenditure credit shown within operating expenses

nodes.label: R&D EQUIPMENT & FACILITIES
nodes.formula_human: R&D Equipment Depreciation + R&D Lab / Office Space + R&D Cloud Compute
nodes.definition: Equipment and facility costs dedicated to R&D activities.
nodes.example: A biotech company spends $8M on R&D facilities: $2M equipment depreciation, $4M lab/office rent, and $2M cloud compute for genomic data processing.
nodes.classification_notes: Equipment used exclusively in R&D with no alternative future use must be expensed at acquisition under ASC 730. Equipment with alternative future use is capitalized and depreciated, with depreciation allocated to R&D. Facility costs should be allocated between R&D and other functions if space is shared.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new R&D lab or facility buildout, (2) increased cloud compute for AI/ML workloads, (3) equipment purchases with alternative future use entering depreciation, (4) lease renewals at higher rates
playbook.if_decreased: (1) equipment becoming fully depreciated, (2) lab consolidation or closure, (3) migration from on-premise to cloud (shifts to OpEx), (4) sublease of underutilized R&D space

comparability.variations: Capital-intensive R&D (pharma, semiconductor) has high equipment and facility costs. Cloud-native companies may have minimal physical equipment but significant cloud compute spend. Some companies allocate corporate facility costs to R&D based on headcount rather than tracking dedicated R&D facilities.

examples.treatment: Massive R&D fab and equipment costs; billions in R&D equipment depreciation
R&D infrastructure dominated by cloud GPU compute costs
Dedicated R&D labs and equipment across pharmaceutical and medical device divisions
