nodes.label: R&D Cloud Compute
nodes.definition: Cloud computing costs for R&D model training, testing, and experimentation (separate from production infrastructure in COGS).
nodes.example: An AI company's GPU compute costs for training new models before deployment.
nodes.classification_notes: Only cloud compute used for R&D activities (model training, experimentation, testing) should be classified here. Production cloud infrastructure serving customers belongs in COGS. The line between R&D and production compute can be blurry for AI companies -- classification should be based on whether the workload generates revenue. Pre-production staging environments are typically R&D.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new AI/ML model training runs requiring GPU clusters, (2) expansion of R&D testing environments, (3) cloud provider price increases, (4) shift from on-premise to cloud infrastructure
playbook.if_decreased: (1) model training completion, (2) efficiency improvements reducing compute needs, (3) negotiated reserved instance pricing, (4) migration of workloads to on-premise GPUs

comparability.variations: AI companies have rapidly growing R&D cloud compute costs, often exceeding personnel costs. Traditional software companies have modest R&D compute. Non-tech companies have minimal to zero R&D cloud compute. The boundary between R&D and production compute is a key classification judgment.

examples.treatment: Massive GPU cloud compute costs for LLM training classified as R&D
R&D cloud costs for platform development and internal testing
R&D compute for testing new features on their own cloud platform

nodes.label: R&D Equipment Depreciation
nodes.definition: Depreciation on equipment used exclusively for research and development.
nodes.example: A semiconductor company depreciates $50M in wafer fabrication test equipment over 5 years, recording $10M/year in R&D equipment depreciation.
nodes.classification_notes: Equipment used exclusively for R&D with no alternative future use is expensed immediately under ASC 730 (not depreciated). Equipment with alternative future use is capitalized under ASC 360 and depreciated, with the depreciation charge allocated to R&D. This line captures the latter case. Common methods: straight-line over 3-7 years for lab equipment.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new R&D equipment purchases entering depreciable base, (2) shorter useful life estimates accelerating depreciation, (3) lab equipment upgrades, (4) acquired company's R&D equipment added
playbook.if_decreased: (1) R&D equipment becoming fully depreciated, (2) equipment disposals or retirements, (3) extension of useful life estimates, (4) shift from on-premise equipment to cloud services

comparability.variations: Semiconductor and pharma companies have the highest R&D equipment depreciation. Tech/software companies have minimal R&D equipment. Some companies do not break out R&D-specific depreciation, instead including it in total D&A on the income statement.

examples.treatment: Significant R&D equipment depreciation for lithography system development
R&D equipment depreciation for genomic sequencing instrument development
R&D equipment depreciation for chip design and testing labs

nodes.label: R&D Lab / Office Space
nodes.definition: Allocated or dedicated facility costs for research labs and development offices.
nodes.example: A biotech company leases 50,000 sq ft of lab space at $80/sq ft, resulting in $4M/year in R&D facility costs allocated to research activities.
nodes.classification_notes: Includes rent, utilities, maintenance, and property taxes for dedicated R&D facilities. Under ASC 842, lease costs are recognized as ROU asset amortization and interest, but the total cost is still allocated to R&D. Shared facilities must be allocated based on square footage or headcount. Lab space typically costs more than standard office space due to specialized requirements.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new R&D lab or campus buildout, (2) lease renewals at higher market rates, (3) expansion into additional R&D locations, (4) reclassification of shared space to R&D
playbook.if_decreased: (1) R&D facility consolidation, (2) shift to remote/hybrid work reducing office needs, (3) sublease of excess R&D space, (4) lease expirations not renewed

comparability.variations: Biotech and pharma companies have high lab facility costs due to specialized requirements (clean rooms, biosafety). Tech companies allocate office space to R&D based on engineering headcount. Some companies own R&D facilities, in which case depreciation replaces rent.

examples.treatment: Dedicated South San Francisco R&D campus costs allocated to research
R&D office space allocated from corporate campuses based on headcount
Specialized mRNA research lab facilities with high per-sq-ft costs

nodes.label: R&D MATERIALS & SUPPLIES
nodes.formula_human: Laboratory & Research Supplies + Prototype Materials + R&D Software & Development Tools
nodes.definition: Consumable materials, supplies, and prototype components used in R&D activities.
nodes.example: A hardware company spends $4.5M on R&D materials: $1.2M in lab supplies, $2.8M in prototype components, and $0.5M in software development tools.
nodes.classification_notes: Materials used in R&D must have no alternative future use to be expensed under ASC 730. If materials have alternative future use, they are capitalized as inventory and expensed as consumed. Prototype materials are always expensed. Software tools used in R&D are included here if subscription-based; perpetual licenses may be capitalized.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new product development entering prototype phase, (2) expanded lab testing requirements, (3) supply chain cost inflation, (4) new R&D projects initiated
playbook.if_decreased: (1) shift from hardware to software R&D, (2) project completions or cancellations, (3) efficiency improvements reducing material waste, (4) bulk purchasing agreements

comparability.variations: Hardware and pharma companies have high materials costs (30-50% of R&D). Software companies have minimal materials cost. Biotech companies include reagents, cell cultures, and assay kits as R&D materials.

examples.treatment: Significant R&D materials for medical device prototyping and testing
R&D materials include prototype chip fabrication and testing components
R&D supplies include lab chemicals, biological materials, and clinical supplies

nodes.label: Laboratory & Research Supplies
nodes.definition: Consumable lab supplies, chemicals, reagents, and research materials.
nodes.example: A pharmaceutical company's lab chemicals used in drug discovery.
nodes.classification_notes: Includes consumable items such as chemicals, reagents, cell cultures, assay kits, glassware, and disposable lab equipment. Must be expensed as incurred if no alternative future use. If lab supplies have alternative future use (e.g., can be used in production), capitalize as inventory until consumed.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new drug candidates entering preclinical testing, (2) expanded testing protocols, (3) supply cost inflation for specialty chemicals, (4) new lab facility opening
playbook.if_decreased: (1) project completions or cancellations, (2) lab closures, (3) negotiated volume discounts with suppliers, (4) shift to computational/in-silico research methods

comparability.variations: Pharma and biotech companies have the highest lab supply costs. Hardware companies include testing components. Pure software companies have minimal to zero lab supplies.

examples.treatment: Significant lab supply costs for diagnostic and pharmaceutical R&D
Lab supplies for internal R&D, also a major supplier to other companies
Lab materials including biological reagents and cell culture media for antibody research

nodes.label: Prototype Materials
nodes.definition: Materials used to build product prototypes during development.
nodes.example: An EV manufacturer spends $2.8M on battery cell prototypes and $1.5M on chassis components for next-generation vehicle development.
nodes.classification_notes: Prototype materials are always expensed under ASC 730 because prototypes built during R&D have no alternative future use. Includes raw materials, components, and assemblies used to build test units. If a prototype can be sold (e.g., pre-production unit), it should be reclassified to inventory.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new product entering physical prototyping phase, (2) multiple design iterations required, (3) component cost increases, (4) expanded product line development
playbook.if_decreased: (1) product reaching production stage, (2) shift to simulation-based design reducing physical prototypes, (3) project cancellations, (4) design reuse from prior products

comparability.variations: Hardware, automotive, and consumer electronics companies have the highest prototype material costs. Software-only companies have zero. Medical device companies include prototype materials subject to FDA design controls.

examples.treatment: Significant prototype costs for new vehicle models and battery technology
Extensive prototyping costs for consumer product development (thousands of iterations)
Prototype materials for medical devices under strict design control requirements

nodes.label: R&D Software & Development Tools
nodes.definition: Licenses for development environments, IDEs, testing tools, and research software.
nodes.example: A SaaS company spends $800K/year on R&D tools: $300K for GitHub Enterprise, $200K for JetBrains IDE licenses, $150K for Jira/Confluence, and $150K for testing and CI/CD tools.
nodes.classification_notes: Includes SaaS subscriptions for IDEs, code repositories, CI/CD pipelines, testing frameworks, project management, and specialized research software. Subscription/SaaS costs are expensed as incurred. Perpetual licenses may need to be evaluated for capitalization under ASC 350-40. Only tools used primarily for R&D should be classified here; general-purpose tools used across departments belong in SG&A.

playbook.if_increased: (1) engineering headcount growth increasing per-seat licenses, (2) adoption of new development tools, (3) vendor price increases on renewals, (4) migration to more expensive enterprise tiers
playbook.if_decreased: (1) engineering headcount reductions, (2) tool consolidation, (3) switch to open-source alternatives, (4) renegotiated vendor contracts

comparability.variations: Software companies have moderate tool costs (1-3% of R&D). Companies using proprietary/expensive simulation software (semiconductor, automotive) have higher costs. Some companies build tools in-house, reducing this line item.

examples.treatment: Development tool costs included in R&D; heavy investment in internal tooling
Uses own EDA tools internally; minimal external tool spend
Specialized simulation and CAD software licenses for aerospace R&D

nodes.label: R&D PERSONNEL
nodes.formula_human: R&D Salaries & Wages + R&D Benefits + R&D Bonuses & Incentive Pay
nodes.definition: Compensation for employees engaged in qualifying research and development activities.
nodes.example: A SaaS company with 200 engineers spending $35M in R&D personnel: $28M salaries, $5M benefits, $2M bonuses.
nodes.classification_notes: Includes all compensation for employees whose primary function is R&D. Stock-based compensation for R&D staff is typically included here or broken out separately. Shared employees must be allocated between R&D and other functions based on time spent.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new engineering hires for product development, (2) salary inflation in competitive tech labor markets, (3) increased stock-based compensation grants, (4) acquisitions adding R&D headcount
playbook.if_decreased: (1) R&D workforce reductions or layoffs, (2) offshoring to lower-cost geographies, (3) shift from employees to contractors, (4) natural attrition not backfilled

comparability.variations: Personnel is typically 60-80% of total R&D spend for software/tech companies. Pharma companies may have a lower ratio due to significant materials and clinical trial costs. Some companies disclose SBC separately from base R&D personnel costs.

examples.treatment: R&D personnel costs are the dominant component; disclosed as part of total R&D expense
R&D personnel embedded within research and development expenses alongside clinical costs
R&D personnel costs included in product development expense

nodes.label: Payroll Taxes — R&D
nodes.definition: Employer payroll taxes attributable to R&D workforce.
nodes.example: A software company pays $1.8M/year in employer FICA, FUTA, and state unemployment taxes on $23M of R&D engineering salaries across 150 developers.
nodes.classification_notes: Includes employer-side FICA (Social Security + Medicare), FUTA, and state unemployment taxes for R&D staff. Does not include employee benefits like health insurance or 401(k) matching, which are tracked separately. FICA taxes cap at the Social Security wage base, causing Q1 seasonality in per-employee costs.

playbook.if_increased:
1. Grew R&D headcount increasing total payroll tax base
2. Annual salary raises increased taxable compensation
3. Social Security wage base ceiling increased year-over-year
4. Hired more employees in high-tax jurisdictions
5. Q1 seasonality reset where all employees restart FICA accumulation
playbook.if_decreased:
1. R&D layoffs or attrition reducing headcount
2. Shifted R&D workforce to contractor model (no employer taxes)
3. Relocated R&D staff to lower-tax jurisdictions
4. Q3-Q4 effect where high-earners exceed Social Security wage cap

comparability.variations: Most companies do not separately disclose payroll taxes by department; they are bundled into total R&D expense. International companies may have significantly different employer tax rates (e.g., European social contributions are much higher).

examples.treatment: Includes payroll taxes within total research and development expense without separate disclosure
Bundles payroll taxes into R&D personnel costs alongside salaries and benefits
Reports payroll taxes within R&D expense, noting higher rates for Australian employees vs. US staff

nodes.label: R&D Benefits
nodes.definition: Health insurance, retirement, and benefits for R&D employees.
nodes.example: A biotech company provides $18K/year per R&D employee in benefits (health, dental, 401k match) for 100 scientists, totaling $1.8M in R&D benefits.
nodes.classification_notes: Includes health/dental/vision insurance, 401(k) matching, life insurance, disability insurance, payroll taxes (employer portion of FICA), and other fringe benefits for R&D employees. Stock-based compensation is sometimes included here but more commonly shown separately.

playbook.if_increased: (1) healthcare premium increases, (2) R&D headcount growth, (3) richer benefits packages to attract talent, (4) increased 401(k) matching rates
playbook.if_decreased: (1) R&D headcount reductions, (2) shift to high-deductible health plans, (3) reduction in employer retirement matching, (4) increased use of contractors (no benefits)

comparability.variations: Benefits as a percentage of base salary typically range from 20-35% in the US. Companies with large international R&D teams may have different benefit structures. European subsidiaries often have higher mandatory social contributions.

examples.treatment: R&D benefits bundled into total R&D expense; comprehensive benefits package
R&D benefits reflect Swiss and global statutory requirements; higher percentage of salary
R&D benefits included in technology and content costs

nodes.label: R&D Bonuses & Incentive Pay
nodes.definition: Performance bonuses for R&D staff tied to innovation milestones.
nodes.example: A tech company pays $3.2M in annual bonuses to R&D staff: $1.5M in milestone bonuses for shipping a new product and $1.7M in annual performance bonuses.
nodes.classification_notes: Includes annual performance bonuses, project milestone bonuses, signing bonuses, and retention bonuses for R&D employees. Stock-based compensation (RSUs, options) may be classified here or in a separate SBC line. Accrual timing can create quarter-to-quarter variability.

playbook.if_increased: (1) strong product launch triggering milestone bonuses, (2) increased target bonus percentages to retain talent, (3) signing and retention bonuses in competitive hiring market, (4) company-wide performance exceeding targets
playbook.if_decreased: (1) company underperformance reducing bonus pools, (2) R&D headcount reductions, (3) shift from cash bonuses to equity compensation, (4) project cancellations eliminating milestone payouts

comparability.variations: Tech companies often emphasize equity (RSUs, options) over cash bonuses. Pharma companies may tie bonuses to clinical trial milestones. Bonus as a percentage of base salary typically ranges from 10-30% for R&D roles.

examples.treatment: Favors higher base salary over bonuses; minimal R&D bonus component
R&D bonuses tied to pipeline milestones and clinical trial progress
R&D incentive pay includes significant equity component tied to performance milestones

nodes.label: R&D Salaries & Wages
nodes.definition: Base salary and wages for scientists, engineers, and developers engaged in R&D.
nodes.example: A mid-stage SaaS company pays $140K average salary to 150 software engineers, totaling $21M in R&D salaries annually.
nodes.classification_notes: Only base salary and wages for employees whose primary role is R&D. If an employee splits time between R&D and other functions (e.g., customer support), allocate based on time records. Overtime and shift differentials for R&D staff are included here.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new engineering hires, (2) annual merit increases and cost-of-living adjustments, (3) competitive salary benchmarking adjustments, (4) insourcing previously contracted work
playbook.if_decreased: (1) R&D layoffs or reduction in force, (2) attrition without backfill, (3) offshoring to lower-cost regions, (4) reclassification of roles to other departments

comparability.variations: Silicon Valley companies pay significantly higher base salaries than other regions. Companies with large offshore R&D centers (India, Eastern Europe) have lower per-capita salary costs. Some companies bundle SBC into salary line items.

examples.treatment: R&D salaries included in research and development expense; top-of-market compensation
R&D personnel costs reflect lower-cost geography; significant offshore engineering
R&D salaries within research and development; global engineering workforce

nodes.label: Stock-Based Compensation — R&D
nodes.definition: Equity award expense for R&D employees (ASC 718).
nodes.example: A SaaS company recognizes $12M/year in SBC expense for RSU grants to its 400-person engineering team, vesting over 4 years with quarterly tranches.
nodes.classification_notes: Typically the largest SBC allocation for technology companies given the size of engineering teams. Non-cash expense under ASC 718. R&D SBC is commonly added back for non-GAAP metrics. Includes RSUs, stock options, ESPP discounts, and performance shares for R&D staff. Capitalization under ASC 350-40 for internal-use software may apply to some SBC.

playbook.if_increased:
1. Expanded engineering team with competitive equity packages
2. Annual refresh grants layering on top of prior unvested awards
3. Rising stock price increasing grant-date fair value of new awards
4. Accelerated vesting from acquisitions triggering change-of-control provisions
5. Retention grants to prevent attrition during competitive talent market
playbook.if_decreased:
1. Large prior-year grants fully vested reducing ongoing amortization
2. Engineering layoffs causing forfeiture of unvested equity awards
3. Stock price decline reducing fair value of new option grants
4. Shifted compensation mix from equity to cash for R&D staff

comparability.variations: R&D SBC is the largest functional allocation at most tech companies. Companies with high SBC-to-revenue ratios face investor scrutiny. Some companies capitalize a portion of R&D SBC under ASC 350-40 for internal-use software, reducing the P&L impact.

examples.treatment: Reports very high R&D SBC as percentage of revenue, separately disclosed in the SBC footnote by function
Allocates SBC to R&D and other functions, with R&D being the largest allocation given engineering-heavy workforce
Discloses R&D SBC separately in operating expense breakdown, representing a significant portion of total R&D expense

nodes.label: Depreciation & Amortization (D&A)
nodes.formula_human: Depreciation of PP&E + Amortization of Intangible Assets
nodes.definition: The non-cash allocation of the cost of long-lived assets over their useful lives. Often embedded within COGS, SG&A, or R&D rather than shown as a separate line item. When disclosed separately, it represents total D&A from all functions.
nodes.example: A manufacturing company with $500M in PP&E and $200M in acquired intangibles may record $80M in annual D&A.
nodes.classification_notes: Whether D&A is shown separately or embedded within functional categories is a PRESENTATION choice -- the underlying sub-items are the same. For EBITDA calculations, total D&A must be gathered from the cash flow statement or notes if not separately presented on the income statement.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new capital expenditures entering depreciable base, (2) acquisitions adding intangible assets, (3) change in depreciation method or useful life estimates, (4) accelerated depreciation from impairment indicators
playbook.if_decreased: (1) assets reaching end of useful life (fully depreciated), (2) asset disposals or sales, (3) change to longer useful life estimates, (4) reduced capital spending in prior years

comparability.variations: D&A presentation varies significantly. Capital-intensive companies (manufacturing, telecom) show large D&A. Asset-light companies (SaaS, consulting) have minimal depreciation but may have significant amortization from acquisitions.

examples.treatment: Depreciation and amortization (separate line, very large)
Embedded in cost of revenues and operating expenses; total in cash flow statement
Depreciation and amortization shown in operating expenses

nodes.label: AMORTIZATION OF INTANGIBLE ASSETS
nodes.formula_human: Customer Relationship Amortization + Technology / IP Amortization + Trade Name Amortization + Capitalized Software Amortization + Right-of-Use Asset Amortization
nodes.definition: Allocation of acquired intangible asset cost over useful life (ASC 350). Applies to acquired assets; internally developed intangibles are generally expensed as incurred.
nodes.example: After a $500M acquisition, a company identifies $150M in intangible assets: $60M customer relationships (10-yr life), $50M technology (7-yr life), $25M trade names (15-yr life), and $15M software (5-yr life), totaling ~$18M/year in amortization.
nodes.classification_notes: Only finite-lived intangible assets are amortized; indefinite-lived intangibles (goodwill, certain trade names) are tested for impairment instead. Acquired intangibles from business combinations (ASC 805) are the primary source. Internally developed intangibles are generally expensed as incurred (except capitalized software under ASC 350-40). Amortization is often excluded from non-GAAP metrics as acquisition-related.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new acquisitions adding intangible assets, (2) capitalized software development entering amortization, (3) change in useful life estimates, (4) accelerated amortization patterns for revenue-based methods
playbook.if_decreased: (1) intangible assets becoming fully amortized, (2) impairment write-downs reducing carrying value, (3) fewer acquisitions in recent periods, (4) disposal of businesses with associated intangibles

comparability.variations: Serial acquirers (tech, pharma) have the highest intangible amortization. Companies that grow organically have minimal amortization. Many companies exclude acquisition-related amortization from non-GAAP earnings, creating significant GAAP vs non-GAAP differences.

examples.treatment: Significant intangible amortization from acquisitions (LinkedIn, Nuance, Activision); excluded from non-GAAP
Massive acquired intangible amortization; key non-GAAP adjustment
Customer relationship and trade name amortization from Optum acquisitions

nodes.label: Capitalized Software Amortization
nodes.definition: Amortization of internally capitalized software development costs per ASC 350-40 (application development stage only).
nodes.example: A SaaS company capitalizes $12M in internal-use software development during the application development stage and amortizes it over 3 years, recording $4M/year in software amortization.
nodes.classification_notes: Internal-use software (ASC 350-40): costs capitalized during application development stage only; preliminary project and post-implementation costs are expensed. Software for sale (ASC 985-20): costs capitalized after technological feasibility. Cloud computing arrangements (ASC 350-40): implementation costs for hosted arrangements may be capitalized. Typical useful lives are 3-5 years. Amortization method is usually straight-line.

playbook.if_increased: (1) increased software capitalization from major platform development, (2) prior-year capitalized projects entering amortization, (3) shorter useful life estimates, (4) aggressive capitalization policy
playbook.if_decreased: (1) capitalized software becoming fully amortized, (2) impairment of capitalized software, (3) shift in policy to expense more costs, (4) reduced software development investment

comparability.variations: SaaS companies frequently capitalize internal software development costs, creating significant amortization. Companies with aggressive capitalization policies show lower R&D expense but higher amortization. Some companies present software amortization in COGS (cost of revenue) rather than D&A. Capitalization policies vary significantly across companies, impacting comparability.

examples.treatment: Significant capitalized software amortization in cost of subscription revenue
Internal software development capitalized and amortized; shown in cost of cloud and software
Capitalized internal-use software amortized over 3-year useful life

nodes.label: Customer Relationship Amortization
nodes.definition: Amortization of customer relationship intangibles acquired in a business combination.
nodes.example: A company acquired for $100M with $20M attributed to customer relationships, amortized over 7 years.
nodes.classification_notes: Customer relationships are identified as a separate intangible asset in purchase price allocation (ASC 805). Typical useful lives are 5-15 years. Amortization method should reflect the pattern of economic benefit -- accelerated methods may be appropriate if customer attrition is front-loaded. Backlog (existing contracts) is a separate intangible with a shorter life. Non-compete agreements are also separate.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new acquisitions with significant customer relationship intangibles, (2) purchase price allocations assigning more value to customer relationships, (3) shorter useful life estimates for acquired relationships
playbook.if_decreased: (1) customer relationship intangibles becoming fully amortized, (2) impairment of customer relationships due to customer losses, (3) disposal of business units with associated customer intangibles

comparability.variations: Customer relationships are often the largest acquired intangible asset (30-50% of intangible value in many deals). B2B companies typically receive higher customer relationship valuations than B2C. SaaS companies may classify this as customer contracts and backlog. Some companies use accelerated amortization reflecting declining customer retention curves.

examples.treatment: Significant customer relationship amortization from Slack, Tableau, and MuleSoft acquisitions
Serial acquirer with large customer relationship amortization across life sciences businesses
Customer relationship amortization from tuck-in waste hauling acquisitions

nodes.label: Right-of-Use Asset Amortization
nodes.definition: Amortization of finance lease right-of-use assets (ASC 842).
nodes.example: A company enters a 10-year finance lease for equipment valued at $5M, recording $500K/year in ROU asset amortization (separate from the interest component of the lease payment).
nodes.classification_notes: Only finance lease ROU assets are amortized (similar to owned assets). Operating lease ROU assets are not amortized -- instead, a single lease expense is recognized on a straight-line basis. Finance lease cost has two components: (1) ROU asset amortization (in D&A or operating expenses) and (2) interest on lease liability (in interest expense). Amortization is typically straight-line over the lease term or useful life of the asset, whichever is shorter.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new finance leases entered (equipment, real estate), (2) reclassification of operating leases to finance leases, (3) lease modifications extending term, (4) sale-leaseback transactions classified as finance leases
playbook.if_decreased: (1) finance lease expirations, (2) early lease terminations, (3) lease buyouts converting to owned assets, (4) reclassification to operating leases

comparability.variations: Airlines and retailers with significant finance leases have the highest ROU amortization. Most office and warehouse leases are operating leases (no ROU amortization). The finance vs operating lease classification significantly affects where costs appear on the income statement. Companies transitioning from legacy capital leases under ASC 840 to ASC 842 maintain finance lease classification.

examples.treatment: Significant finance lease ROU amortization on aircraft and ground equipment
Finance lease ROU amortization on select retail locations and equipment
Finance lease amortization on data center equipment and fulfillment center assets

nodes.label: Technology / IP Amortization
nodes.definition: Amortization of acquired patents, trademarks, and developed technology intangibles.
nodes.example: A tech company acquires a startup for $200M, identifying $40M in developed technology with a 5-year useful life, recording $8M/year in technology amortization.
nodes.classification_notes: Includes acquired developed technology, patents, and proprietary processes identified in purchase price allocation. Distinct from in-process R&D (IPR&D), which is not amortized until the project is completed. Technology intangibles typically have shorter useful lives (3-7 years) than customer relationships due to faster obsolescence. Patent amortization follows the remaining legal life of the patent.

playbook.if_increased: (1) acquisitions of technology companies, (2) patent portfolio purchases, (3) completion of acquired IPR&D beginning amortization, (4) shorter useful life estimates reflecting rapid technology change
playbook.if_decreased: (1) technology intangibles becoming fully amortized, (2) technology impairment due to obsolescence, (3) fewer technology acquisitions, (4) disposal of technology assets

comparability.variations: Tech acquirers (Cisco, Oracle, Microsoft) have the highest technology amortization. Pharma companies amortize developed drug formulations and manufacturing processes. Some companies present technology amortization within COGS (cost of revenue) rather than operating expenses.

examples.treatment: Large technology amortization from decades of technology acquisitions; shown in cost of sales
Significant developed technology amortization from cloud and database acquisitions
Technology amortization on acquired drug formulations and manufacturing IP from Allergan

nodes.label: Trade Name Amortization
nodes.definition: Amortization of acquired trade names with finite useful lives.
nodes.example: A consumer goods company acquires a brand for $30M, with $10M allocated to the trade name (finite life of 20 years), recording $500K/year in trade name amortization.
nodes.classification_notes: Only trade names with finite useful lives are amortized. Many acquired trade names are determined to have indefinite lives and are instead tested for impairment annually. The finite vs indefinite determination depends on whether the company plans to use the name indefinitely. Trade names being phased out or transitioned to a parent brand have finite lives. Typical useful lives range from 5-30 years.

playbook.if_increased: (1) acquisitions with finite-lived trade name intangibles, (2) reclassification of indefinite-lived trade names to finite-lived, (3) brand portfolio rationalization assigning end dates to brands
playbook.if_decreased: (1) trade names becoming fully amortized, (2) impairment of brand value, (3) fewer acquisitions with trade name intangibles, (4) determination that acquired trade names have indefinite lives

comparability.variations: Consumer products and hospitality companies often have the largest trade name intangibles. Many well-known brands are classified as indefinite-lived (not amortized). The finite vs indefinite classification is a key judgment area. Some companies rebrand acquisitions quickly, resulting in short-lived trade name amortization.

examples.treatment: Many acquired trade names classified as indefinite-lived; some finite-lived names amortized
Starwood brand trade names with varying finite and indefinite life determinations
Large trade name intangibles; mix of indefinite and finite-lived brands

nodes.label: DEPRECIATION OF PROPERTY, PLANT & EQUIPMENT
nodes.formula_human: Machinery & Equipment Depreciation + Vehicles Depreciation + Building & Improvement Depreciation + Furniture & Fixtures Depreciation
nodes.definition: Allocation of PP&E cost over its useful life (ASC 360). Method: straight-line, declining balance, or units-of-production.
nodes.example: A manufacturing company with $1.2B in gross PP&E records $120M in annual depreciation: $60M machinery, $25M buildings, $20M vehicles, $15M furniture and fixtures.
nodes.classification_notes: Depreciation method (straight-line, declining balance, units-of-production) and useful life estimates are accounting policy choices that significantly affect the amount. Land is not depreciated. Leasehold improvements are depreciated over the shorter of useful life or lease term. Component depreciation may be required for significant asset components with different useful lives.

playbook.if_increased: (1) significant capital expenditures in prior periods entering depreciable base, (2) acquisitions adding PP&E, (3) change to shorter useful life estimates, (4) accelerated depreciation methods adopted
playbook.if_decreased: (1) assets reaching end of useful life (fully depreciated), (2) asset disposals, retirements, or sales, (3) change to longer useful life estimates, (4) reduced prior-year capital spending

comparability.variations: Capital-intensive industries (manufacturing, energy, telecom) have very high PP&E depreciation. Asset-light companies (SaaS, consulting) have minimal PP&E depreciation. Airlines depreciate aircraft over 20-30 years. Technology equipment is typically 3-5 years.

examples.treatment: Massive PP&E depreciation on refineries, pipelines, and production equipment
Aircraft depreciation over 25-30 years; fleet age affects total depreciation
Significant depreciation on stores, distribution centers, and fixtures

nodes.label: Building & Improvement Depreciation
nodes.definition: Depreciation on owned buildings and leasehold improvements.
nodes.example: A company owns a $50M headquarters building depreciated over 39 years ($1.3M/year) plus $5M in leasehold improvements depreciated over the 10-year lease term ($500K/year).
nodes.classification_notes: Buildings are typically depreciated over 25-40 years (IRS: 39 years for commercial, 27.5 for residential). Leasehold improvements are depreciated over the shorter of useful life or remaining lease term. Land is never depreciated. Building components (HVAC, electrical, roofing) may be separately depreciated with different useful lives. Tenant improvement allowances from landlords reduce the depreciable base.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new building acquisitions or construction completions, (2) major renovations or leasehold improvements, (3) acquisitions adding owned properties, (4) component replacements (new roof, HVAC)
playbook.if_decreased: (1) building sales or dispositions, (2) buildings becoming fully depreciated, (3) lease expirations with associated improvements fully amortized, (4) impairment write-downs reducing carrying value

comparability.variations: REITs and property-heavy companies have the largest building depreciation. Many tech companies lease rather than own buildings, so their building depreciation is minimal. Retail companies with owned store locations have significant building depreciation. Leasehold improvements can be substantial for companies that heavily customize leased spaces.

examples.treatment: Massive building depreciation on owned shopping centers and malls
Significant depreciation on owned branch locations and headquarters buildings
Leasehold improvement depreciation across thousands of store locations

nodes.label: Furniture & Fixtures Depreciation
nodes.definition: Depreciation on office furniture, fixtures, and minor tangible assets.
nodes.example: A company furnishes a new 200-person office for $1.5M (desks, chairs, conference tables, monitors) depreciated over 7 years, recording $214K/year.
nodes.classification_notes: Includes desks, chairs, cubicles, conference room furniture, filing cabinets, shelving, and non-IT office equipment. Useful life typically 5-10 years (IRS: 7 years for furniture and fixtures). Items below the company's capitalization threshold are expensed immediately. Some companies group IT equipment (monitors, docking stations) with fixtures.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new office openings requiring furniture, (2) office renovation and refurnishing, (3) headcount growth requiring additional workstations, (4) acquisitions adding furnished offices
playbook.if_decreased: (1) furniture becoming fully depreciated, (2) office closures with furniture disposals, (3) downsizing reducing furniture needs, (4) shift to remote work

comparability.variations: Furniture depreciation is typically a small percentage of total D&A for most companies. Retail and hospitality companies may have higher fixture costs (display cases, store fixtures). Companies with high capitalization thresholds expense more items immediately, reducing this line.

examples.treatment: Significant furniture and fixture depreciation across co-working locations
Store fixtures depreciation across thousands of retail locations
Office furniture depreciation in global consulting offices

nodes.label: Machinery & Equipment Depreciation
nodes.definition: Depreciation on production machinery, manufacturing equipment, and heavy machinery.
nodes.example: A steel manufacturer depreciates $200M in blast furnaces and rolling mills over 20 years, recording $10M/year in machinery and equipment depreciation.
nodes.classification_notes: This captures depreciation on non-production general-purpose machinery and equipment reported within the D&A operating expense line. Production machinery depreciation is typically in COGS. Useful lives vary: office equipment 3-7 years, heavy machinery 10-20 years. Salvage value assumptions affect annual depreciation amount.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new machinery and equipment purchases, (2) business acquisitions adding equipment, (3) shorter useful life estimates, (4) accelerated depreciation for technology equipment
playbook.if_decreased: (1) equipment becoming fully depreciated, (2) asset disposals and retirements, (3) longer useful life estimates, (4) reduced capital spending in prior years

comparability.variations: Heavy industry companies (mining, oil and gas, construction) have the highest machinery depreciation. Useful life assumptions vary significantly by industry and can differ between companies, impacting comparability. Some companies use units-of-production for machinery directly tied to output.

examples.treatment: Significant machinery depreciation on manufacturing and construction equipment
Rental fleet depreciation is a major cost component
Diverse machinery depreciation across multiple manufacturing segments

nodes.label: Vehicles Depreciation
nodes.definition: Depreciation on company-owned vehicles.
nodes.example: A logistics company with a fleet of 500 delivery trucks at $80K each depreciates them over 7 years, recording $5.7M/year in vehicle depreciation.
nodes.classification_notes: Includes depreciation on company-owned cars, trucks, vans, forklifts, and specialty vehicles. Leased vehicles under finance leases are also included (ROU asset amortization). Operating lease vehicles are excluded -- those costs appear as lease expense. Salvage value for vehicles is typically 10-20% of original cost. IRS MACRS allows 5-year recovery for most vehicles.

playbook.if_increased: (1) fleet expansion with new vehicle purchases, (2) transition from leased to owned vehicles, (3) higher vehicle acquisition costs, (4) shorter useful life estimates for high-mileage vehicles
playbook.if_decreased: (1) vehicles reaching end of useful life, (2) fleet downsizing, (3) shift from owned to leased vehicles, (4) vehicle sales and trade-ins

comparability.variations: Delivery, logistics, and transportation companies have the highest vehicle depreciation. Many companies lease rather than own vehicles, which moves cost from depreciation to lease expense. EV transitions may change useful life assumptions and residual values.

examples.treatment: Large fleet depreciation on delivery vehicles and aircraft
Significant depreciation on collection trucks and specialized vehicles
Delivery fleet depreciation included in selling and distribution costs

nodes.label: Non-Operating Income & Expenses
nodes.formula_human: Non-Operating Income − Non-Operating Expenses
nodes.definition: Income and expenses that arise from activities outside the company's core operations. These items fall BELOW the Operating Income (EBIT) line. Including them in operating income would distort the measure of core operational performance. Key analytical principle: separating operating from non-operating items allows analysts to assess sustainable earnings vs. one-time or financing-driven items.
nodes.example: Interest expense is non-operating because it reflects financing decisions (how much debt the company has), not operating efficiency.
nodes.classification_notes: Non-operating items bridge the gap between Operating Income and Pre-Tax Income. The net amount can be positive (net non-operating income) or negative (net non-operating expense). Financial services companies have a different operating/non-operating boundary since interest income is part of core operations for banks.

playbook.if_increased: (1) investment gains or higher interest income on cash balances, (2) gains on asset disposals, (3) favorable FX movements, (4) reduced debt lowering interest expense
playbook.if_decreased: (1) higher interest expense from new debt or rising rates, (2) impairment charges on investments, (3) restructuring charges classified below EBIT, (4) unfavorable FX movements, (5) loss on asset disposals

comparability.variations: Presentation varies widely. Some companies show 'Other income (expense), net' as a single line. Others break out interest expense, interest income, and other items separately. Financial services companies treat interest as operating.

examples.treatment: Other income/(expense), net
Other income, net
Interest income, Interest expense, Other income (expense) — shown separately

nodes.label: NON-OPERATING INCOME
nodes.formula_human: Interest Income + Dividend Income + Gain on Investments + Gain on Foreign Exchange + Gain on Sale of Assets + Other Non-Operating Income
nodes.formula_machine: fintree:InterestIncome + fintree:DividendIncome + fintree:GainOnInvestments + fintree:GainOnForeignExchange + fintree:GainOnSaleOfAssets + fintree:OtherNonoperatingIncome
nodes.definition: Gains and income from activities outside core operations.
nodes.example: Apple reported $3.9B in other income in FY2023, primarily from interest income on its $166B investment portfolio.
nodes.classification_notes: Non-operating income includes all revenue-like items outside core operations. For financial services companies, interest and dividend income may be operating. Gains can be realized or unrealized. One-time vs. recurring distinction is critical for forecasting.

playbook.if_increased: (1) higher interest rates boosting yield on cash/investments, (2) realized gains from selling investments at a profit, (3) favorable foreign exchange movements, (4) asset sales above book value
playbook.if_decreased: (1) lower interest rates reducing yield on cash, (2) unrealized investment losses in mark-to-market portfolio, (3) fewer asset disposals, (4) unfavorable FX movements reducing translated gains

comparability.variations: Many companies net non-operating income and expenses into a single line. Others break out interest income separately. Financial services companies include interest income in operating revenue.

examples.treatment: Other income/(expense), net — nets interest income against other non-operating items
Investment gains — massive line item due to equity portfolio mark-to-market under ASC 321
Other income, net — includes interest income and net gains on investments

nodes.label: Dividend Income
nodes.definition: Dividends received from equity investments (typically minority stakes, not consolidated subsidiaries).
nodes.example: Berkshire Hathaway receives approximately $5.5B annually in dividend income from its equity portfolio, including $900M from Coca-Cola and $850M from Apple.
nodes.classification_notes: Recognized when the right to receive payment is established (ex-dividend date). For equity method investments (20-50% ownership), the investor records its share of investee earnings, not dividends — dividends reduce the investment balance instead. Distinguish from intercompany dividends eliminated in consolidation.

playbook.if_increased: (1) investee companies raising their dividend payouts, (2) new equity investments in dividend-paying stocks, (3) larger ownership stakes increasing pro-rata share, (4) special one-time dividends from investees
playbook.if_decreased: (1) investee companies cutting or suspending dividends, (2) sale of dividend-paying equity positions, (3) investees shifting capital allocation to buybacks over dividends, (4) reduced ownership percentage

comparability.variations: Most non-financial companies have minimal dividend income. Insurance companies and holding companies often have significant dividend income. May be combined with interest income under investment income.

examples.treatment: Dividend income reported as major line item — $5.5B from large equity portfolio
Net investment income — combines dividend and interest income on insurance investment portfolio
Dividends from equity method investees shown separately in income from investments

nodes.label: Gain on Foreign Exchange
nodes.definition: Realized and unrealized gains from currency rate movements on foreign-denominated assets/liabilities.
nodes.example: A US exporter with EUR 50M in receivables gains $3.2M when the euro strengthens from 1.05 to 1.11 against the dollar during the quarter.
nodes.classification_notes: Transaction gains (ASC 830-20) arise from remeasuring foreign-currency-denominated monetary items and flow through the P&L. Translation adjustments (ASC 830-10) from consolidating foreign subsidiaries go to OCI, not here. Companies may net FX gains and losses into a single line. Hedging gains under ASC 815 may offset transaction losses if hedge accounting is applied.

playbook.if_increased: (1) strengthening of foreign currencies against the functional currency on receivables, (2) weakening of functional currency on foreign-denominated assets, (3) increased unhedged foreign currency exposure, (4) favorable settlement timing on foreign transactions
playbook.if_decreased: (1) stable exchange rates reducing remeasurement gains, (2) effective hedging programs neutralizing FX movements, (3) reduced foreign-denominated receivables or assets, (4) netting against FX losses

comparability.variations: Many companies combine FX gains and losses into a net line. Some report within Other income/expense without separate disclosure. Multinationals with significant hedging programs may show minimal net FX impact.

examples.treatment: Foreign exchange gains/losses included in Other non-operating income — significant due to operations in 180+ countries
Effect of exchange rates on cash disclosed separately; transaction gains/losses in Other income
Foreign exchange gains shown as separate line item — major impact from USD/JPY movements

nodes.label: Gain on Investments
nodes.definition: Mark-to-market gains or realized gains from equity investments.
nodes.example: Berkshire Hathaway reported $35.5B in investment gains in FY2023, driven primarily by unrealized appreciation in its Apple and other equity holdings under ASC 321.
nodes.classification_notes: Under ASC 321 (post-ASU 2016-01), equity securities with readily determinable fair values are marked to market through the income statement — creating potentially large, volatile gains/losses that do not represent cash flow. Realized gains occur on actual sale. Analysts often exclude unrealized gains from recurring earnings. Debt securities classified as available-for-sale record unrealized gains in OCI, not P&L.

playbook.if_increased: (1) rising equity markets boosting unrealized gains on mark-to-market portfolio, (2) sale of appreciated investments at a gain, (3) new investments that appreciated quickly, (4) favorable sector rotation benefiting held positions
playbook.if_decreased: (1) declining equity markets reducing mark-to-market values, (2) sale of investments at lower gains, (3) reduced investment portfolio size, (4) shift from equity to fixed-income investments with less price appreciation

comparability.variations: Post-ASU 2016-01, all equity securities flow through P&L, creating massive volatility for large holders. Some companies present gains/losses net; others separate realized from unrealized. Many companies add non-GAAP adjustments to exclude unrealized gains.

examples.treatment: Investment gains/losses — enormous line item ($35B+) driven by Apple and equity portfolio mark-to-market
Gain on investments — Vision Fund marks startup portfolio to fair value each quarter
Gain on equity securities — includes gains/losses on venture investments

nodes.label: Gain on Sale of Assets
nodes.definition: Proceeds in excess of book value from selling property, equipment, or investments.
nodes.example: A manufacturer sells a factory with a $12M net book value for $18M, recording a $6M gain on sale of assets.
nodes.classification_notes: Gain = Sale proceeds minus net book value (cost less accumulated depreciation). Non-operating because asset sales are not core business activity. If the asset qualifies as a discontinued operation (ASC 205-20), report below the line instead. Sale-leaseback transactions have special treatment under ASC 842. Gains on sale of investments go to Gain on Investments, not here.

playbook.if_increased: (1) selling appreciated real estate or equipment above book value, (2) strategic divestitures of non-core assets, (3) rising market values for used equipment, (4) asset-light transformation selling owned facilities
playbook.if_decreased: (1) fewer asset disposals in the period, (2) assets sold near book value with minimal gain, (3) fully depreciated assets with zero book value sold for scrap, (4) declining market values for used assets

comparability.variations: Some companies report gains and losses on asset sales as a net figure. Others separate gains from losses. Real estate companies may have frequent gains from property sales as quasi-operating items. Classification as operating vs. non-operating depends on whether asset sales are part of the business model.

examples.treatment: Gain on sale of business units reported separately — e.g., WarnerMedia divestiture
Gain on disposal of long-lived assets within Other income (expense)
Gain on sale of real estate — frequent and quasi-operating for REITs

nodes.label: Interest Income
nodes.definition: Interest earned on cash deposits, money market funds, and fixed income investments.
nodes.example: Apple earned $3.7B in interest income in FY2023 from its $166B cash and marketable securities portfolio, benefiting from rising interest rates.
nodes.classification_notes: Non-operating for most companies. For banks and financial institutions, interest income is an operating item and the primary revenue source. Includes interest on bank deposits, money market funds, Treasury bills, corporate bonds, and other fixed income securities. Accrue using effective interest method per ASC 835-30.

playbook.if_increased: (1) rising interest rates increasing yield on cash and investments, (2) larger cash/investment balances, (3) shift to higher-yielding fixed income securities, (4) proceeds from equity raise or asset sale parked in interest-bearing accounts
playbook.if_decreased: (1) falling interest rates reducing yield, (2) lower cash balances from capex or M&A spending, (3) shift to lower-yielding or equity investments, (4) debt repayment reducing investable cash

comparability.variations: Banks report interest income as a primary operating revenue line. Non-financial companies report it as non-operating. Some companies net interest income against interest expense into a single line.

examples.treatment: Interest income shown within Other income/(expense), net footnote detail
Interest income — primary operating revenue line ($89B in 2023)
Interest income reported separately within Other income (expense)

nodes.label: Other Non-Operating Income
nodes.definition: Catch-all for non-operating income items not classified above (sublease income, government grants, etc.).
nodes.example: A retailer earns $2.4M from subleasing excess warehouse space and $800K from a government energy efficiency grant, totaling $3.2M in other non-operating income.
nodes.classification_notes: This is the residual category for non-operating income. Items here should not fit neatly into interest, dividends, investment gains, FX gains, or asset sale gains. Common items include sublease income, royalty income from non-core IP, insurance recoveries, and government grants. If an item becomes material, consider breaking it into its own line.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new sublease arrangements generating income, (2) government grants or incentive payments received, (3) insurance recovery proceeds, (4) settlement income from lawsuits, (5) royalty income from licensing non-core IP
playbook.if_decreased: (1) expiration of sublease agreements, (2) no government grants in current period, (3) prior-period insurance recoveries not recurring, (4) reclassification of items to specific non-operating income lines

comparability.variations: Companies differ widely in what falls into this catch-all. Some lump all non-operating income here; others break out each component. Size and materiality drive the level of disaggregation.

examples.treatment: Other income (expense), net — includes miscellaneous items not broken out separately
Other gains and losses — includes non-recurring items like insurance proceeds
Other income — includes royalty income and miscellaneous non-operating receipts

nodes.label: NON-OPERATING EXPENSES
nodes.formula_human: Interest Expense + Foreign Exchange Loss + Loss on Sale of Assets + Impairment Charges + Restructuring Charges + Other Non-Operating Expenses
nodes.formula_machine: fintree:InterestExpense + fintree:ForeignExchangeLoss + fintree:LossOnSaleOfAssets + fintree:ImpairmentCharges + fintree:RestructuringCharges + fintree:OtherNonoperatingExpenses
nodes.definition: Costs outside core operations — primarily financing costs and exceptional charges.
nodes.example: A highly leveraged retailer reports $45M interest expense, $8M restructuring charges from store closures, and $12M goodwill impairment, totaling $65M in non-operating expenses.
nodes.classification_notes: Non-operating expenses reduce pre-tax income but are excluded from operating income. Interest expense is typically the largest and most recurring component. Impairment and restructuring charges are non-recurring but can be substantial. For capital-intensive or highly leveraged companies, interest expense can exceed operating income. Analysts separate recurring (interest) from non-recurring (restructuring, impairment) items.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new debt issuance or refinancing at higher rates, (2) goodwill or asset impairment charges triggered by declining business performance, (3) restructuring program announced with severance and facility closure costs, (4) FX losses from unfavorable currency movements, (5) loss on sale of assets below book value
playbook.if_decreased: (1) debt repayment reducing interest expense, (2) refinancing at lower interest rates, (3) no impairment or restructuring charges in current period, (4) favorable FX movements, (5) fewer asset disposals at a loss

comparability.variations: Some companies show a single Other expense line. Others disaggregate interest expense, restructuring, and impairment separately. Interest expense is almost always disclosed separately due to SEC requirements. Capital-intensive industries have proportionally higher interest expense.

examples.treatment: Interest expense shown separately; impairment and restructuring as distinct lines
Interest expense shown separately — relatively low due to equity-heavy capital structure
Multiple non-operating expense lines including interest, restructuring, and goodwill impairment

nodes.label: Foreign Exchange Loss
nodes.definition: Realized and unrealized losses from adverse currency movements on foreign-denominated items.
nodes.example: A US company with EUR 80M in receivables records a $4.8M FX loss when the euro weakens from $1.12 to $1.06 during the quarter.
nodes.classification_notes: Transaction losses (ASC 830-20) arise from remeasuring foreign-currency monetary items when exchange rates move unfavorably. Distinguished from translation adjustments (OCI). Companies with significant international operations may have large FX losses. Hedging programs (ASC 815) can mitigate but rarely eliminate FX losses. Some companies net FX gains and losses into one line. Analyze alongside Gain on Foreign Exchange for the net FX impact.

playbook.if_increased: (1) weakening of foreign currencies against the functional currency on receivables/assets, (2) strengthening of foreign currencies on payables/liabilities, (3) increased unhedged foreign currency exposure, (4) hedge ineffectiveness leaving residual FX risk, (5) large foreign-denominated debt revaluation
playbook.if_decreased: (1) stable exchange rates reducing remeasurement losses, (2) effective hedging programs covering foreign currency exposures, (3) reduced international operations or foreign-denominated items, (4) natural hedging from matching foreign revenues and costs

comparability.variations: Companies often net FX gains and losses. Some report a single net FX line in Other income/expense. Multinationals disclose FX impact in MD&A. The distinction between transaction (P&L) and translation (OCI) losses is critical for analysis.

examples.treatment: FX losses included in Other non-operating — significant exposure across 180+ countries
Currency impact disclosed in organic growth reconciliation — large FX headwinds in strong-dollar periods
Foreign currency exchange losses reported in financial income/expense — euro-based reporting with global revenue

nodes.label: INTEREST EXPENSE
nodes.formula_human: Interest on Long-Term Debt + Interest on Revolving Credit Facility
nodes.definition: The cost of borrowed capital — interest payments on debt instruments. The primary non-operating expense for most companies. Reflects financing decisions, not operational performance.
nodes.example: AT&T reported $6.8B in interest expense in FY2023 on its $137B total debt, reflecting a weighted average interest rate of approximately 5%.
nodes.classification_notes: Interest expense includes coupon payments on bonds, interest on term loans, revolving credit facilities, capital lease interest (ASC 842), and amortization of debt issuance costs/discounts. Capitalized interest on qualifying assets (ASC 835-20) reduces the P&L charge. For banks, interest expense is an operating cost. Interest coverage ratio (EBIT / Interest Expense) is a key credit metric.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new debt issuance for M&A or capital projects, (2) rising benchmark interest rates on variable-rate debt, (3) refinancing at higher rates due to credit downgrade, (4) amortization of debt discount accelerating, (5) lease liability interest under ASC 842
playbook.if_decreased: (1) debt repayment or retirement reducing outstanding principal, (2) refinancing at lower rates, (3) shift from debt to equity financing, (4) interest rate swaps converting floating to lower fixed rate, (5) capitalization of interest on qualifying construction projects

comparability.variations: All companies with debt report interest expense. SEC requires separate disclosure. Some companies report interest expense net of capitalized interest. Banks report interest expense as a primary operating line item. Interest on finance leases (ASC 842) is included here.

examples.treatment: Interest expense — $6.8B separate line item reflecting heavy debt load
Interest expense shown within Other income/(expense), net — modest relative to cash position
Interest expense — operating line item ($35B+) as a bank

nodes.label: Amortization of Debt Issuance Costs
nodes.definition: Amortization of financing fees paid to issue debt instruments (treated as an interest expense component under ASC 835).
nodes.example: A company issued $500M in bonds and paid $4M in underwriting and legal fees; it amortizes $800K per year over the 5-year term as a component of interest expense.
nodes.classification_notes: Under ASU 2015-03, debt issuance costs are presented as a direct deduction from the carrying amount of the debt, not as a separate asset. The amortization flows through interest expense, not amortization expense. Distinguish from loan origination fees received by lenders (ASC 310).

playbook.if_increased:
1. New debt issuance with significant underwriting fees
2. Refinancing of existing debt triggering accelerated amortization of old costs
3. Shorter debt maturity concentrating amortization into fewer periods
4. Write-off of unamortized costs on early extinguishment
playbook.if_decreased:
1. Debt maturity reached and fully amortized
2. Shift from debt to equity financing reducing outstanding issuance costs
3. Longer-term debt instruments spreading costs over more periods

comparability.variations: Some companies combine debt issuance cost amortization into a single interest expense line; others break it out separately. IFRS companies may use different effective interest method calculations under IFRS 9.

examples.treatment: Reports amortization of debt issuance costs within interest expense on the income statement, disclosed separately in the notes
Includes debt issuance cost amortization within automotive interest expense, given large bond portfolio
Amortizes significant content-debt issuance costs over bond terms, disclosed in interest expense footnotes

nodes.label: Finance Lease Interest
nodes.definition: Interest component of finance lease payments (ASC 842) — treated as interest expense on the P&L.
nodes.example: A company with a $5M finance lease (5-year term, 6% implicit rate) recognizes $300K in finance lease interest in year 1, declining over the lease term as the liability is amortized.
nodes.classification_notes: Finance leases (formerly capital leases) split the P&L impact into two components: (1) depreciation of the ROU asset (in depreciation expense) and (2) interest on the lease liability (here, in interest expense). This differs from operating leases which show a single straight-line lease expense. Finance lease classification triggers when lease transfers substantially all risks/rewards of ownership. Interest declines over the lease term as the liability balance decreases (front-loaded expense pattern).

playbook.if_increased: (1) new finance lease agreements entered into, (2) lease modifications increasing the liability balance, (3) higher incremental borrowing rates on new leases, (4) acquisition bringing new finance leases onto the balance sheet, (5) reclassification of operating leases to finance leases
playbook.if_decreased: (1) natural decline as lease liability is paid down (declining interest pattern), (2) finance leases reaching end of term, (3) early termination or buyout of leased assets, (4) refinancing at lower rates, (5) shift to operating lease structures

comparability.variations: Finance lease interest appears below EBIT in interest expense. Companies with heavy equipment (airlines, trucking, manufacturing) have significant finance leases. Under IFRS 16, all leases are treated similarly to finance leases, creating comparability differences with US GAAP. The split between depreciation and interest for finance leases creates a front-loaded total expense pattern vs. straight-line for operating leases.

examples.treatment: Significant aircraft finance leases; interest component disclosed in interest expense footnotes
Fleet and facility finance leases; finance lease interest separately disclosed under ASC 842

nodes.label: Interest on Long-Term Debt
nodes.definition: Interest on bonds, term loans, and other long-term borrowings.
nodes.example: A company with $500M in bonds at 5% coupon records $25M/year interest expense, plus $1.2M amortization of debt issuance costs for a total of $26.2M.
nodes.classification_notes: Includes stated coupon interest on bonds, interest on term loans, and amortization of debt issuance costs and original issue discount using the effective interest method. Most long-term debt is fixed rate, so interest expense is predictable. If issued at a discount or premium, the effective interest rate differs from the coupon rate. Callable bonds may result in make-whole premiums on early retirement.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new bond issuance for M&A or growth capex, (2) refinancing maturing debt at higher rates, (3) additional term loan drawdowns, (4) accelerated amortization of debt discount on early repayment
playbook.if_decreased: (1) scheduled debt maturity and retirement without refinancing, (2) voluntary prepayment of term loans, (3) bond buyback at or below par, (4) refinancing at lower coupon rates

comparability.variations: Most companies combine all interest expense into one line. Only the debt footnote breaks out interest by instrument. Companies with complex capital structures may disclose senior vs. subordinated interest separately.

examples.treatment: Substantial long-term debt interest ($6B+) disclosed in debt footnote by maturity tranche
Automotive interest expense separated from Ford Credit (financial services) interest
Interest on senior notes — historically large as Netflix funded content with debt

nodes.label: Interest on Revolving Credit Facility
nodes.definition: Interest on drawn balances of revolving credit lines.
nodes.example: A company draws $100M on its $500M revolving credit facility at SOFR + 150bps (total 6.8%), incurring $6.8M in annual interest plus $1.5M in unused commitment fees.
nodes.classification_notes: Revolving credit facilities typically carry variable rates tied to SOFR (or formerly LIBOR) plus a credit spread. Interest cost depends on the drawn balance, which fluctuates with working capital needs. Commitment fees on undrawn portions are also expensed here. Revolver interest is more volatile than fixed-rate long-term debt interest. Seasonal businesses may show significant quarter-to-quarter variation.

playbook.if_increased: (1) higher drawn balances due to working capital needs or cash flow timing, (2) rising SOFR/benchmark rates increasing variable rate cost, (3) credit downgrade widening the applicable spread, (4) seasonal peak borrowing periods
playbook.if_decreased: (1) repayment of drawn balances from cash flow generation, (2) falling benchmark interest rates, (3) credit upgrade reducing the applicable spread, (4) replacement with cheaper term loan or bond financing

comparability.variations: Most companies do not separately disclose revolver interest vs. term loan interest on the income statement. Detail is typically in the debt footnote. Companies with large revolvers (retail, manufacturing) have more variable interest expense profiles.

examples.treatment: Seasonal revolver draws for inventory build — interest spikes in Q3 ahead of holiday season
Revolver interest included in total interest expense footnote — supports dealer financing
Revolver draws disclosed in liquidity section — drawn during COVID for cash preservation

nodes.label: Impairment Charges
nodes.definition: Write-down of long-lived assets or goodwill when carrying value exceeds recoverable amount (ASC 350, ASC 360).
nodes.example: Kraft Heinz recorded a $15.9B goodwill and intangible asset impairment charge in 2018 (announced February 2019) related to its Kraft and Oscar Mayer brands, one of the largest write-downs in US corporate history.
nodes.classification_notes: Goodwill impairment (ASC 350) uses a one-step quantitative test comparing reporting unit fair value to carrying amount. Long-lived asset impairment (ASC 360) triggers when undiscounted cash flows are below carrying value, then measured at fair value. Impairments are non-cash charges that signal overpayment in past acquisitions or declining business outlook. Once recognized, impairments cannot be reversed under US GAAP. Analysts typically exclude from recurring earnings but view as an important signal about management capital allocation quality.

playbook.if_increased: (1) declining business performance triggering goodwill impairment test failure, (2) M&A overpayment becoming evident as acquired business underperforms, (3) market downturn reducing fair value of reporting units, (4) strategic pivot abandoning previously acquired capabilities, (5) rising discount rates reducing present value of future cash flows
playbook.if_decreased: (1) no triggering events requiring impairment testing beyond annual test, (2) strong performance of acquired businesses validating purchase prices, (3) prior write-downs already recognized leaving lower carrying values, (4) conservative acquisition pricing providing headroom above carrying value

comparability.variations: Classification varies — some companies report impairment within operating expenses, others as non-operating. Goodwill impairment is always disclosed separately when material. Industries with heavy M&A activity (tech, media, pharma) tend to have more impairments. IFRS allows reversal of asset impairments (not goodwill); US GAAP does not.

examples.treatment: Goodwill and intangible asset impairment — $15.9B write-down on Kraft and Oscar Mayer brands (2018, announced Feb 2019)
Goodwill impairment after merger — reported as separate operating line item
Impairment on equity method investments — wrote down Didi and other stakes

nodes.label: Loss on Sale of Assets
nodes.definition: Book value in excess of proceeds when selling property, equipment, or investments below carrying value.
nodes.example: A retailer closing underperforming locations sells store fixtures with a $3.5M net book value for $1.2M, recording a $2.3M loss on sale of assets.
nodes.classification_notes: Loss = Net book value minus sale proceeds. Non-operating because asset sales are not core business. If the asset qualifies as a discontinued operation (ASC 205-20), report below the line instead. Losses on disposal of investment securities go to investment losses, not here. Assets held for sale (ASC 360-10-45) are measured at the lower of carrying amount or fair value less cost to sell, with any write-down recorded upon reclassification.

playbook.if_increased: (1) forced sale of assets in distressed conditions at below-book prices, (2) technology obsolescence reducing resale value of specialized equipment, (3) store or facility closures requiring asset liquidation, (4) declining used equipment market prices
playbook.if_decreased: (1) fewer asset disposals in the period, (2) improving secondary market conditions for used equipment, (3) assets fully depreciated before disposal (zero book value), (4) better disposal planning maximizing sale proceeds

comparability.variations: Some companies net gains and losses on asset sales. Others report losses separately from gains. Classification as operating vs. non-operating depends on frequency and business model. Companies undergoing restructuring may have elevated losses on asset sales.

examples.treatment: Loss on sale of assets included in automotive Other expenses — plant closure disposals
Significant losses on store asset disposals during wind-down — reported separately
Losses on disposal of business units reported within Other income (expense)

nodes.label: Other Non-Operating Expenses
nodes.definition: Miscellaneous non-operating charges — legal settlements, regulatory fines, and other exceptional costs.
nodes.example: A pharmaceutical company records $4.5M in legal settlement costs and $1.2M in regulatory fines, totaling $5.7M in other non-operating expenses.
nodes.classification_notes: Residual category for non-operating expenses not fitting interest, FX losses, asset sale losses, impairment, or restructuring. Common items include litigation settlements, regulatory penalties, early debt extinguishment costs, and charitable contributions classified as non-operating. If an item becomes material, it should be broken out as a separate line item per SEC guidance.

playbook.if_increased: (1) legal settlement payments or accruals for pending litigation, (2) regulatory fines from government agencies, (3) early debt retirement penalties or make-whole premiums, (4) charitable donation commitments, (5) environmental remediation charges
playbook.if_decreased: (1) resolution of pending litigation without payment, (2) no regulatory actions in current period, (3) prior-period charges not recurring, (4) reclassification of items to specific expense categories

comparability.variations: Companies vary widely in what they classify here. Some include legal costs in operating SG&A. Others classify litigation settlements as non-operating. The boundary between operating and non-operating miscellaneous expenses is judgment-driven.

examples.treatment: Legal settlements and FTC fines classified within operating expenses, not here
Regulatory penalties and remediation costs shown in non-interest expense
Litigation expense — talc-related settlements disclosed as separate non-operating line

nodes.label: Restructuring Charges
nodes.definition: Costs of significant reorganization — severance, facility closures, contract terminations. Non-recurring. Required to be disclosed separately when material.
nodes.example: Meta announced 11,000 layoffs in 2022, recording ~$4.2B in Q4 2022 restructuring charges including ~$975M in severance, ~$1.88B in facilities consolidation costs, and ~$1.34B in data center asset write-offs ($4.6B full year 2022).
nodes.classification_notes: ASC 420 governs recognition of exit/disposal costs. Severance is accrued when communicated to employees (one-time benefit) or when probable and estimable (ongoing benefit plan). Lease termination costs are recognized at cease-use date. Contract termination penalties recognized when contract is terminated. Companies must disclose the nature, timing, and expected costs. Serial restructurers effectively make these recurring — analysts should evaluate the pattern. Often excluded in non-GAAP earnings but should be scrutinized if recurring.

playbook.if_increased: (1) major layoff program announced with severance accruals, (2) facility closures or consolidation with lease termination costs, (3) strategic exit from business lines or geographies, (4) post-M&A integration and synergy-driven headcount reductions, (5) technology platform migration abandoning legacy systems
playbook.if_decreased: (1) restructuring program completed in prior period, (2) reversal of excess accruals as actual costs come in below estimates, (3) stable operating model without reorganization, (4) smaller-scale efficiency actions not meeting restructuring threshold

comparability.variations: Some companies classify restructuring within operating expenses; others as non-operating. SEC requires separate disclosure when material. Companies like Cisco and HP have had recurring restructuring charges for years, making the non-recurring label questionable. Under IFRS (IAS 37), provisions for restructuring follow similar but not identical criteria.

examples.treatment: Restructuring charges — ~$4.2B in Q4 2022, $4.6B full year 2022 (Year of Efficiency program), shown as separate operating line
Restructuring charges — shown as separate line within operating expenses during EV transition
Restructuring and other charges — recurring annual line item despite non-recurring label

nodes.label: Income Tax Expense
nodes.formula_human: Current Tax Expense + Deferred Tax Expense (Benefit)
nodes.definition: Total income tax charge on the income statement, comprising current and deferred tax components. Governed by ASC Topic 740. May differ significantly from cash taxes paid due to deferred tax mechanisms.
nodes.example: A company with $100M pre-tax income and a 21% US corporate rate records approximately $21M income tax expense, adjusted for deferred items.
nodes.classification_notes: Income tax expense is the last deduction before Net Income. The effective tax rate (tax expense / pre-tax income) is a key metric. Differences from the statutory 21% rate arise from state taxes, international operations, R&D credits, and permanent differences.

playbook.if_increased: (1) higher pre-tax income, (2) unfavorable discrete tax items (audit settlements, valuation allowance increases), (3) shift in geographic income mix to higher-tax jurisdictions, (4) expiration of tax credits
playbook.if_decreased: (1) lower pre-tax income, (2) favorable discrete items (R&D credits, stock option windfalls), (3) shift to lower-tax jurisdictions, (4) new tax incentives or credits

comparability.variations: All companies report income tax expense. Key variation is the effective tax rate, which varies widely by company based on geographic mix, credits, and incentives. Some companies report 'Provision for income taxes' vs. 'Income tax expense'.

examples.treatment: Provision for income taxes (~15% ETR in FY2023 due to Ireland structure; rose to ~24% in FY2024 following EU tax ruling)
Provision for income taxes (variable ETR due to SBC deductions)
Income taxes (high ETR due to domestic income concentration)

nodes.label: CURRENT TAX EXPENSE
nodes.formula_human: Federal Income Tax — Current + State & Local Income Tax — Current + Foreign Income Tax — Current
nodes.definition: The income tax payable to tax authorities for the current period based on taxable income. Computed using the applicable statutory tax rates applied to taxable income per the tax return.
