nodes.example: Apple reported $16.7B in current income tax expense in FY2023, split across federal ($6.2B), state ($1.2B), and foreign ($9.3B) jurisdictions.
nodes.classification_notes: Current tax expense is the closest proxy for cash taxes paid (though timing differences exist between accrual and cash payment). Split into federal, state, and foreign components in the tax footnote. The current tax amount is computed on taxable income (which differs from book pre-tax income). Key permanent differences (non-deductible expenses, tax-exempt income) and timing differences (depreciation, revenue recognition) cause taxable income to differ from book income.

playbook.if_increased: (1) higher pre-tax income driving more tax on the current return, (2) shift in geographic income mix toward higher-tax jurisdictions, (3) fewer permanent tax benefits (credits, deductions) in current year, (4) expiration of tax holiday or incentive
playbook.if_decreased: (1) lower pre-tax income or tax losses, (2) R&D tax credits or other credit-based incentives, (3) shift of income to lower-tax foreign jurisdictions, (4) utilization of NOL carryforwards reducing current taxable income, (5) tax law changes reducing statutory rates

comparability.variations: All profitable companies report current tax expense. The geographic split (federal vs. state vs. foreign) reveals a company's tax planning structure. Companies with significant international operations may have foreign current tax exceeding US federal tax.

examples.treatment: Current tax expense — foreign component exceeds domestic due to international operations
Current tax relatively low due to R&D credits and stock compensation deductions
Large current foreign tax from international production operations with high host-country rates

nodes.label: Federal Income Tax — Current
nodes.definition: US federal corporate income tax due for the current year (21% flat rate for corporations as of 2026).
nodes.example: A domestic manufacturer with $50M in US taxable income records $10.5M in federal current tax expense at the 21% statutory rate, reduced to $8.9M after $1.6M in R&D tax credits.
nodes.classification_notes: The 21% flat corporate rate was established by the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) in 2017, down from 35%. Federal current tax is computed on US taxable income, which differs from book income due to permanent differences (meals deduction limits, municipal bond interest exclusion) and timing differences. R&D credits (IRC Section 41), foreign tax credits, and other tax incentives reduce the federal tax below the statutory rate. Companies with significant NOL carryforwards may show zero or negative federal current tax.

playbook.if_increased: (1) higher US domestic pre-tax income, (2) expiration or reduction of R&D or other tax credits, (3) statutory rate increase by Congress, (4) fewer permanent deductions in current year, (5) full utilization of prior NOL carryforwards
playbook.if_decreased: (1) lower US domestic pre-tax income, (2) R&D tax credits and other credit incentives, (3) NOL carryforward utilization offsetting current income, (4) income shifting to foreign jurisdictions, (5) increased tax-exempt income (municipal bonds)

comparability.variations: All US corporations face the same 21% statutory rate. Effective rates differ due to credits, deductions, and permanent differences. Companies with significant R&D (tech, pharma) often have lower effective federal rates. Companies with mostly domestic operations have larger federal tax relative to total tax.

examples.treatment: Federal current tax — large domestic component reflecting US-centric operations
Federal current tax reduced by energy-related credits and stock option deductions
Federal current tax — R&D credits and foreign income exclusions lower effective rate

nodes.label: Foreign Income Tax — Current
nodes.definition: Income taxes payable in foreign jurisdictions on income earned outside the US.
nodes.example: Apple paid $9.3B in foreign current income taxes in FY2023, reflecting taxes in Ireland, China, UK, and other jurisdictions where it earns significant revenue.
nodes.classification_notes: Foreign current tax is computed under each jurisdiction's local tax law. Rates vary widely (Ireland 12.5%, Germany 30%, Singapore 17%, UK 25%). The OECD Pillar Two global minimum tax (15%) affects multinationals starting 2024. GILTI (Global Intangible Low-Taxed Income) adds a US tax on certain foreign earnings. Foreign tax credits offset US tax on the same income. Transfer pricing rules (IRC Section 482) govern intercompany pricing and affect the allocation of income across jurisdictions.

playbook.if_increased: (1) higher foreign pre-tax income, (2) foreign jurisdictions raising statutory tax rates, (3) OECD Pillar Two minimum tax imposing top-up tax, (4) transfer pricing adjustments increasing foreign taxable income, (5) expiration of foreign tax holidays or incentives
playbook.if_decreased: (1) lower foreign pre-tax income, (2) tax holidays or incentives in developing markets, (3) transfer pricing strategies shifting profits to lower-tax jurisdictions, (4) foreign tax credits reducing the effective foreign rate, (5) income mix shifting to lower-rate countries

comparability.variations: Multinationals with significant international operations (tech, pharma, consumer products) have large foreign current tax. Domestic-focused companies have minimal foreign tax. The ratio of foreign to domestic tax reveals geographic income allocation strategies.

examples.treatment: Foreign current tax exceeds US federal — reflects significant international income booking
Large foreign current tax — major operations in Ireland and other favorable jurisdictions
Foreign current tax from franchise royalty income earned across 100+ countries

nodes.label: State & Local Income Tax — Current
nodes.definition: State and local corporate income taxes due for the current period. Rates vary by jurisdiction.
nodes.example: A California-headquartered SaaS company with $80M in apportioned state taxable income pays $7.2M in state income taxes (California at 8.84%), plus $1.8M across other states where it has nexus.
nodes.classification_notes: State income tax rates vary from 0% (Nevada, Wyoming, Texas franchise tax instead) to 11.5%+ (New Jersey). Income is apportioned across states using sales, payroll, and property factors (many states now use single-sales-factor). Nexus rules determine which states can tax a company. SALT deduction on the federal return increases the effective benefit. Companies can manage state tax through entity structuring, headquarters location, and economic incentive negotiations. Net of SALT deduction, the incremental state rate is typically 3-5%.

playbook.if_increased: (1) revenue growth in higher-tax states shifting apportionment, (2) state tax rate increases, (3) expanded nexus from new physical presence or economic nexus thresholds, (4) expiration of state tax incentives or credits, (5) increased overall pre-tax income
playbook.if_decreased: (1) revenue shift to lower/zero-tax states, (2) state tax incentive programs or credits, (3) restructuring to reduce nexus in high-tax states, (4) state rate reductions, (5) lower overall pre-tax income

comparability.variations: Companies with concentrated operations in high-tax states (CA, NY, NJ) have higher state tax burdens. Companies in zero-income-tax states show minimal state tax. Multi-state operations require complex apportionment. The blended state rate in the ETR reconciliation is typically 2-5% after federal benefit.

examples.treatment: State tax significant due to operations in all 50 states — blended rate ~3.5% after federal benefit
State tax reduced after moving headquarters from California to Texas (zero income tax)
Significant New York state and city income taxes due to NYC headquarters

nodes.label: DEFERRED TAX EXPENSE (BENEFIT)
nodes.formula_human: Deferred Tax Benefit — NOL Carryforward + Deferred Tax Expense — Depreciation Timing + Other Deferred Tax Items
nodes.definition: The change in deferred tax liabilities and assets arising from temporary differences between GAAP book income and taxable income (ASC 740). When GAAP income exceeds taxable income, a deferred tax liability arises (more tax will be paid later); when taxable income exceeds GAAP income, a deferred tax asset arises.
nodes.example: A company using accelerated depreciation for taxes but straight-line for GAAP recognizes a deferred tax liability because it is paying less tax now (will pay more later). If it has $200M in accelerated depreciation timing differences, it records $42M in deferred tax liability at 21%.
nodes.classification_notes: Deferred tax expense is a non-cash component of total tax expense. Positive deferred tax expense means deferred tax liabilities increased or deferred tax assets decreased (tax will be paid later). Negative (benefit) means the opposite. Key sources of temporary differences: depreciation methods, revenue recognition timing, stock compensation, warranty reserves, pension obligations. A valuation allowance reduces deferred tax assets when it is more likely than not they will not be realized. Changes in valuation allowance can cause significant deferred tax swings.

playbook.if_increased: (1) large capital expenditures creating accelerated depreciation timing differences, (2) revenue recognition timing differences expanding, (3) release of valuation allowance increasing deferred tax benefit recognition, (4) new temporary differences from acquisitions
playbook.if_decreased: (1) reversal of depreciation timing differences as assets age, (2) establishment of valuation allowance against deferred tax assets, (3) utilization of NOL carryforwards reducing DTA, (4) tax rate changes reducing the value of deferred tax balances

comparability.variations: Capital-intensive companies (manufacturing, utilities) tend to have large deferred tax liabilities from depreciation. Tech/SaaS companies may have large deferred tax assets from stock compensation and NOLs. The deferred tax footnote reveals the major temporary difference categories.

examples.treatment: Large deferred tax benefit driven by accelerated depreciation on massive infrastructure and stock compensation deductions
Significant deferred tax liability from accelerated depreciation on oil & gas assets
Large deferred tax asset from accumulated NOLs with partial valuation allowance

nodes.label: Deferred Tax Benefit — NOL Carryforward
nodes.definition: Deferred tax asset recognized for net operating loss carryforwards expected to reduce future taxes.
nodes.example: A SaaS startup with $300M in cumulative NOLs records a $63M deferred tax asset (at 21%), offset by a $40M valuation allowance due to uncertainty about future profitability, resulting in a net DTA of $23M.
nodes.classification_notes: Under TCJA, post-2017 NOLs have no expiration but can only offset 80% of taxable income in any year. Pre-2017 NOLs had 20-year expiration. IRC Section 382 limits NOL usage after ownership changes (>50% in 3 years). A valuation allowance is required when it is more likely than not that some or all of the DTA will not be realized. Releasing a valuation allowance (when the company becomes consistently profitable) creates a large one-time deferred tax benefit. This is a key metric for early-stage companies transitioning to profitability.

playbook.if_increased: (1) company achieves sustained profitability, releasing valuation allowance, (2) new losses generating additional NOL carryforwards, (3) tax rate increase raising the value of existing NOLs, (4) favorable Section 382 analysis confirming no ownership change limitation
playbook.if_decreased: (1) utilization of NOLs against current taxable income, (2) establishment of valuation allowance against uncertain future realization, (3) Section 382 limitation triggered by ownership change, (4) tax rate decrease reducing the value of NOLs, (5) expiration of pre-2017 NOLs

comparability.variations: Companies with long histories of losses (early-stage tech, biotech, airlines post-crisis) have large NOL DTAs. The valuation allowance is a key judgment — its release or establishment signals management's confidence in future profitability. Investors closely watch this for turnaround companies.

examples.treatment: Massive NOL DTA ($5B+) — partially offset by valuation allowance; released as profitability improved
Released valuation allowance in 2020 as sustained profitability was established — large one-time tax benefit
Pre-COVID NOLs fully utilized during vaccine profitability surge — DTA drawn down rapidly

nodes.label: Deferred Tax Expense — Depreciation Timing
nodes.definition: Deferred tax arising from different depreciation methods for book vs. tax (most common source).
nodes.example: A manufacturer purchases $100M of equipment. Book depreciation (straight-line, 10 years) is $10M/year. Tax depreciation (MACRS, 5 years) is $20M/year initially. The $10M annual timing difference creates a $2.1M annual deferred tax liability at 21%.
nodes.classification_notes: The single largest source of deferred tax liabilities for capital-intensive companies. Tax depreciation (MACRS) is typically faster than book depreciation (straight-line). Section 179 expensing and bonus depreciation (100% under TCJA, phasing down) accelerate the timing difference further. The DTL reverses over time as tax depreciation declines below book depreciation in later years. A growing company with continuous capex may never see the DTL reverse in aggregate.

playbook.if_increased: (1) large capital expenditures creating new timing differences, (2) bonus depreciation provisions allowing immediate tax deduction, (3) shorter MACRS lives for new asset classes, (4) expanding asset base that prevents DTL reversal
playbook.if_decreased: (1) reduced capital expenditures allowing historical timing differences to reverse, (2) phase-out of bonus depreciation (TCJA phase-down starting 2023), (3) aging asset base where book depreciation catches up to tax depreciation, (4) asset disposals eliminating associated DTL

comparability.variations: Capital-intensive industries (utilities, manufacturing, oil & gas, telecom) have large depreciation-related DTLs. Asset-light companies (SaaS, consulting) have minimal depreciation timing differences. Companies using similar book and tax lives will have smaller differences.

examples.treatment: Massive DTL ($30B+) from accelerated depreciation on telecom network infrastructure
Large DTL from accelerated depreciation on data center and logistics infrastructure
Minimal depreciation DTL — asset-light SaaS model with limited PP&E

nodes.label: Other Deferred Tax Items
nodes.definition: Deferred taxes from revenue recognition timing, stock compensation, warranty reserves, and other temporary differences.
nodes.example: A SaaS company with $150M in deferred revenue (taxed on cash receipt but recognized over time for GAAP) holds a $31.5M deferred tax asset. Separately, $80M in stock compensation expense (book, not yet tax-deductible) creates a $16.8M DTA.
nodes.classification_notes: Catch-all for deferred tax items not related to NOLs or depreciation timing. Common sources: (1) deferred revenue — taxed on receipt but deferred for book (DTA), (2) stock-based compensation — booked before tax deduction (DTA), (3) warranty and litigation reserves — accrued for book but deducted for tax only when paid (DTA), (4) pension obligations — different measurement timing (DTA or DTL), (5) unrealized gains on investments — recognized for book but not tax (DTL). The SBC deduction at exercise often exceeds book expense, creating windfall tax benefits.

playbook.if_increased: (1) growing deferred revenue balances from subscription business growth, (2) increasing stock compensation expense creating larger DTAs, (3) higher warranty or litigation reserve accruals, (4) pension liability increases from actuarial assumption changes, (5) new temporary differences from acquisitions
playbook.if_decreased: (1) recognition of previously deferred revenue reducing the DTA, (2) stock option exercises creating tax deductions that reduce the SBC DTA, (3) warranty claims paid reducing the reserve and associated DTA, (4) pension plan contributions or assumption changes reducing obligations, (5) tax rate changes re-measuring deferred tax balances

comparability.variations: The composition of other deferred tax items varies significantly by industry. SaaS/subscription companies have large deferred revenue DTAs. Tech companies have significant SBC-related DTAs. Manufacturing companies have warranty reserve DTAs. The deferred tax footnote is essential for understanding the company-specific mix.

examples.treatment: Large DTA from deferred revenue (multi-year licenses) and stock compensation
Significant DTAs from warranty reserves, pension obligations, and long-term contract timing
DTA from content amortization timing differences and stock compensation

nodes.label: BELOW-THE-LINE ITEMS
nodes.formula_human: Discontinued Operations + Extraordinary Items + Cumulative Effect of Accounting Changes
nodes.definition: Items reported AFTER Net Income from continuing operations, required to be presented separately by GAAP (ASC 205) because they relate to discontinued or extraordinary activities. Including these in operating results would distort the assessment of ongoing business performance.
nodes.example: GE reported $2.1B in discontinued operations losses (net of tax) in 2023 related to its legacy insurance and financial services businesses as it completed its three-way split.
nodes.classification_notes: Below-the-line items appear after Income from Continuing Operations and before Net Income. They are presented net of their own tax effect. Post-ASU 2015-01, extraordinary items are eliminated as a separate category. Today, the primary below-the-line item is discontinued operations (ASC 205-20). Cumulative effect of accounting changes is rare but occurs when transitioning to new standards. Analysts focus on continuing operations for valuation and exclude below-the-line items.

playbook.if_increased: (1) strategic divestiture of a business segment classified as discontinued, (2) adoption of a new accounting standard requiring cumulative catch-up adjustment, (3) impairment of discontinued operations held for sale, (4) operating losses from segments awaiting disposal
playbook.if_decreased: (1) completion of segment disposal eliminating ongoing discontinued operations losses, (2) no new accounting standard adoptions, (3) gain on final sale of discontinued operations, (4) no segments meeting the held-for-sale criteria

comparability.variations: Most companies have zero below-the-line items in a typical year. Only companies undergoing major divestitures or accounting standard transitions will show material amounts. Presentation is standardized under GAAP — always shown net of tax, after income from continuing operations.

examples.treatment: Discontinued operations — reported for years during breakup of GE Capital and business separations
Discontinued operations during three-way split into Dow, DuPont, and Corteva
Discontinued operations for Garrett Motion and Resideo spin-offs

nodes.label: DISCONTINUED OPERATIONS
nodes.definition: Results of a component of the business that has been disposed of or classified as held-for-sale and represents a separate major line of business or geographic area (ASC 205-20). Shown net of tax.
nodes.example: GE reported $2.1B in discontinued operations losses in 2023 as it completed its three-way split, reclassifying GE HealthCare and GE Vernova results from continuing to discontinued operations.
nodes.classification_notes: ASC 205-20 requires discontinued operations treatment when a component (1) has been disposed of or is held for sale AND (2) represents a strategic shift that has (or will have) a major effect on operations and financial results. Reported net of tax as a separate line item below income from continuing operations. Prior period income statements must be restated to reclassify the discontinued component. Includes both operating results during wind-down and gain/loss on disposal. EPS must be presented separately for continuing and discontinued operations.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new strategic divestiture announced and classified as held for sale, (2) operating losses from discontinued segment during wind-down period, (3) impairment write-down of held-for-sale segment to fair value less costs to sell, (4) loss on final disposal below carrying amount
playbook.if_decreased: (1) gain on sale of discontinued segment exceeding operating losses, (2) completion of disposal eliminating ongoing discontinued results, (3) improved operating performance of segment during hold period, (4) upward revision of disposal price

comparability.variations: Companies only report discontinued operations when divestitures meet the strategic shift threshold. Many asset sales do not qualify and are recorded as gain/loss on sale within continuing operations. The threshold tightened under ASU 2014-08, requiring a major strategic shift rather than just a component disposal.

examples.treatment: Discontinued operations reported for GE Capital, GE HealthCare, and GE Vernova during multi-year breakup
Kenvue consumer health spin-off — discontinued operations for the separated business
PayPal spin-off results reclassified to discontinued operations in the separation year

nodes.label: Expenses — Discontinued Operations
nodes.definition: Operating costs attributable to the discontinued business component.
nodes.example: A conglomerate divesting its media division reports $45M in operating expenses (salaries, rent, content costs) of that segment as expenses from discontinued operations during the wind-down period.
nodes.classification_notes: Under ASC 205-20, a component qualifies as discontinued when it represents a strategic shift (e.g., disposal of a major geographic area, line of business, or equity method investment). Must be reported net of tax, below the line. Prior periods must be retrospectively reclassified. Costs to sell are included.

playbook.if_increased:
1. Extended wind-down period for discontinued segment
2. Additional severance and restructuring costs during phase-out
3. Contractual obligations (leases, vendor commitments) that cannot be terminated early
4. Unexpected operating losses in the discontinued segment during transition
playbook.if_decreased:
1. Faster-than-expected sale or closure of discontinued operations
2. Buyer assumption of liabilities reducing wind-down costs
3. Completion of the disposal period
4. Favorable contract termination negotiations

comparability.variations: All US GAAP companies present discontinued operations the same way (below the line, net of tax), but the threshold for what qualifies changed under ASU 2014-08, narrowing the definition. IFRS 5 uses similar but not identical criteria. Some companies have continuing involvement that complicates clean separation.

examples.treatment: Reported GE Capital operations as discontinued during its separation, with detailed expense breakdowns in notes
Reported Kenvue consumer health segment expenses as discontinued operations during the 2023 separation
Reported PayPal operating expenses as discontinued operations during its 2015 spin-off

nodes.label: Gain / Loss on Disposal
nodes.definition: The net gain or loss recognized upon actual or expected disposal of the discontinued component.
nodes.example: A technology company sells its hardware division with a book value of $200M for $275M, recognizing a $75M pre-tax gain on disposal of discontinued operations.
nodes.classification_notes: Reported net of tax, below the line within discontinued operations per ASC 205-20. The gain/loss equals sale proceeds minus the net carrying amount of the disposed component (assets minus liabilities). If disposal is expected but not yet completed, an estimated loss must be recognized immediately but a gain is deferred until realized. Distinguish from gain/loss on sale of individual assets (ASC 360), which is above the line.

playbook.if_increased:
1. Sale price exceeds net book value due to favorable market conditions
2. Strategic buyer paying premium for synergies
3. Previously impaired assets sold at recovery above written-down value
4. Favorable resolution of contingencies from prior disposals
playbook.if_decreased:
1. Distressed sale at below book value due to market conditions
2. Additional impairment charges prior to disposal
3. Higher-than-expected costs to sell (transaction fees, separation costs)
4. Unfavorable working capital adjustments at closing
5. Indemnification claims reducing net proceeds

comparability.variations: All US GAAP companies present disposal gains/losses the same way (within discontinued operations, net of tax). However, the threshold for discontinued operations treatment varies in practice. IFRS 5 has similar requirements but differences in measurement (lower of carrying amount and fair value less costs to sell).

examples.treatment: Reported gain on disposal of its managed infrastructure services business (Kyndryl spin-off) within discontinued operations
Reported gain on disposal of its consumer healthcare joint venture (Haleon) within discontinued operations
Reported gain/loss on disposal of its Nutrition & Biosciences segment within discontinued operations

coa_mapping.netsuite: 9110 - Gain Loss on Disposal Disc Ops

nodes.label: Revenue — Discontinued Operations
nodes.definition: Revenue attributable to the discontinued business component, shown separately.
nodes.example: A technology conglomerate reports $320M in revenue from its divested hardware division for the 9 months before the sale closed, shown separately as discontinued operations.
nodes.classification_notes: Under ASC 205-20, a component qualifies as discontinued operations when it has been disposed of or is classified as held for sale and represents a strategic shift. Revenue is reported net of tax as a single line below continuing operations. Prior periods must be restated to reclassify the discontinued component for comparability.

playbook.if_increased:
1. Discontinued business unit performed well during wind-down period
2. Extended transition period before divestiture close increased reported revenue
3. Additional business components classified as held for sale
playbook.if_decreased:
1. Divestiture completed and no longer generating revenue
2. Discontinued unit's operations wound down ahead of final sale
3. Revenue decline in discontinued unit accelerating strategic exit
4. Prior period included full-year discontinued revenue vs. partial year

comparability.variations: Discontinued operations reporting makes year-over-year comparison of total revenue unreliable. Analysts must exclude discontinued operations to assess organic continuing operations growth. Some companies provide pro forma continuing operations revenue for comparability.

examples.treatment: Reported GE Capital revenue as discontinued operations during its multi-year divestiture, restating prior periods
Reported PayPal revenue as discontinued operations in the period leading up to the 2015 spinoff
Classified consumer health business (Kenvue) revenue as discontinued operations during the separation period

nodes.label: EXTRAORDINARY ITEMS
nodes.formula_human: Legacy Extraordinary Items
nodes.definition: Under US GAAP (post-ASU 2015-01), extraordinary items as a separate classification were eliminated. However, legacy filings and certain context (e.g., insurance proceeds from natural disasters) still use this nomenclature. Retained here for historical reference and AI context.
nodes.example: Pre-2015: A company received $50M in insurance proceeds from a hurricane-destroyed factory. The $50M gain was classified as an extraordinary item (unusual and infrequent) and shown net of $10.5M tax.
nodes.classification_notes: ELIMINATED under US GAAP by ASU 2015-01 (effective Jan 2016). Previously required items to be both unusual in nature AND infrequent in occurrence. Now, unusual or infrequent items are disclosed within continuing operations with separate line-item presentation if material. This node exists for: (1) parsing historical financial statements pre-2016, (2) AI context when users reference extraordinary items, (3) IFRS comparisons where the concept also does not exist. No new extraordinary items should be recorded under current US GAAP.

playbook.if_increased: (1) legacy filing analysis — pre-2016 natural disaster gains/losses, (2) historical data with government expropriation of assets, (3) pre-2016 early debt extinguishment gains/losses (prior to ASU 2015-01)
playbook.if_decreased: (1) this category is eliminated under current GAAP — should be zero for filings after January 2016, (2) historical items reclassified under restatements, (3) no unusual/infrequent events in legacy period

comparability.variations: Eliminated under US GAAP since 2016. IFRS never had this category (IAS 1 prohibits extraordinary items). When analyzing pre-2016 filings, extraordinary items were shown net of tax between discontinued operations and cumulative effect of accounting changes.

examples.treatment: Extraordinary gain/loss — shown net of tax, required to be both unusual and infrequent
Hurricane and catastrophe losses sometimes classified as extraordinary
N/A — category eliminated; unusual/infrequent items now within continuing operations

nodes.label: Legacy Extraordinary Items
nodes.definition: Pre-2015 classification for unusual and infrequent items. No longer a separate GAAP category; unusual/infrequent items are now disclosed within continuing operations.
nodes.example: Pre-2016: A mining company lost a $200M open-pit mine due to government expropriation in a foreign country, recording a $200M extraordinary loss net of $42M tax benefit, for a net impact of $158M.
nodes.classification_notes: This leaf exists solely for historical data compatibility. No new items should be classified here for filings after January 2016. Common legacy extraordinary items included: natural disaster gains/losses, government expropriation, early debt extinguishment (pre-ASU 2002), and prohibition-era legal changes. When encountered in historical data, these items should be understood as net-of-tax, below-the-line amounts that were both unusual AND infrequent.

playbook.if_increased: (1) analyzing pre-2016 filings with large natural disaster events, (2) government expropriation events in historical data, (3) early debt extinguishment gains in older filings
playbook.if_decreased: (1) should always be zero in post-2016 filings, (2) reclassification of historical items under restatement, (3) smaller magnitude events in legacy periods

comparability.variations: Only appears in pre-2016 US GAAP filings. IFRS never had this category. When comparing across time periods, analysts must recognize that post-2016 unusual items appear within continuing operations rather than as extraordinary items.

examples.treatment: Extraordinary item, net of tax — required dual criteria of unusual AND infrequent
N/A — items previously classified here now shown within continuing operations

nodes.label: CUMULATIVE EFFECT OF ACCOUNTING CHANGES
nodes.formula_human: Cumulative Effect of Principle Change
nodes.definition: The catch-up adjustment when a company changes an accounting principle (ASC 250). Recorded in the period of change, net of tax, as a direct adjustment to opening retained earnings (most changes) or as a separate income statement line for certain changes.
nodes.example: When adopting ASC 606 (Revenue Recognition) in 2018, a software company recorded a $45M cumulative catch-up adjustment to opening retained earnings, reflecting the difference between old and new revenue timing.
nodes.classification_notes: Most accounting standard adoptions today use the modified retrospective method, recording the cumulative effect as an adjustment to opening retained earnings rather than on the income statement. Only certain transitions (where the standard specifically permits) use prospective or full retrospective methods. Key recent transitions: ASC 606 (Revenue, 2018), ASC 842 (Leases, 2019), ASC 326 (Credit Losses/CECL, 2020). Analysts must understand that the income statement may not show this — check the equity rollforward and transition footnotes.

playbook.if_increased: (1) adoption of a major new accounting standard with significant measurement change, (2) voluntary change in accounting principle requiring catch-up adjustment, (3) change from one acceptable method to a preferable one under ASC 250, (4) large gap between old and new measurement basis
playbook.if_decreased: (1) no new accounting standards requiring adoption in the period, (2) immaterial differences between old and new accounting methods, (3) standard adopted using prospective method with no catch-up, (4) gradual transition over multiple periods

comparability.variations: The impact depends on the specific standard adopted and the company's business model. SaaS companies had large ASC 606 impacts; banks had large CECL impacts; real estate companies had large ASC 842 impacts. Transition disclosures are required in the adoption year.

examples.treatment: CECL adoption (ASC 326) — $2.7B increase to allowance recorded as retained earnings adjustment in 2020
ASC 606 adoption — modified retrospective with cumulative catch-up to retained earnings
ASC 842 lease adoption — significant impact from operating lease capitalization

nodes.label: Cumulative Effect of Principle Change
nodes.definition: One-time P&L impact from the transition to a new accounting standard (e.g., adoption of ASC 842 lease accounting).
nodes.example: A bank adopting CECL (ASC 326) in 2020 recorded a $1.8B cumulative catch-up increase to its loan loss allowance, with a $1.4B after-tax reduction to opening retained earnings.
nodes.classification_notes: This records the P&L or retained earnings impact of transitioning to a new accounting principle. Most modern standard transitions use modified retrospective (retained earnings adjustment) rather than income statement recognition. Voluntary changes in principle (e.g., switching from LIFO to FIFO) require retrospective application to all prior periods. Mandatory changes follow transition guidance in the specific ASU. The cumulative effect captures the difference between old and new measurement for all assets/liabilities affected as of the adoption date.

playbook.if_increased: (1) major new standard with fundamentally different measurement basis (e.g., CECL vs. incurred loss), (2) large portfolio of affected items amplifying the cumulative difference, (3) voluntary accounting change where preferable method produces materially different results, (4) deferred adoption concentrating impact in a single period
playbook.if_decreased: (1) new standard produces similar measurements to the old approach, (2) early adoption spread the impact over prior periods via retrospective method, (3) small portfolio of affected items, (4) standard adopted prospectively with no catch-up adjustment

comparability.variations: Impact varies dramatically by industry and the specific standard adopted. CECL hit banks hardest; ASC 606 hit tech/SaaS; ASC 842 hit asset-light companies with large operating lease portfolios. Transition disclosures in Year 1 footnotes are essential for understanding the magnitude.

examples.treatment: CECL adoption — $3.3B increase to allowance, $2.5B after-tax retained earnings reduction
ASC 606 cumulative catch-up — deferred revenue timing changes from subscription model
ASC 842 adoption — $22B operating lease right-of-use assets recognized on balance sheet

industry_overlays.label: Financial Services
industry_overlays.description: Overlay for banks, insurance companies, asset managers, and fintech firms. Emphasizes interest income/expense, regulatory costs, and financial instrument gains/losses. Suppresses physical manufacturing and inventory nodes.

add.label: Fee & Commission Income
add.description: Revenue from advisory fees, management fees, brokerage commissions, and service charges

add.label: Provision for Credit Losses
add.description: Reserve for expected loan and receivable defaults (ASC 326 / CECL)

industry_overlays.notes: Financial services P&Ls differ fundamentally from product companies. Net interest margin (NIM) drives bank profitability. Provision for credit losses is the dominant risk expense. Regulatory capital requirements (Basel III/IV) constrain balance sheet strategy. Fee income diversification is a key analyst metric.

industry_overlays.label: Manufacturing
industry_overlays.description: Overlay for companies that produce physical goods. Emphasizes COGS breakdown (raw materials, direct labor, factory overhead), inventory flow, and production-related depreciation. Suppresses software/SaaS-specific nodes.
industry_overlays.notes: Manufacturing P&Ls center on the COGS waterfall: raw materials -> WIP -> finished goods. Inventory valuation method (FIFO/LIFO/weighted-average) significantly affects gross margin. Production variances (yield loss, scrap) are critical KPIs.

industry_overlays.label: Professional Services
industry_overlays.description: Overlay for consulting firms, law firms, accounting practices, staffing agencies, and other labor-intensive service businesses. Emphasizes personnel costs, utilization metrics, and project-based revenue. Suppresses manufacturing and inventory nodes.
industry_overlays.notes: Professional services firms are measured on utilization rate, revenue per employee, and realization rate (billed vs. standard hours). Personnel costs typically represent 60-75% of revenue. Hiring pace and attrition are leading indicators. Travel and subcontractor costs are the primary variable expenses.

industry_overlays.label: Retail & E-Commerce
industry_overlays.description: Overlay for companies that sell merchandise to consumers. Emphasizes inventory management, merchandise margins, store/fulfillment costs, and promotional discounts. Suppresses R&D and SaaS infrastructure nodes.
industry_overlays.notes: Retail P&Ls focus on merchandise margin, same-store sales growth, and inventory turnover. Shrinkage and markdowns are critical cost drivers. E-commerce adds fulfillment and payment processing as major COGS components. Seasonality heavily influences quarterly comparisons.

industry_overlays.label: Software as a Service (SaaS)
industry_overlays.description: Overlay for subscription-based software companies. Emphasizes recurring revenue streams, cloud infrastructure costs, R&D headcount, and customer acquisition. Suppresses physical inventory and manufacturing nodes.
industry_overlays.notes: SaaS P&Ls are evaluated on ARR/MRR growth, gross margin (target >70%), net revenue retention, and the Rule of 40 (growth rate + FCF margin). Cost of revenue is dominated by hosting and support, not physical goods. R&D and S&M typically represent the largest opex categories.

non_gaap_measures.label: Adjusted EBITDA
non_gaap_measures.description: EBITDA further adjusted to exclude stock-based compensation, restructuring charges, impairment charges, and other non-recurring items. The most commonly reported non-GAAP metric in public company earnings releases.
non_gaap_measures.sec_regulation_g: Must be reconciled to Net Income via EBITDA. Each adjustment must be individually identified and quantified. "Adjusted" label requires clear disclosure of what is being adjusted and why management believes the measure is useful to investors.
common_adjustments: Gain/loss on sale of assets or business units
non_gaap_measures.notes: Adjusted EBITDA is the dominant metric in private equity and growth-stage company valuations. SEC has increased scrutiny of "adjusted" metrics — companies must explain why each adjustment is appropriate. The gap between GAAP Net Income and Adjusted EBITDA is itself an important analytical signal.

non_gaap_measures.label: EBITDA
non_gaap_measures.description: Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation, and Amortization. The most widely used non-GAAP profitability measure, used to approximate operating cash flow before capital structure and tax effects.
non_gaap_measures.sec_regulation_g: Must be reconciled to Net Income (the nearest GAAP measure) in SEC filings. Cannot be presented on a per-share basis. Cannot be described as "cash flow."
common_adjustments: Depreciation of property, plant, and equipment
Amortization of intangible assets (customer relationships, technology, trade names)
non_gaap_measures.notes: EBITDA is not defined by GAAP and varies across companies. Some include stock-based compensation in D&A add-backs (technically incorrect). EV/EBITDA is a standard valuation multiple; typical ranges vary by industry.

non_gaap_measures.label: Non-GAAP Operating Income
non_gaap_measures.description: Operating Income adjusted to exclude stock-based compensation, amortization of acquired intangibles, and restructuring charges. Commonly used by technology companies to show "underlying" operating performance.
non_gaap_measures.sec_regulation_g: Must be reconciled to GAAP Operating Income. Cannot exclude normal, recurring cash operating expenses. Amortization of acquired intangibles is the most commonly accepted adjustment due to its acquisition-driven, non-cash nature.
non_gaap_measures.notes: Non-GAAP operating income is preferred over Adjusted EBITDA by companies that want to show the impact of their capital allocation (interest, D&A on owned assets) while excluding M&A accounting noise. Common in large-cap tech (Microsoft, Salesforce, Google). The non-GAAP operating margin derived from this metric is a key comparability indicator across acquirers.
